- - THE SUNBEAM'S SONG. "They are coining., coming, cmning. Sang the sunbeams rine bright day, When the Winter winds Wow- softly. And the frost king sped away. Did I hear them? ay.l heard them, For I'd hearkened, oh. so long! Yes, they sang, the flowers are coming," All that golden, simbright threng. Then the bees took up the ditty, And the tuneful chorus grew, For the robins chirped their gladness, And the sparrows twittered, too; And all sang, "They're coining, coming— Hear the tramp of tiny feet; From the land of Spring they're basting, Al! their last year's friends to greet." And the rooks caw-cawed and clamoured, And they said their nests they'd mend, While an old owl ceased his hooting, An attentive ear to lend. • And he asked, "Too-boo, who is coming?" 'Twas the doves cooed soft reply, "The flowers, the sweet Spring flowers, Whom we bade a sad good-bye." How the brooklets sang and babbled; And up leaped the fishes all; • The tree-tops shook with laughter, As they beard the sunbeams call: " Ho ! the flowers are coming, coming— Hear the tread of twinkling feet." Ah ! the sunbeams' song exceeded In rapturous etclence sweet. For they anew they long had wooed them, 'Mid dark Winter's frost and snow; .Ay. and 'neath the clods had sought them, They had loved the flowerets so. :Now. dear children, catch my moral, And 'mid Spring's tumultuous joy, Say. "I'll be a human sunbeam, To every happy girl and boy." —Little Folks' Alaga:ine.

Beauty unaccompanied by virtue is as a flower with- out perfume. If you want to succeed in the world, you must make 'your own opportunities as you ;,,o on. Under all speech that is good for anything there lies a silence that is better. Silence is deep as eternity; speech

is shallow as time. Rescuer (who has nulled a man out of the water) 'Gracious! Your head is bleeding. Flow did you cut it?" Rescued man: "On the water's edge, I guess." .Good nature and evenness of temner will give you an <easy companion for life; virtue and good sense an agree- able friend; love and constancy a good wife and bus-
band. "The signal service does four times as much predict- ing now as it used to do?' "Is that so?" "Yes; where it formerly made one indication' it now makes fore-

casts." When a clergyman remarked that there would be a 'nave in the new church the society was building, an old lady whispered that she "knew the party to whom he referred." "Do great calamities move in cycles?" asked Brown. " They frequently do in bicycles,' said Smithers, who had recently left three layers of his nasal cuticle on a macadamised road. your daughter, sir, to be my wife." Old Dukkets: "Wait a year!" "It's a long time to wait, sir!" Dukkets : "Oh, I don't mean for you to wait here. Call again in about a year." "Yes, Augustus, we believe it is better to have loved and lost than never to have loved at all. It is better for the jeweller, and the florist, and the messenger boy— and sometimes for the lawyers." "I have this evening been preaching to a congregation of idiots," said a conceited young parson. "Then that was the reason you always called then 'beloved brethren," said a strong-minded young werease Mrs. Figg : "Isn't there any way to get rid of that young Jinx who keeps calling on Clara without positively insulting him?" Mr. Figg : "Why, certainly. Just give him the baby to hold the next time he comes." Jones and his friends were discussing the latest lion accident. "Why, I've been in the cage myeelf a dozen I times." boasted that inveterate joker. "And vou weren't afraid ? " "Of course not; the lions had been taken out" ' The child was very ill, and his mother fed him almost exclusively on "teething powders." "This is not right." seid the doctor, gravely. "Well, sir," eras the indignant reply, "I think I might be allowed to know, seeing I've buried three already." Who was the first man?" asked a Sunday school -teacher of a little girl. She answered that' she did not know. The question was put to the next, an Irish child, who answered loudly, "Adam, sir!" with apparent I -satisfaction. "Law," said the first child contemptu- ously, "you needn't feel so grand about it—he wasn't an Irishman." The followinrf story illustrates the disadvantage of having an article in common use called after one's own name. The chief of the clan Mclntosh once had a dispute with a cabman about his fare. "Do you know who I am?" indignantly exclaimed the Highlander. "I am the Mclntosh." • I don't care if you are an umberella," replied the cabby; "I'll have my rights." A good story is told concerning the late Rev. W. Barnes, the Dorsetshirapoet, which will interest spelling reformers: "One d sy he went into a village school where a little boy and girl were sitting together. The girl was crying, and when he asked the reason, she said that Johnny had had the word • Psalm' to write in his copy- book, "and." she said with a fresh burst of the tears, "he ha' scrope out the •P' with his elbow !" Then Johnny fired up, and said, "What if I did scrope of en out? He didn't spell naught, and what was the good of en?" A small boy was one day calling on a school friend, and fell into conversation with his friend's mother. He finally remarked that it was getting very hard to tell, from the places in which people live, whether or not they are entitled to social consideration. "Now there's Blank-street," he said, "you wouldn't. think anybody was much that lived in Blank-street, would you? But -there's Mr. T—, he lives there." "And is Mr. T— • much '?" "Mr. T—?" with astonishment. " shcfuld think he was! He's an awful swell. Why, he won't speak to my fathef The famous regiment of Buffs, which used also to be known as the 3rd Foot, once rejoiced for a while in the nickname of the "Nutcrackers." This was after the battle of Albuera,-which was fought on the 18th May,' 1811. In this terribly fierce conflict they attacked the Polish Lancers, whose heads they cracked. Fhen. after -the fashion of the nutcrackine tool, they opened to avoid the charge of the Polish Horse, and retreated. In a few minutes, however, they again took the field, and once more proceeded—like brave British soldiers—to flght with all their well-known courage for king and -country. Caueser zss TIIE SLING.—Some time since, while a swallow was flying about a house It caught its foot in a I sling that was hanging from a pipe on the roof. Of course the bird got frightened at becoming an unwilling. prisoner.' It struggled and fluttered to no purpose, and when the poor thing was thoroughly tired it simply hung helpless by its leg. Meanwhile its sad case had roused the pity of its swallow mates, which all flocked round it from every quarter. After a good deal of twitter-talk amongst themselves, it seemed as if they bad at last decided upon a plan; for presently one bird after anoaher struck at the sling with its beak, and after half-an-hour's steady work they succeeded in 'cutting the cord and in setting the captive free.—" Little Folks" Naga:int.' °DOMES OF EATING AND DRINEING.—A gentleman farmer in the Midlands some time since engaged a ploughman, to whom he gave permission, in tho middle of the first day's work, to retire from the field to the kitchen, and eat some bread and cheese. The cook placed a whole double Gloucester and a peck loaf before the man, and invited him to help himself. After waiting upwards of an hour, the gewleman grew impatient, and went. to the kitchen to See what the man was about. lie found the fellow munching at the last orust of the loaf, and more than half the cheese consumed. In answer to the inquiry as to what detained him so long, the man replied, "Oh, master, you don't consider what a time it takes to eat up a whole cheese, especially when there is only one loaf—and no beer!' Great appetites were rather common in that part of the country, and a cer- tain carter in the neighbourhood had earned an envied reputation in that direction. The gentAs in in farmer was so impressed by the gormandising powers of his new ploughman, that he determined to match him against the carter to eat for a wager at a public-house in the village. Unfortunately, the squire was obliged to be absent in London on the day appointed, hut his interest in the affair was sufficient to cause him to arrange for tele- grams to be sent to him by his bailiff, announcing the pro- gress nnd termination of the contest A telegram was re- ceived dated 6 p.m., and ran as follows: "The men sat down at 12. At this time our man is ahead of the other by, a poiind of sausages, half a roast pig, and an apple pie." The ploughman won. A gentleman named Austin once made a bet that he would cook a big pudding 10 feet below the surface ot the Thames. Be accomplished the teat in the following manner:—He put the:pudding into a large tin vessel, and enclosed that in a sackful of lime, and sank sack, pan, and pudding to the required depth at Rotherhithe. At the end of two else and a half he hauled the pudding up, when it. was discovered to be well cooked, and was eaten with much relish. The only fault that waefound with it was that it was a trifle over-baked. It is not a little remarkable that one of the most elaborate treatises on foods and eating that was ever written, was compiled by Dr. Reich, of Berne, dur- ing such a period of hunger, cold, and wretchedness, that, in closing the preface to the first part, the author said he was on the brink of the grave, and might not survive to complete what he had so laboriously cm m- menced. A few months ago a well-dress,,d man entered a Boston restaurant, and called for a raw egg and a glass of sherry. The order was executed, and a few minutes afterwards he -desired a repetition of the sea° dose. For seven hours the man sat at the same table, and kept on drinking eggs in sherry until he had consumed a. He paid his bill, and quietly left the restaurant, apparently none the worse.—Cassell's Saturday Journal.

div.head: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
div.p: " CAPITAL " CHAT.
-- -- V It is reported from St. Petersburg, that the Shah's wife will come to Europe, making the Russian capital her first stopping place. She will consult several medical specialists.

I hear that Mr. Gladstone is as emphatic as the rest of the world in his condemnation of -Mr. Matthews's monstrous decision In the case of the brothers Davies. If George Davies was justly re- prieved, Richard Davies was unjustly hung. This seems to be the universal verdict.

Sir Edwin Arnold's friends in London say that he is never coming back to England. He is fascinated with Japan, where he has settled down with his daughter, in a villa built under his special super- vision, and he says he has found the ideal country. He is making new studies for poeins.

William Wetmore Story, the Sculptor, is small of stature, white of moustache, and musical of voice; he discusses statuary and art with an air of easy mastery. His charming manners make him much sought after in society. at Rome, where he has re- sided in the Barbanna palace for nearly forty years.

The Sunday evening services which Dean Lefroy has established in the nave of Norwich Cathedral are drawing very large congregations, who are at- tracted both by the bright character of the shortened service,and by the Dean's very eloquent and interest- ing sermons. Dean Lefroy was formerly Arch- deacon of Warrington.

The Queen goes from Aix-les-Bains to Darmstadt, next week, travelling direct through Geneva, Basle, Freiburg, and Heidelberg. The Queen, who has not visited Darmstadt for five years, will stay there for five or six days, and is then to travel direct to Flushing', where she will embaik on board the Royal yacht Victoria and Albert for Port Victoria, the whole journey from Darmstadt to Windsor being completed in about eighteen hours.

The "woman who puts you into mourning," though quite a recent invention, has become indis- pensable in America. She sees to everything in the shape of gowns, bonnets, note paper, and cards, fills in the necessar shadows in the rooms of the house, and lifts the burden of thought off those upon whom it would fall but for her and her novel pro- fession. America thinks that she is an importation from England, but she is as yet unknown in this country.

It is not difficult to recognize to whom the fol- lowing paragraph in "The Man of the World" refers, and as to how far the statement is correct time will show :—" Before the year is out we may expect the announcement of the ,marriage of a dis- tinguished politician, the eldest son of a duke, who has hitherto being regarded as a confirmed bache- lor." It is a pity that some indication is not given of the identity of the lady who is supposed to have fascinated Lord Hartington.

Prince Bismarck's pension has been represented as being a very large one by the daily papers. This is a mistake. as it amounts to only 18,000 marks, or not quite £9OO per annum. This is no very great amount when his services for his country are brought into consideration, and we need only look at the sums of money such men as Pitt, Nelson, and Wellington received for their services to understand that the Chancellor has been a cheap workman. They do these things differently in Germany.

The Labor Electoral Congress has done well to place the return of Labor representatives at muni- cipal and local elections in the front of its pro- gramme. Every year that passes will see more and more powers for the benefit of the workers entrusted to local authorities, and such powers cannot pos- sibly be effectively exercised without the presence of Labor representatives on the bodies that exercise them. From this point of view it is also perfectly fair that, as the Hanley Congress haa declared, the interests of Labor should be looked to before any other consideration.

Mr. and Mrs. Gladstone, before going to Aston Clinton, attended St. Margaret's Church, Westmin- ster, to witness the christening of their youngest grandchild, the daughter of the Rev. Harry and Mrs. Drew. The Rev. Canon Purse officiated. The in- fant was baptised in the names of Dorothy Mary Catherine, the sponsors being Mr. Spencer Lyttleton, Miss Helen Gladstone, Miss Kate Wickham, Lady Cowell Stepney, Canon Holland, of St. Paul's, Mr. Gould Drew, and Mr. G. W. E. Russell. Among those present were the Earl of Rosebery, Lord Dalmeny, Miss Buxton, Miss Farquhar, and Mr. and Mrs. Wickham. St. Margaret's Church was chosen because the parents were married there in February, 1888.

Charles Wyndham told a good story not long ago which merits publication. While getting into a railroad carriage bound for Folkestone, he recog- nised in his compartment a well-known detective. Presently a dissenting minister got in, and with the three locked in by the guard, the train started. The detective was in pursuit of a criminal who had gone by a previous train He soon began to study the photograph of. the fugitive, and of course was ab- sorbed over it. This attracted the attention of the minister. who presently observed: "You have, per- chance. lost a dear friend ?" " Dear ? yes, very dear indeed," answered the detective. "Take comfort, brother, he has but gone before." continued the holy man, who was not a little shocked wi,en he got for a reply : "Yes, curse him. and got three hours' start of me; but I'll follow him if it's to Hades."

Mr. Navarro, who is engaged to Mary Anderson, is thirty. He is by profession a lawyer. He has travelled extensively abroad, is an acnompliAhed lin- guist, a thorough musician of artistic temperament and tastes, and a strict Catholic: His full name is Antonio Fernando Navarro de Niana. The Navarros claim descent from the ancient house of Niana, con- stables of the old Kingdom of Navarre and Counts of Lerin. this title having passed since, by marriage, to the Fitz James, Dukes of Berwick. As a rule, the Niana Navarros have always followed the sea, either in the merchant service or the Royal Navy, and have often attained the highest rank and dis- tinction in the latter, as in the case of Pedro Navarro, who, after the surrender of Granada, ac- companied Columbus to America in his second voy- age in 1493, and afterwards became so famous in Italy and Atrica,as Count Pedro Navarro,command- ing large fleets and leading great armies as general;

A boredom to which -Oxford is subjected is the constant crowds of tourists which infest the place day and night, and _every day and every night of the year. For these individuals numerous guides have been appointed, but one imaginative man hit upon the following plan by which he could at least always be sure of showing to thtrcrowd one of the live lions of the place. It so happened that Dt Jowett was very busily engaged on his famous I translation of Plato at the time, and unfortunately for him, the guide that we are speaking of learnt that the Professor's study window looked into the Broad-street. Coming with his menagerie under these windows, the guide would begin This, ladies and gentlemen, is Balliol College, one of the very holiest in the Huniversity, and famous for the berudition of its scholars. The 'cad of Balliol College is called 'the Master ' ; the present Master of Balliol is the celebrated Professor Benjamin Jowett, Regius Professor of Greek. Those are Professor Benjamin Jowett's study windows, and there "—here the ruffian would stoop down, take up a handful of gravel, and throw it up against the panes, bringing poor Jowett, livid with fury to the window—" ladies and gentlemen, is Professor Benjamin Jowett himself.'

Eugene C. Field of the "Chicago News" in London, tells this story of Henry Gladatone's wooing Miss Maud Rendel :—" It seems that the two niet last summer at Posillipo, the young lady's father having at, that pictufesque little hamlet on the gulf of Naples's a lovely villa. One beautiful evening the two were in the garden overlooking the water upon which the moonlight hung like a misty gauze ; the soene was one of poetic loveliness—young Gladstone felt that there never could be a fairer spot or a better moment for the confession of his love, so he declared himself to his inamorata with a fervour Which the picturesqueness of the surroundings en- hanced, if it did not inspire Instead, however, of answering him, the pretty girl covered her face with her hands and fled precipitately into the villa, Of course this astonished the young lover; he could not understand it at all; should he interpret the maiden's conduct as a rejection? If so, it were better for him to leave Posillipo at once. But no; his Scotch instincts came to his' rescue ; he had done the proper thing properly—he would bide his time. Next morning after breakfast, at which his idol did not appear, he sought the garden and meandered gloomily therein, wondering what tactics he ought to pursue. Suddenly he heard Miss Maud call to him, and turning he beheld that young girl

div.head: AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.
div.p: AGRICULTURAL SOCIETY.

An adjourned meeting of the Royal Manchester, Liverpool, and North Lancashire Agricultural Society was held on Wednesday, at the Lion Hotel, Warrington. Mr. G. C. Hale presided, and amongst those present were Mr. John White, Captain With- ingten, Mr. R. Catterall, Mr. J. Haball, Mr. James Birch, Mr. James Warburton, Mr. J. T. Sniith,Mr. R. Lansdale, Mr. T. E. Tattoo, Mr. F. Robinson, Mr. W. Scotson, Mr. Thomas Fair, Mr. James Hatton, Mr. James Southern, Mr. P. Blundell, Mr. T. Wilkinson, Mr. T. Nevett, Mr. C. B. Davies, Mr. J. Kay, Mr. W. Derbyshire, Mr. T. Par- ton.—A deputation, consisting of the Mayor of Bury (Mr. C. Brierley), Mr. T. Statter, and Mr. Walter Muck- low (master of the Holcomb Hunt), attended for the purpose of inviting the society to hold the annual show next year at Bury.—The Mayor of Bury, in a statement, said that if the show were held at Bury, the local com- mittee were prepared, in addition to the £250 required I.sy the society, to offer £lOO, making a total of £350. They had the hearty co-operation of Lord Derby, who had promised to do all he could to promote the success of the show if held at Bury. Mr. Statter said he thought the society would not regret the action if they decided to hold their annual show in Bury next year. They would have no difficulty he thought in raising £l,OOO by subscription, and they would be able to offer very large premiums which would conduce to the success of the show. Within a radius of. five miles of Bury there was a larger population than in any similar area in the country.—The Chairman in thanking the deputation for the invitation and for the interest they had shown in the society mentioned that a decision would not be come to till the meeting in jiffy.— The Chairman, on behalf of the society, presented to Mr. Robert Lansdale a gold medal as an acknowledgment of his services as one of the auditors of the society for about 50 years.—The Secretary said he had obtained a copy of the report of the Committee of the Liverpool Agricultural Society for the year 1832, and a list of the prizes offered in the succeeding year. The document also gave a sort of history of the society down to the year 1834. He gathered from it that the annual meeting of thei society for 1834 was held on October 3, and amongst those present were Lord Winmarleigh, who at that time was Mr. Wilson Patten. The name also appeared, in the records for 1833. He mentioned this matter to show that the society had been in existence for the length of time that had been stated—a fact which there had been a disposition on the part of some persons to doubt. —On.the motion of Mr. Smith, Mr. J. White (Warring- ton) and Mr.. Jacob Fair (Haigh Hall, Wigan) were appointed auditors to act until the annual meeting in October.—This was the principal business.

div.head: TEN MONTHS' SUFFERING IN A HOSPITAL.
div.p: TEN MONTHS' SUFFERING IN A HOSPITAL.

These is an old saying that physicians are a class oi men who pour drugs, of which they know little, into bodies of which they know lesa. This is both true and untrue at the same time. There are good and poor lawyers, and good and poor doctors. The trouble with these medical gentlemen as a profession is that they are clannish, and apt to be conceited. They don't like to be beaten at their own trade by out- siders who have never studied medicine. They there- fore pay, by their frequent failures, the penalty of refusing instruction unless the teacher bears their own " Hall Mark." An eminent physician—Dr. Brown-Sequard, of Paris— states the fact accurately when he says; "The medical profession are so bound up in their self-confidence and conceit that they allow the diamond truths of science to be picked up by persons entirely outside their ranks." We give a most interesting incident, which illustrates this important truth. The steamship" Concordia," of the Donaldson Line, Bailed from Glasgow to Baltimore in 1887, having on board as a fireman a man named Richard Wade, of Glasgow. He had been a fireman for fourteen years on various ships sailing to Ameriea, China, and India. He had borne the hard and exhausting labour, and had..been healthy and strong. On the trip we now name he began for the first time to feel weak and ill. His appetite failed, and he suffered from drowsiness, heartburn, a bad taste in the mouth, and costiveness and irregularity of the bowels. Sometimes when at work he had attacks of giddiness, but supposed it to be caused by the heat of the fire-room. Quite often he was sisk and felt like vomiting, and had some pain in the head. Later during the passage he grew worse, and when the ship reached Halifax he was placed in the Victoria General Hospital, and the ship sailed away without him. The house surgeon gave him some powders to stop the vomiting, and the next day the visiting physician gave him a ia ix- ture to take every four hours. Within two days Wade was so much worse that the doctors stopped both the powders and the mixture. A month passed, the poor fireman getting worse and worse. Then came another doctor who was to be visiting physician for the next five months. He gave other medicines, but not much relief. Nearly all that time Wade suffered great torture; he digested nothing. throw- Irvg up all he ate. There was terrible pain in the bowels, burning heat in the throat, heartburn, and racking head- ache. The patient was now taking a mixture every four hours, powders one after each meal to digest the food, operating pills one every night, and temperature pills two Pach night to stop the cold sweats. If drugs could cure him at all, Richard had an idea that he took enough to do it. But on the other hand, pleurisy set in, and the doctors took ninety ounces of matter from his right side, a d then told him he was sure to die. Five months ; more rolled by, and there wis another change of visiting physicians. The new one gave Wade a mixture which he said made him tremble tgce a leaf on a tree. At this crisis Wade's Scotch blood asserted itself. He refused to stand any more dosing, and told tlie doctors that if he must die he could die as well without them as with them. By this time a cup of milk would turn sour on his stomach, and lie there for days. Our friend from Glasgow was like a wreck on a shoal, fast going to pieces. We will let him tell the rest of his experience in the words in which he communicated it to the press. He says " When I was in this state a lady whom

had never seen came to the hospital and talked with me. She proved to be an angel of mercy, for without her I should not now be alive. She told me of a medicine called" Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup," and brought me a bottle next day. I started with it, without consulting the doctors, and in only a few days' time I was out of bed calling for liar and eggs for breakfast. From that time, keeping on with Mother Seigel's great remedy, I got well fast, and was soon able to leave the
, hospital and come home to Glasgow. I now feel as if I was in another world, and have no illness of any kind."

The above facts are calmly and inipartially stated,. and the reader may draw his own conclusion. We deem it best to use no names although Mr. Wade gave them in his original deposition. His address is No. 244, StObcross Street, Glasgow, where letters will reach him. Emma.

div.head: OLD COACH ROAD TO LIVERPOOL.
div.p: THE OLD COACH ROAD TO LIVERPOOL.
BY ALFRED RIMIER.

When railways superseded coaches in the con- veyance of passengers end mails, the coach service between Manchester and Liverpcol was alsisost at as high a state of efficiency as it could reach. A very interesting book on coaching days was written by Mr. Stanley Harris, who was himself an expert amateur, and often took the reins from the coach- man. He states twit in 1836 " the average speed of mails, taking both four-horse and pair-horse, was eight miles seven furlongs an hour, and that in the year 1836 then were only six mails that travelled at the rate of ten miles and upwards.' Birmingham to Sheffield and Pontefract to Leeds managed to compass ten miles, but from Liverpoorto Preston ' the rate was ten miles and five furlongs in hour. This, he says, was the fastest speed in ,the kingdom, but it was all day work; it was the night work which reduced averages so very much, for the poorest horses were put on, and a much lower speed had to be maintained. But the fastest record he gives does not seem to have equalled the 'coaches from Manchester to Liverpool even long before. A very careful record ef the mail and post coaches was made by Mr. M. Webb, and corrected down to 1822. Now this was fourteen years before Mr. Stanley Harris's dates, and in the interval an immense improvement had taken place both in roads and coaches. According to Mr. Webb, the coaches on week days averaged some three hours over the journey. This indeed was the advertised time, and after carefully measuring the dis- tance from Manchester to Liverpool, I find that this would be at the rate of ten miles seven furlongs per hour. The first coach which left Manchester for Liverpoolon Sunday was the Regulator, and this started from the Palace Inn, in Market-it., at 5 a.m., reaching the Gold m Lion, in Dale-st., Liverpool, at 10. The Defiance and the True Blue left at 9.30 and 10 respectively, and arrived at the Saracen's Heed, Liverpool,flve hours after- wards. It is not very easy to say why the Sunday 'journeys were some two hours longer than those of the week days; but doubtless as there were no business places open the journey was not pressing, and the brief space which we so often see complained of in old times as allowed for refreshments was liberally extended at the hotels. The Umpire left the Swan Inn at 12.30, and arrived at the Crown, Red Cross-st., in Liverpool, an inn which has disappeared. There would be some half- dozen more coaches in all that left Manchester for Liver- pool on Sundays. On week days there were fifteen which regulsrly left and made some four stoppages between Manchester and Warrington. From Eccles the road ran through Patricroft and Barton-on-Irwell to Islam, a die- tance of five miles, but there is little interest in the coun- try ; it partakes of the flat character of Chat Moss, and indeed stands on its outskirts. It is about a mile from Cadishead, a place whose inhabitants were occupied in fustian-cutting for Manchester houses, and also in agriculture, which still flourishes well. Warrington is reached through Woolston and Padgate. In coaching days it was a country town of great interest and beauty. It was the town where the county aristoc- racy congregated, for here was the noble residence of the Patten family, which is the present Town Hail, and many others. The church, which is seen from a great distanee, has been rebuilt, and the Nag's Head, the principal inn, was only a plain structure. There is a point Mr. Stanley Harris mentions in his work which is interesting in connection with the present movement to facilitate the distribution of parcels, for this, of course, is the work the Manchester and Liverpool coaches are to perform. I refer to the terrible tax of toll-gates. The heavy weight of these in the old coaching days may be judged from the following table :—From London to Brighton per day, £1 4s. ed., to Manchester £5 13s. 5d., to Birmingham £3 lie. 9d., to Liverpool £5 4e. 7d. It is true that the coaches which carried mails were exempt, but their exemption cost them heavily. The contractors were never to wait for a passenger. Their horses and harness were to be the very best, even for night work, and any of them might be condemned by a Government inspector. The coachmen were not to go single stages but Government distances. No parcels could be carried on the roof of a coach. No staao was ta be so long that the horses required watering, and the number of passen- gers was strictly limited. There were many other con- ditions which the mail contractors had to sign for , exemption from tolls, and sometimes a trifling lommis- • sion had to be paid. All this, of course, has been greatly changed .—From" The Jfanehester Guardian.'

div.head: WILL OF THE LATE MR. TWIS&
div.p: WILL OF THE LATE MR. TWIS&

The will of the late Mr. Edward Twiss„ of 81, Wilderspool-cause way,WarringtOn,hasrecently been proved at Chester. The testator, who was a retired cordwainer, devisee the farm at Fenketh to his son William. He bequeaths to him all his pro- perty in Academy and Mersey-streets, Warrington ; also the property in Irlam-st., with three cottages in Smith-st., and to his daughter for her life, absolutely free from control of any present or future husband and at her death to her children should they survive her, the eight houses in Orford-st., beginning at the end nearest the Central Station ; also Nos. 82 and 84, Wilderspool-causeway,. Warrington, subject to the same conditions. He bequeaths to her his 38 share's in the Manchester Ship Canal, and to his son Edward the two cottages in Upper James-street, formerly Bowcock-st. also the three small cottages behind the same; also the two freehold houses Nos. 48 and 50 Wilderspoohcauseway, Warrington, the cottages fronting and back on the opposite side of the way, No. 49, Ste., for his life, and to his wife if she should survive him. He bequeaths to his son Joseph the three houses in Orford-et., Warrington, adjoining hisdaughter Mary's property ; also two cottages in Cockhedgc-iane, also all his property in Manchester-road. He bequeaths to his wife, Mary Elizabeth, the house in which he lived and the next door, Nos. 80 and 78, Wilderspool-causeway, Warrington ; also his eight cottages in tostock-et., Warrington, and his. nye housesin Ilaydock-st., Warring- ton. He also bequeaths the newly erected property, Stafford Villas, at Virilderspool, to his wife. Four houses known as Stafford .Villas be bequeaths, instead of the distribution in his will, No. 1 to his grandson William .Tohn Twiss No. 4to his grandson Walter, No. 2 to his grandson Josiah, No. 3 to his granddaughter Elizabeth, subject to their coming into benefit of posseadon at the age of 21 years.

There was a good deal of expense to be incurred in restoring it to its former state, but he did not mind that, he said, for it had taught him a lesson, and be at once sot to work to alter the con- struction, so that it would be impossible for such an

, accident to occur again. In fact it Was quite a month before he once more handed over the keys to the manager; but there was no inaugural banquet upon this occasion, and, for some reason or another, upon receiving them, Mr. Elopstock looked anything but pleased. Matters went on at the great establishment in a very unpleasant way. Martin had, on the strength of his accident, been for a few days quite a hero, but as that wore off, and he seemed less disposed than ever to give up his careless ways, Mr. Klopstock began to speak severely, and Mark would go home of an evening pondering upon the possibility of obtaining his brother a post in some other establishment, and whether it would not be better to try and get him to go abroad. He broached the I,tter idea to Miss Klopstock on evening, and instead of sympathising and trying to help, she merely laughed. "How much would it cost?" she said, on seeing the

.• Pained look in Mark's countenance. "It depends upon what colony he goes to, and the extent of the farming operations attempted. He must not go penniless. Passage money, outfit, purchase of land, and stock; why, in the very smallest way it would take five hundrA pounds." "Well," replied Miss Klopstock, "say five hundred vounds. Of course, you would have to find this?" "Oh! of course. Martin would not be pre- pared with any." 'Five hundred pound 4! Take the money then, and go down to Waterloo-bridge, and drop it into the water. It will be just as sensible a thing to do." Mark frowned, and then smiled in the old lady's face. " Ah, you may smile, my dear boy, but I mean it If I had your faith in him, and you were doing such a thing as you propose, I'd give him another hundred pounds when he started; but it would be no good, Mark—no good at all." " I need have some faith," said Mark to himself, cheerfully; "and I must hold to my brother and help him, for he has not many friends." Just about this time Mr. Klopstock was taken very unwell, and had to keep his room fur a few days, the management devolving upon Mark, who soon had a little trouble on bis hands, for Mr. Samson Hall was seized with a fit, and his wife came to report the in- cident to Mark, who expressed his sorrow, and hoped the poor fellow would soon be better. "Let'. see," he said; "he had one of these fits about three months ago, did be not?" "Yes, sir; he generally has about four every year.' "Well, go and attend to him," said Mark. "Fli see that his wages are not stopped; and if he needs any special advice, come over again." Very large trees grow out of leery small seeds, and from the consequences of one of Mr. Samson Hall's fits came ruin and destruction to Mark Woolford. For though named Samson, Mr. Hall was an ex- teedingly weak man, and upon occasions would fly to strong things for support, the consequence being that from his ignorant*, of Om relative potency, of the medicinal, he administered to himself, mingled wide toe irre,ter and repr, the.ie terrible lit., as his wits teem, used to euperrene. Mee. Hall lived with her spouse in the pleasantly- named road, Song-bird-lane, in the rural district of P3ow. It was a charming spot, arid upon occasion a song bird could be heard twittering in a cage; but it was not to ell a rural country lane, inasmuch as the hedges were little four-roomed boilers, which ran down to the great gates of a gasworke, whose etrengly-pervading odour was known all over the district, but declared by the inhabitemts to be very healthy. Mrs. Hall was a very little thin woman, who had once been very pretty, but an attack of small-pox had so puckered and pitted her face that there was nothing pretty left but her eyes, and her heart, which was deeply devoted to the great eix feet high broad. shouldered potter, who led her as miserable a life as a poor woman could live. Samson Hall's income was thirty shillings pee week, for somehow or another, when he left the army, he missed getting a pension, and all he bad to show for twelve years' service was a very uprrgl erriege, strong language, suppressed at Humphreys', ':o come out the more powerful at home; and the move-named periodical fits. Poor Mrs. Hall was very proud of h:r lord, but she lived in a constant state of fear. Now this dread was not reep eoting any injury the. _

he might do her during one of his att-acks'—fo"r be war 4 given to being plaTful at such times, and throwing his boots at her, caressing her with pieces of crockery, and lovingly Promising to throw her out of window—but for fear that he should show himself some day at the great place of business while suffering from ono of his fits. . .

Poor woman! She had a hard task, for when unwell the 'prevailing idea in Mr. Samson Hall's brain was-- and he constantly said it—that be wns never better in his life ; and on Monday mornings after a seizure, which always began in the City on Saturday niehts, and was very bad all through Sunday, be used to make strenuous efforts to go down to the office, show himself to Mr. Bloetsock, and lose his post. So to prevent this, poor little Mrs. Hall used to set her wits to work, hiding her husband's bxas, his her, and on occasions, when he was very bad perhaps,. the whoie of his garments, thus forcing hint to lie its bed all day, and fill the haise with bad language that could be heard as tar is; the gas-works' gates. These plans had Mem iaely been successful, for Samson retained his old military discipline as far as dressing himself cleenlv, smartly, and well, making himeell thereby a well-known and decidedly ornamen- tal addition to Humphrey s' esenelishinent ;. but clever as were poor little Mrs. Hall's plans, they could not always be expected to succeed; and it so. happened that at the time when Mr. Alopstock was ill, and the poor woman had gone down to report the fit to Mark Woolf ord, that Semson Hall began to play al; " Hot boiled beans, and very good butter," without any one being there to tell him when he was growing warm or burnine. satisfaction, displaying tne neatly pinned-up bundle rather sooty—but that only appertained to the big blue-check bundle handkerchief—which, upon being unfolded, revealed the missing coat perfectly clean. The result was that, properly clothed, but atill oaf- tering considerably from his fit, Samson Efel itarra:d out of the street, and reached the main road, eiroesing over to catch an omnibus, to the top of which he mounted, just as, on the other side of the way, clever little Nelly, his wife, alighted from the interior of another omnibus, just returned from the City, happy and satisfied—poor little body I—at having once snore staved off the danger that threatened their bumble home. Chuckling and self-satisfied, Samson Hall went on Cityward, assuring himself several times over that he never felt better in his life; and so well was he that on slighting in Gracechurch-street, he turned up a court to one of those dispensaries with strapped-back swing- ing doors, where he partook of more medicine; went on a hundred yards, and turned up another long court to another dispensary, where he took something to take the taste out of his mouth, and no wonder, for *ome medicines are so nasty Then, walking very stiff and straight, as if he were snaking for points like a surveyor carrying a chain, he went right away to Humphreys', walked through into the large office, saluted the assembled clerks military fashion, and smiled upon them benignantly. " Hallo:" said Martin, looking up. "You there, Samson? Why, your wife's been here, and said you had a fit." "Tenth!" he exclaimed, contemptuously. "Mad woman. Never was batter in my life." "Suppose, not," said Martin, laughing, to a fellow elerk. "You look capital." "Never was better in my life, Mr. Martin," said Hall, nodding. "There now.' "That's wed," said Martin. "Here, take this paper into Mr. Wool'ord's room." "No, au,' said a fellow clerk. "Don't send him ku, Martin. He'll be all right soon. Here, Hall, go awl lit down in your place," "No, no," said Samson, sternly, "I am not to be played with by junior elerlo?. Mr. Martin Woolford odd I was to take in that paper, and I'm going to take

it in, sir." _ _ Say ing which, he snatched the form from Martin's desk, and walked straiebt to the chief clerk's room. " It's too bad ofyou;Woolford," said Bev ; "you'll get the fellow sent off." "Serve him right," said Martin. "No business to send his wife here to say he is in fits. The blackguard's boea;drinking." " A thing whieh you never do," said another. " I never come to the office if I have been," said Martin, meekly. " Then you must indulge pretty well," said another, "for you come late, and stay away pretty often." " You mind your own laisinfes; Martin. "I do," was the retort; "and it would make it pleasanter for all of us if you minded yours." "Hear, bear!" cried several. " Oh, yes," said Martin. "You are nice model ern. ple:as, all of you. I never met such a set of die• agreeable cads. I just send that fellow in for a bit of fun to see what ley stuck-up brother will say to him and then you all set to bajing at me like a pack of curs." " At a strange dog," said another, laughing. " Well, never mind, Martin Woolford, I say it was a nasty, malicious trick on both old Hall and Mr. Woolford, and I hope it won't turn out awkward for any one." " Bah ' said Martin, contemptuously; end he went on with his writing. Meanwhile Samson Halt had walked, without knocking, straight into Mark Woolford's room, and dabbed the paper down before him with a defiant air, afterwards drawing hirnselr up and looking down with an eye of contempt upon his superior. "Why, Hall," exclaimed Mark, .ring, "I thought you were at home, suffering from a tit.", "Never was better in my life," said the porter, mapping his fingers. "There, who says I'm not right ? ' I do," said Mark, sternly, as he rose. "How dare you come here, sir, in such a state! It is d.sgraneful. Go home, and do not come back here for a week Meanwhile I will consult with Mr. Klopstock on what is to be done." •Wha-a-at?" cried the porter. "You foolish fellow," cried Mark. "So these are your fits for which you have received charitable dona- tions from the firm. Hall. you a man of fifty, in a trusted responsible situation, and to behave like this There, leave the room, and do not return to the office for a week." Mark did not intend to mention the matter to Mr. Klopstock, but trusted, by reading the man a severe lesson, to make him amend his ways; but fate was against him then. His words partly sobered Hall, sufficiently to bring him to a knowledge of his position, and to rouse the temper that mastered him when he had been drinking. "Look here you, Mr. Woolford," he cried, mena- cingly. "I'm not blind, you knew. If I was your young sneak of a brother, and I'd come like this, you wouldn't have said a word." "Leave the room, sir." "Not till I've done: so there. Look here. I know what your brother has done, and what he does, and how you bide it, so don't you make an enemy of me.' "You insolent scoundrel!" cried Mark; "bays the place." "Good! I'll go then," said Samson, screwing his, hands together. "It's to be 'enemies then? Very well. I warned you, so you can look out for youreelf, Tour day to-day, Mark Woolford ; mine to-morrow. to look out." Without another word the man strode out of tI- rOOM with a malignant grin upon his face; and. as t door closed, trifling as the incident seemed, Mn ViToolford read mischief in the porter's enmity, and cloud of danger threatening his future through brother's folly, thoueh he could not see how CLIST_` ar-Q danger that cloud would prove,

div.p: CHAPTER XL MARTIN'S WAY OF TIIORNS.

" HALLO " said Martin Woolford, as the porter came striding back through the great office. "Did you I leave the paper?" The question was put more out of bravado than anything else, for Martin wanted to show his fellow elerks how little he cared for their opinion. Hall carne as far as his deA, and then stopped. short, showing in nowise that he had been drinking, save in his defiant language. "rye told him," he Enid, angrily," I've tad him' "Look here," said the clerk, who bad reproved Martin for sending the porter to his brother's, room. "You take my adrne, 11,11, and go home.i" "I'll ask for your advice, sir, when tweet aid the man, sharply. "I was addressing Mn. Martin Woolford here, it you please." "Yes, yes, I koow," said the clerk; "'but„ look here, /fall, I don't want to see you get Into trouble." Lawson, the clerk, left his desk, and. laid his band upon the portr r's shoulder. "Thanky, Mr. Lawson, sir, you've gentlemein--tbat you are," said Sainson ; "and if you had your desserts, sir,vou'd bah, ad man here instead of a.peck of hingry wolves—Woolfords." He looked round for approval after- this atiemid, at witticism, and several of the younger clerks. who had not learned to realise the horrors el intemperance, began to laugh. "I tell him," continued Sam.cir4, "as I told his brother, that they're blots on this establishment; and, if I dteln't tell his brother, I tell tam to his face --him. elartin Woolford, who's done enough a hundred times over to belicked out of any respectable house." "Why. you in, client blackguard!' cried Martin, rising in his seat. "Which it's, yourself you, mean," said Sam , drawing himsell up very stiffly, and settling his +wok in his stiff odlitiary stock. " And if I'd done what 1; liked, I shouhl have left you, stout sip in the big safe, which wail be the safest place for you." "Kick him out of the offikiiN Lawson," said Martilt4 scornfullyt "No, OA*. ountinned Samson, crossing his aim- upon hie breast. "I Anti not he kicked out or', the °face. I any one is kicke.-I mut of the office, it will be you and year brother too. , said before, acid 'II say ago*, you two are blots upon the establishment; and as an, old and faithful' servant of Humpktips end Company I shall scratch you both out." "To be sure; yes, Hall, of course YOU will,' said Lawson, smiling; "and being such a fine bit oV ste,l as you are, I should juat go quietly borne and get ground." "Right, Mr. Lawson, sir," said Samson, todding "You're a gentleman, sir, and I resnect you. I have been insulted bore this morning, sir; but never mind. The enemy is in front, sir, and just now be is strong ; but we can be strong, too, and we will retire, air, and take up fresh position on the right—do you bear you Woelford. on the right—on the right, I say. on the right. Ten—tion! Grenadier company. Rest stand fast. Right about Noe. By your right. Ma-r-r-r -ch." Ile swung round sharply upon his heels, and with his arms straight down to his sides, he marched straight out of the office, and along the street, to make the best of his way home, leaving the clerks convulsed with laughter, saving Martin Woolford, who set his teeth fast as he bent over the writing upon which he was engaged. "What a pity!" said Lawson, returning to his desk. "A quiet, respectabli fellow like that to break out and be so stupid. Yo-ar brother won't be very hard upon biR, I hope. Woolf ord."

1115 t litaskupora atm Tr I say that if the blackguard is allowed to enter the doors again it will be positively disgraceful." "Oh, I don't know," said Lawson. "Of course, I'd punish him; but if we never met with anything but mach stern judgment, we should; some of us, come badly " Look here, Lawson, none of your dirty insinua tiona, Rime. I maybe your fellow clerk, but recollect that in brother is manager here." "Indeed!" said Lawson, coolly. "I thought Mr. Klopstock held that position." "Mr. Klopstock !" cried Martin, oontemptuoudy. "An imbecile old man, kept on by the principals because they don't like to send him away. No, sir, my brother lathe head here, and perhaps some of you will find it "Perhaps so," said Lawson; "but I say, Martin Woolford, isn't that rather an indiscreet speech of yours ? What would Mr. Klopstock say if he heard - of it r "Yon can go and tell hula if you like," retorted Martin, who bitterly regretted having made ths remark; "I don't mind his knowing my opinion." "No," said Lawson, quietly, as he went on writing; "tale bearing and carrying foolish people's hasty words to others for the sake of making mischief is not in nil way.' "You can tell him if you like," said Martin, with mourned coolness. "Well, what is it r This was to a boy who acted as messenger, and who stow handed a note to Mark's brother. "Letter for you, sir; and gentleman said he'd wait for a hanswer. Lawson could not resist the ternetation to glance sidewise, and in his quick glance be saw that the envelope was ill-directed, and that Martin had turned Very pale. "All right:" he said, cavalierly, " call when I've written the answer." Martin Woolford's bands trembled as he tore the note open, and it was very hard work to preserre calm, unruffled aspect, when all the time he knew that a number of eyes were watching him from the different desks. But he kept up the mask pretty well, opened the paper, and read, screwing his lips as if it were some contemptible affair, though his heart %vas beating painfully, and a strange sinking sensation of dread threatened to rob him of his composure. Throwing the note aside, he wrote a few lines upon a wrap of paper—selected an envelope that did not bear the stamp of the firm, directed it, and beckoned to the boy, who came up to his desk. " Give that to the bearer," he said, calmly; and theft went on with his writing, but with his ears painfully attent upon what was going on around. "Old Martin's in for it again," said one. "Only his washerwoman's bill," replied another. "There'll be a regular row one of these days," whispered the first speaker. Lawson said nothing, only watched while apparently. busy over his work. At the ead of five minutes Martin began to shiver« for be saw the boy coming back, and try how be wonld' to nerve hiinseff for what was coming, it was in vain. "Plea, sir, the gent says as that won't do. Lie' wants to see "Tell him I'm engaged," said Martin, with a despe- rate attempt at calmness; "and that he must make an, appointment for this evening." " Yes, air." The boy went away, and Martin went on writing, but it was mechanically, for the brain had ceased to. guide the pen, and the words he wrote were discon- tweed and without meaning. The next minute the boy was back, and there was In twinkle in his eye, as he said aloud: "Gent says he must see you, sir, and he slcall stop here till he do." " Tut—int—tut! e ejaculated Martin, with a look of peeviah annoyanee. "How vapid to to sure!" And leaving his stool in a careless, nonchalant way, he' slowly went into the lobby, and took down his hat, conscious all the while that his fellow eerks were• exchanging glanoes and reading his shallow pretence at calmness through and through. It was bravely done, though the pity was that an' much self-restraint had n.a been called into action for a worthier purpose. As soon, though, as he had passed' the door, Martin Woolford's countenance changed to one of fierce rage, and, hurrying aleng the street, he turiseclup a narrow passage, and, after a glance roind to see that be was not observed, darted in between 5
_ temple of swing doors. (To be Continued.)

SELLING BAD FISH AT WARRINGTON.
HEAVY PENALTIES.

At the Warrington Police Court, yesterday morn- ing, before Mr. John White and Alderman Harrison, Evan Goodwin Ilughes and Alfred Hughes, of Latchford., were summoned to show cause why they should not be fined for having, on the 29th ult., ex- posed for sale a quantity of unwholesome fish, that had 'been seized by Inspector Norman, and des- troyed by order of a magistrate. The fish seized weighed )31.11be. Mr. J. Lyon Whittle, town clerk, appeared to prosecute, and said that Inspector Norman on the date mentioned, noticed a quantity of fish exposed for sale in the market. A strong smell emanated from it, and the Inspector examined it and found that it was unfit for human food. It was also examined by a magistrate, who ordered that it should be destroyed. If the Bench were satisfied that the defendant knew the condition of the fish, he should ask them to inflict a heavy penalty. Inspector Norman gave evidence to the effect that when he seized it the fish was going putrid, and Dr. Gornall, medical officer, deposed that it was in an advanced stage of decomposition, and quite unfit for human food; it stunk horribly. The magistrates fined each of the defendants, who did not appear, £5 and costs, or the alternation of two months' imprisonment. A second case was then heard, in which James Smith, of Wigan, fishmonger, was charged with a similiar offence, also committed on the 29th ult. The fish seized on his stall weighed 1491b5. He said that he did not know the fish was bad. He was fined 40s. and costs, or a month's imprisonment in default, and he was further fined ss. and costs for using obscene language on the occasion 1 when the seizure was made.

div.head: RUSSIAN STUDENTS.
div.p: THE RUSSIAN STUDENTS.

A St. Petersburg correspondent sends adetailed account of the Russian Student Agitation, which has now assumed unprecedented proportions, and spread to all the Universities and Academies. The Government may be compelled to close all these institutions. A Berlin cor- respondent sends the text of a manifesto which has been circulated among all tke students embodying their de- mands.

div.head: FUNERAL OF THE DUKE OF MA.NOHESTER.
div.p: FUNERAL OF THE DUKE OF MA.NOHESTER.

--- --- The remains of the late Duke of Manchester were in- terred on Wednesday afternoon in the family vault at Kimbolton Parish Church. Most of the shops were closed. The service was read by the Venerable Archdeacon Vesey, of Huntingdon, and the Rev. Mr. Young, vicar of Tillbrook. Wreaths were sent from the Queen, the Prince and Princess of Wales, and the Duke an Duchess of Fife. The present Duke, Lord Mandeville, Lord Charles Montague, the Duke of Hamilton, and Lord Esme Gordon were chief mourners.

div.head: DRUGGED AND ROBBED.
div.p: DRUGGED AND ROBBED.

An extraordinary case of alleged robbery came before the magistrate at Dalston, on Monday. Mr. Augustus Andrew de Metz, a civil engineer, swore that he was in- duced by a man he supposed to be a neighbour to enter a house near his own residence at Stoke Newington, and there to drink what was represented to be ale and gin, but which made him drowsy. While in this condition he was robbed of his money and jewellery. William Wilson, a dealer, giving an address at Whitechapel, was charged with being concerned with a woman in com- mitting the theft, and was now sent for trial.

div.head: MR. CAINE AND WORKING-CLASS REPRESENTATION.
div.p: MR. CAINE AND WORKING-CLASS REPRESENTATION.

Mr. Caine, M.P., addressed a meeting at Barrow on Wednesday night on labour legislation and kindred sub- jects. He advocated the payment of members of Parlia- ment, in order that there might be fuller representation of the working classes. In regard to the Eight Hours Bill, he considered foreign competition was a great diffi- culty in the way of the adoption of such a measure. Before anything satisfactory could be achieved in this direction it would be necessary that the scheme should have international sanction and approval.

div.head: ACTION FOR LIBEL AGAINST MR. T. W. RUSSELL, M.P.
div.p: THE ACTION FOR LIBEL AGAINST MR. T. W. RUSSELL, M.P.

The action brought by Mr. Patrick O'Brien, M.P. against Mr. T. W. Russell, M.P., for libel, was concluded on Wednesday, at Cork Assizes, before Mr. Justice Andrews. The jury, after a protracted deliberation, asked his lordship if a statement published without malice might be a libel. His lordship said if the words complained of tended to Ignore, disparage or degrade the plaintiff they would be libellous. Subsequently the jury found a verdict for the plaintiff, damages £l5O. Judgment for plaintiff with costs was therefore entered.

div.head: LABOUR ELECTORAL ASSOCIATION.
div.p: LABOUR ELECTORAL ASSOCIATION.

The annual congress of the Labour Electoral Associa- tion was concluded on Tuesday at Hanley. A resolution was adopted in favour of concerted action at municipal and local elections. The practice of sweating by work- ing-men in the form of the employment of underhands, which was said te exist to a large extent amongst mem- bers of Birmingham Trades Unions, was thoroughly condemned. Another resolution expressed regret at the determined opposition of Mr. Bradlaugh to the Em- ployers' Liability Bill, as the working-men of the country desired it to be passed, and refused to recognise Mr. Bradlaugh as a labour representative. A metien in favour of State payment of members was adopted, and London was selected as the next place of meeting. Mr. G. D. Kelley (Manchester) was elected president, and Mr. W. J. Davis (Birmingham), treasurer.

div.head: MIL CHAMBERLAIN ON THE LAND BILL
div.p: MIL CHAMBERLAIN ON THE LAND BILL

Mr. J. Chamberlain, M.P., presided on Thursday night at a banquet in connection with the inauguration of the Birmingham Liberal Unionist Club, and in proposing success to it, asserted that the Unionists had really done most useful work and influenced legislation. He charged Mr. Gladstone and his followers with divorcing politics from ethics, and said the Unionist party were not at all prepared to admit that Horne Rule was a question of ex- pediency. Hecriticised the attitude of the Liberal party on the question of free education, and then referred to I Mr. Balfour's Irish Land Purchase Bill. Ile found one flaw, in the Bill which he thought could easily be re- medied, and he held that the scheme of land purchase was a sound one, for the Government would simply be in the position of a banker, and could guard against loss. He added that the Government had pledged themselves to bring in a Bill for the local government of Ireland, and he hoped they would produce it before the Land Purchase Bill left the House of Commons. What they had to insist upon was the honest payment of rent, and to promote public opinion in favour of the fulfilment of just and reasonable obligations. As to the reunion of the Unionists with the Radical party, he feared it was far distant, for the third party in English politics with which he was now asseciated,could not surrender its old Liberal principles.

div.head: ATHERTON MURDER.
div.p: THE ATHERTON MURDER.

The condemned man William Chadwick. who lies in Birkdale Gaol. awaiting execution for the murder of a pawnbroker's assistant, at Atherton. in July last, still asserts hi st innocence as firmly as he did during his re- cent trial at the Assizes. The convict has not been visited by any of his friends, but exhibits a cheerful demeanour, and attends earnestly to the ministrations of the Protes- tant chaplain of the gaol, the Rev. 0. F. Pigott. On Sun- day Chadwick was present at the Divine service con- ducted by Mr. Pigott. Unless the Home Secretary should intervene, the execution will take place on Tuesday, the 15th inst., and the Governor of the Gaol has nearly com- pleted the preparations for the solemn event.

. . . THE CONDEMNED MAN INTERVIEWED. Chadwick was on Wednesday visited by his sister, Mrs. Kay, the wife of a stonemason at Whitefield, with whom he formerly lodged. It was while living at their house in Radcliffe, and employed at Wild's paper I mill, that the condemned man lost a finger which formed an important feature in the identification. He was born in Pendleton, and there he married his wife, Polly Shaw. , The interview lasted half an hour. On again emerging from the prison Mrs. Kay said her brother was looking very ill and weary, but was delighted to see her. He said at once that he owned to being a bad one, but that he was not guilty of murder. He declared, however, that 11 he would die like a man, and affirm his innocence on the scaffold next Tuesday morning. "Only five 1 more days, my dear sister," he said, and then went on to tell her how he wished he could have had another chance, and added that he would have been better if he had been caught sooner for some of his misdeeds. He begged his sister never to forsake his wife, observing, "No matter what I've been, Folly's innocent enough." Over and over again he declared his innocence of the murder. " I admit all, tell my friends," said he, "except murder." When the time was up he said "Good morning." "I think it is good-bye dear brother," replied his sister, and then he cried bitterly. Four times over she asked him if he killed Davies, and each time he raised his hand and said be didn't, and would repeat the same on the scaffold. His wife visited him a few days ago, and is going again. The culprit is also anxious to see his brother Thomas. and his sister's eldest daughter. No efforts have been made to obtain the reprieve of the culprit.

THE various Easter Vestry Meet- Vestry inas which have been hold in this Meetings. part of the country have,with a few exceptions, passed off without noteworthy incident. At Frodsham, Mr. ROBERT FOULKES, the redoubt- able and irrepressible, came upon the scene and trotted out his objection& to everything which he imagined had a smack of POpery. But it would seem that, if the parishioners are going down hill to destruction, they are perfectly willing to go, for Mr. FOULKES ryas not supported by even a single follower. He objected to a vote of thanks to the ladies who had supplied flowers to the Church, and to the use of Hymns Ancient and Modern ; but he was as the voice of one crying in the wilderness, for no heed was paid to anything he said. At the vestry meeting, on Tuesday, of the Warrington Parish Church there was a contest of ' a more serious nature. Tho new Rector (the Rev. F. W. Willis) has shown himseli a thoughtful, earnest and practical worker; and. he hae already organised various institutions which are calculated to be of great benefit to his parishioners. But he is a High Churchman, and his Ritualistic practices have given offence to a considerable portion of those who have been in the habit of regularly attending the Parish Church. All went smoothly however- at the meet- ing, on Tuesday, until the nomination of Mr. ALFRED WOODS as people's warden in succession to the Mayor, who retires from office. It would appear that the nomination of Mr. Woons had been arranged by "the officials of the church ; " but it was not allowed to pass unehallenged,for Dr. CANNELL was also moved and seconded; and it was soon apparent that the doctor was "on the job," for he quickly made it known that if his proposer and seconder demanded a poll he should "certainly stand because of the illegal practices carried on in the church." Dr. CANNeLfaproposer accordingly demanded a poll ; but prudently withdrew on being told by the Clerk that he would be held responsible. for the whole of the costs. This bugbear did not, however, terrify the valiant doctor, who, with a courage equal to his convictions, demanded a poll on his own behalf. It was, in vain that he was appealed to to let the matter drop. He answered that he objected to have " Roman and Popish principles" brought into the church, and he should therefore go to the poll. As the matter stood at the close of the meeting, it was arranged that there should be a poll to-day (Saturday) on the election of people's warden for the ensuing year. The voting was to take place at the I Parochial Schools, between ten in the morning and six in the evening; and it was open, it was said, to every ratepayer in Warrington to vote on the question. But there will be no poll, after all ; for, following upon the adjournment, objection was taken to Dr. CANNELL'S seconder on the ground that he is neither a parishioner nor a house- holder. The objection has been ruled by the Law Clerk to be fatal ; and Mr. Woons is declared duly elected. The adjourned meeting of the vestry will be held this (Saturday) evening, and it is not unlikely that considerable discussion will arise out of this curious complication. At the meeting of the parishioners of St. Barna.bas, Warrington, the Vicar (Rev. G. ALLTON) found that a large gathering was hostile to him. He pro- fessed to be willing to give way for the benefit of the church and of the working people of the parish; but it was soon seen that be meant to carry matters, wherever he could, with a high hand, and that the only way he understands is doing his own way. Finding that the meeting was likely to be too many for hire, the reverend chairdian suddenly declared it at an end; and after a little altercation he left the room. The parishioners, however, concluded that they could exist and even have a meeting without the Vicar. They accordingly elected another chairman, dis- cussed sundry matters, and concluded by passing

div.p: a vote of censure npon their Vicar for abruptly' closing tho meeting. It is not much that parishioners can do at the Easter Vestries; their power is on the whole ridiculously small; and they are therefore quite justified in exercising that power whenever they deem it necessary to give a hint, or administer a rebuke, to their spiritual pastors and masters.

SIR JOHN LuneoeE is not to have it ShopmPn's Flalf-Holiday-. all his own way in striving to get a half-holiday for shop-assistants, one day in each week. Mr. BLuNnELL MApr..a is a. competitor with him in the field of legislation ; and, as the bill which Air. MAPLE has prepared follows the line of least resistance, we are inclined to think it will be the first to find a place upon the Statute book. The object of the bill which Sir Joux LUBBOCK has brought in" is to enable loca/ authorities to establish a weekly half-holiday for shops." This means that shops are to be closed one afternoon in each week; but before this can be done the local authority must have evidence that two-thirds of the shop-keepers in the district with.- in which action is taken are in favour of the half-holiday. It has generally been found when attempts have been made to establish a half-holiday by voluntary agreement that it was impossible to obtain absolute un- animity; and it has this happened that one proposal after anotherhas ended in failure. is due to employers as a body to say that by far the larger proportion of them have always show themselves willing to close their shops for half-a- day ; and, if Sir JOHN LUBBOCK'S bill becomes law, a majority of two-thirds will be in a position te emforce the regulation all round. But ought they Ito have that power? That is a question which requires more attention than it has hitherto re- ceived. Mr. MAPLE thinks compulsory closing would be a hardship to a number of small trades- men ; and his way out of the difficulty is not by closing shops, but by ensuring that every she"' assistant shall have a half-holiday one day in each week. His measure is styled "'A bill to give shop' assistants, male and female, one half-holiday each week, without closing the shop.' ll° makes it a condition that a shop-keeper shall not be compelled to give the half-holiday, except to assistants who have been in his employ for three months. The employer is, to beat liberty to select such days for the half-holiday as suit hira best; and he could, for instance, if he had half-er dozen assistants, have one off every afternoon in the week. It is a weak point in the Bill, as 4 seems to us, that the half-holiday doea not cow' mence until "four p.m. on the day selected" ; but it would be an easy matter, whilst the Bill is in Committee, to amend it by making the half-holi- day commence at one, or two p.m. By way of en- suring that the law shall not become a dead letter, a penalty of £4 attaches to its contra' vention ; and there is, besides, to be a half' holiday register which is to be signed bY each assistant as evidence that he has received his half-holiday. We must confess that we he" a liking for Mr. MAPLE'S bill as one which, on th° face of it, can be brought into operation with' out trenching seriously on the liberty of the subjec• But it leaves out of sight the desire which the trada9" man may have to takea holiday ,himself byclosing altogether—on the understanding that his felloW' tradesmen are taking the same course. It would be interesting to hear what shop-keepers. and their assistants think of these bills. It is within their power to shape them as they like, if they will onlY take the trouble to exercise the power which undoubtedly possess.
