div.p: In the course of some conversation on the sup- ply of intoxicants to paupers, which took place at the meeting, on Wednesday, of the Warrington Board of Guardians, Mr. Heaton said "lie had been in some of those great teetotal workhouses where he had had champagne to his dinner and plenty of good whiskey and beer, and he had been to some teetotal places where 'they had zoedone, which,when they came to drink it,they found to be very good whiskey." It is a pet theory of Mr. Heaton's that " teetotalers "take intoxicants on the sly. He does not seem to see that when people take intoxicants they cease to be teetotal- lars ; that they become members of the class so dear to the heart, of Mr. Heaton—namely, the moderate drinkers ; and that, if they act as he says they do, they are hypocrites as well as moderate drinkers.

PRIMITIVE METHODIST CHAPEL, KINGSLEY.—On Mon- day, a sale cf work and "Easter Tree," was held in the above chapel. The two stalls, which displayed a good assortment of fancy and useful articles were presided over by the following ladies :—No. 1 stall: Mrs. J. Littlemore, Mrs. L. Jackson, assisted by Miss Maddock and Miss L. Lewis. No. 2 stall: Miss Clucas, and Miss S. Oultram' • ' whilst Mrs. S. Lewis and the Misses S. Lewis presided over the refreshments, of which there was an ample supply. The sales realised upwards of £25, which goes towards the augumentation of the circuit funds. The proceedings were opened by Mrs. White, of Runcorn. SPRING FASHIONS, Spring Fasidons.-7. & W. Durrosr, 16 and 18, Sankey-et., Warrington.—Advt. FOOTBALL: ST. HELENS RECREATION V. RUNCORN. These strong teams met on the Recs.'s ground at St. Helens, on Thursday night. About 6,000 spectators witnessed a hard-fought game. The home team kicked off, but the Rancorn men quickly went to the front, and Riley gained an unimproved try. Amid cheers Dobie equalised, and these were the only points scored in the first half. •On the resumption the play was fast and exciting, and Crompton dropped a goal for the visitors. Towards the close Pilkington gained a splendid try for the Recs., but the place kick failed. The Cheshire men were thus declared the victors by one goal, one try, and tour minors, to two tries and one minor. FARNWORTH CHURCH OF ENGLAND TEMPERANCE SOCIETY. On Tuesday evening a concert was given in the National School, Farnworth, under the auspices of the Farnworth Church of England Temperance Society. There was a good attendance. The first part of the programme con- sisted of vocal music, which was well tendered by Miss Lewis, Miss A. Holden, and Mr. A. -Er. Davies. The second part consisted of a representation of " Bardell v. Pickwick," the characters of which were admirably im- personated by Messrs. T. Knowles, H. Knowles, W. Knowles, H. Mercer, E. Young, A. Carter, T. Peattie, W. Rawlinson, H. Booth, and J. Little. The entertainment concluded with a sketch. entitled " The Village School," by Mb A. G. Davies, 'which proved very amusing. The proceeds will be devoted to the funds of the society. THE SOCIETY OF ACCOUNTANTS AND AUDITORS. We are pleased to notice that at a recent Coun- cil meeting, held in London, of the Society of Accountants and auditors, Mr. Robert Lowe, ac- countant, &c., of Market Gate Chambers, Warring- ton (late of Rainhili), was elected a Fellow of the Society. SPRING FASHIONS, Spring Fashions.--J. aW. Dirrrox, 16 and 18, Sankeyret., Warrington.---Advt. DROWNED IN A DOLLY-TUB. A sad drowning fatality occurred at St. Helens on Thursday afternoon, the deceased being James Woodward, two years of age, son of William Wood- ward, a collier, residing at 123, Napier-st. The boy was playing in the yard and was left alone for a few .minutes. He was afterwards found lying head downwards in a dolly-tub, which contained about six inches of water. He was immediately pulled out, and it was found that he was quite dead.

div.head: FATAL ACCIDENT AT_ROBY STATION
div.p: FATAL ACCIDENT AT_ROBY STATION

An inquest was held at Liverpool, on Saturday, touching the death of James Marcella, aged 47, a licensed victualler, living at Toxteth. On the pre. vious Wednesday, deceased and his wife were at Roby looking for a house; On the return journey deceased attempted to get into the train3when it was in motion. Missing his footing, he fell between the carriages and the platform, sustaining serious injuries. He was conveyed to the Royal Infirmary, and he died the same evening. The jury returned a verdict of" Accidental death." SPRING FASHIONS, Spring Fashions,—J. &W. Hymns, 16 and 18, Sankey-st., Warrington.—Advt. STRICKEN WITH PARALYSIS. A carter named Philip Davies, belonging to Padgate, brought a man to the Police Station, on Tuesday evening, whom he had found lying help- less by the roadside at Rixton. The man, who could give no account of himself, was taken by P.C. Frank Jones to the Infirmary. He was there examined by the house surgeon, who stated that the man had received a paralytic stroke down the left side. The patient was accordingly detained at the institution Papers found on him show that his name is Peter Fearn, and that he resides at Ice. SPRING FASHIONS, Spring Fashions.—A &W. Dtirrolt, 16 and 18, Sankey-t., Warrington.--Advt. THE Holm 'mix TRADE. The English iron market shows in somewhat better form this week, but the business doing is small. The prices of pig-iron are stronger, and this is partly due to the improved nature of the Cleve- land ironmasters'returns for March, but partly also to a recovery in warrants. Middlesborough pig- iron has gone up 3s. a ton. Scotch makers' iron has also improved slightly for some brands. Besse- mer iron is steady at former rates. There is less firmness in Lancashire pig-iron, and steel is also , quiet. Rails are ss. a ton lower, and steel plates 1 are easier. Shipbuilders are not booking fresh work,l while engineers are not receiving many new en- quiries; still, both branches of trade keep fairly active.—lron RAILWAY SERVANTS MEETING. On Thursday night, a meeting of the railway' , servants of St. Helens and district was held in the Public Hall, Hardshaw-st., St. Helens, in connection with the formation of a local branch of the General Railway Workers' Union. There was a large attendance and Mr. J. Skeldon, of Crewe, who pre- sided, was supported- by Mr. J. Kelly, organism* secretary of the Union of Salford. The notice call- ing the meeting asked railway workers of all classes to show by their presence that they did not intend to remain as they now were "harshly and unfairly treated." After hearing addresses in explanation of the objects of the Union, a resolution in favour of the formation of a local branch was carried with only two dissentients, and local was, were appointed. BOY TIPPLERS AT WIDNBB.--SINGULA.II CASE, At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Peter Rowe and Edward Glover, two boys, aged respectively 15 and 14 years, were brought up charged with steal- ing a bottle of Passover wine and a bottle of rum, on the 4th inst., Valued at 45., the pronerty of Isaac Cohen.—The prosecutor stated that he a joiner, and resided at 29, Eleaner-st., Widnes. On Friday last, about eight o'clock, he put the bottle of wine and bottle of rum on the window sill, in the back yard. They were both full, and the same night he missed •them.—P.C. Wolfenden proved to finding the boys in the hack yard of Mr. Claff. They were both under the influence of drink. Tie bottles pro- duced were lying beside them.—The defendants pleaded guilty, and were each ordered to pay a fine of 10s. REGISTER GRATES.—d. S. Garland, 51, iirldge-street, War rington.—Adrt. INSTITUTE OF JOURNALISTS: WARRINGTON SUB-DISTRICT.

The quarterly meeting of the members of the Warrington sub-district of the Institute of Journal- ists was held, by permission, at the Chatnbcr of Commerce, Bewsey-St., on Saturday, the President (Mr. Wm. Gill) in the chair. Five nominations for membership were made, and, after receiving the sanction of the meeting, ordered to be forwarded to the District Committee for approval. On the motion of Mr. S. Harrison, seconded by Mr. H. Isherwood, the following resolution was passed and the Secretary was instructed to forward copies to the editors of the papers named :—"That this meet- ing of the Warrington sub-district, of the Liver- pool district, of the Institute of Journalists begs unanimously to tender its best thanks to the "Daily News" and" Pall Mall Gazette," for the indepen- dent stand taken against discourtesy to the Press, as recently exemplified at the banquet to Mr. Gladstone at the National Liberal Club." EMIGRATISOL—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan, Aus- tralia, or New Zoaland, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard, Onion, American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent, •• Examiner • Office, Bewsev-st., Warrington.—Advt. A STRUGGLB WITH NIGHT POA.CHBRS.

At the St. Helena County Petty Sessions, on Tues- day. before %fr. W: Pilkington-and Alderman R. Pilkington, Alfred Rothwell, Thomas Houghton and Thomas Garner, three colliers, living at Thatto Heath, were charged with poaching on Lord Derby's estate at Rainford, and the prisoner Houghton was further charged with assaulting Police Constable Simpson. Mr. J. 0. Swift (St. Helens), prosecuted on behalf of Lord Derby,and stated that about half- Past ten on Sunday night last, Police Constable Carer saw the prisoners with a lurcher dog chasing hares. When they, saw the officer they threatened ' that if he followed them he would be thrashed.and thrown into a brook: The Constable accordingly kept some distance away until gamekeeper Barnes, employed by Lord Derby, appeared on the scene. They then seized the three men who became very violent. The constable blew his whistle for assist- ance, and Police Constable Simpson ran to the -pot. ' Simpson took Houghton while the other constable and the gainekeeper kept a hold on Rothwell and Garner. The prisoners, however, were very rough, , and in the struggle Houghton struck Simpson a violent blow with his fist which knocked him to the ground, and the prisonei then kicked him vio- lently about the body. The men were ultimately, secured with some difficulty. The prisoners, who had not been previously convicted for poaching, were each fined .£2 and ,copts,'or one month's im- prisonment, and Houghton was further fined 108. and costs for the assault. SPRING Essinoxs. Spring Fashions.—..T. &W. DUTTON, 16 and 18, Sankey-at., Warrington.—Advt.

div.p: RUNCORN PARISH CHURCH.

Miss Barclay, daughter of the former vicar, has made R handsome Easter offering to Runcorn Parish Church. The gift consists of a beautiful altar cloth, an elaborate brass cross with jewels, and half-a-dozen brass vases for floral decorations.

div.head: TRIPLETS AT RUNCORN.
div.p: TRIPLETS AT RUNCORN.

On Good Friday, Mrs Andrews, wife of a labourer at Weston Point Salt 'Works, who lodges in Penketh-lane, Runcorn, gave birth to triplets; two girls and a boy. The mother and children went or very well until Tues- day morning, when a boy and girl became unwell and died in the course of the day. The Queen's bounty has been applied for.

div.head: SOCIAL TEA MEETING AT WIDNES.
div.p: SOCIAL TEA MEETING AT WIDNES.

A social iahering was held in the Waterloo-road School, on Tuesday evening, in connection with the Wid- nes Parish Church Improvement Society. Between 50 and 60 persons partook of a substantial tea, provided by Mrs. Bray, confectioner, of Widnes. The after proceed- ings were presided over by the Rev. J. Taylor Collins, and songs were given by Misses K. Jones, L. Davies, F. Jovnson, F. Edwards, N. Jones, Messrs. T. Atherton, W. Davies, J. Beattie, Parr, Risley, and Tomlinson. Miss N. Jones acted as accompanist. Games were afterwards indulged in. Bicruns and Tatovouts.—d. S. Garland, :Warrington; Branch, Barleatown. Advt.

div.head: HALTON BURIAL BOARD.
div.p: HALTON BURIAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of the Board was held in the Girl's schoolroom, on Tuesday, the Rev. G. D. Wray in the chair. The following officers were elected to serve the Board for the ensuing year :—Rev. G. D. Wray (chairman), Mr. James Looker (vice-chairman), Mr. H. Rowe (teasurer). Mr. Rutter brought forward the ques- tion of double fees being paid to the sexton for outside parishioners, and it was resolved that the sexton should have the double fees for outsiders. Messrs. Williams and Clay, Warrington, having presented plans of headstones to be erected in the Cemetery for Messrs. Peter Rowlin- son and E. Ruebottom, they were approved. The Chairman having received a letter from the sexton with reference to a complaint having been madeat the Town's meeting by a ratepayer that his wife had been refused admission into the Cemetery, the said ratepayer, Mr. E. Looker, sent an apology to the Board, explaining that he was in error in making the statement, and according- ly withdrew it. -

A CANAL MYSTERY AT RUNCORN. On the 24th March, Cao:ain Stewart, of the S. S. Peri- dot,:of Glasgow, reported to the Runcorn Police that Archibald McGeachy, an able seaman, was missing from the ship. No trace of the missing sailor could be dis- covered, but on Easter Monday when the locks of the Bridgewater Canal were run dry, for the purpose of re- pairing the gates, McGeachy was found wedged between two pieces of wood at the bottom of the rope walk basin., The body was in an advanced state of decomposition. A search of the man's clothes revealed his total possessioas as a broken pocket knife and a halfpenny. On Wednes- day Mr. Worsley held an inquest at the Burial Board office, and a verdict of " Found drowned "was returned. The coroner remarked that this was the first inquest he had held in Runcorn this year. Never during the 15 years he had been connected with these affairs, had there been so long a period without an inquest. It showed a very great improvement. BASINETTES, new designs.—Garland, Ironmonger, War- rington.—.Advt. THEFT Or FOWLS AT FANNWORTH.

- - - Michael Windale, of Farnworth, was brought up in custody at the Widnes Police Court, on Monday, charged with stealing three fowls, valued at 125., the property of William Appleton. Inspector Keighley opened the case for the police, and called Lydia Appleton, the prosecu- tor's wife, who stated that on Saturday night she fastened up the fowls in a cote at the back of the house. The dobr was securely fastened with a padlock, which on the following morning she found had been broken. P.C. Thompson stated that from information he received he went to the prisoner's house, and searched it. In the pantry he found the chisel produced, and found that the marks on the hencote corresponded with the point of the chisel. He found the fowls produced among the flocks in the bed on which the defendant had been lying. He charged the prisoner with stealing them, and he replied, I "I know nothing about them, they were brought in while I was asleep." The prisoner was ordered to pay a fine of 205., or one month in default. SPRING FastrioNs, Spring Fashions.—J. & W. Dorrox, 16 and 18, Sankey-st.. Warrington.—Advt.

, A WIDNES BUTCHER'S EASTER RECREATION. James Williams, a respectably dressed young man, of Albert-road, was summoned to Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, for assaulting John Wm. Hardy, (14), son of a relief signalman on the London and North Western Railway.—Mr. Knowles, who appeared for the complain- ant. said the defendant, although he only 'coked a lad, was a butcher in business for himself, and was married and had a family. On Good Friday the defendant was playing marbles with Hardy and two other boys. Hardy was winning the " stonies," and the defendant got ex- asperated and he called Hardya cheat. He then seized hold of the boy's writ and twisted his arm, and when the boy kicked to release himself the defendant knocked him to the floor with a blow of his fist. He dragged him to his feet by his coat collar, and then felled him to the , ground again. The boy bled from the nose and mouth, 1 and had since suffered pain in his head. The defendant said if the boy had not kicked him on the " shin" and he had not been in a temper, he would not have done it. The Chairman : You will have to pay for your little temper, 10s. and costs 9s. 6d. A WIDNES FARMER AND HIS HORSES.

At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, John Kilsall, sen., farmer, of Lowerhouse-lane, was summoned for causing a horse to be worked while in an unfit state. John Kilsall, jun., his son, was charged with working the animal.—P.C. Almond stated that on the afternoon of the 2nd inst. he saw young Kilsall in charge of two , horses, which were drawing two harrows in a field. A' black horse was lame, and the other horse had almost to drag it along. The horse was in a very poor condition, and weak. He said, "It is a pity to work that horse, John." and the driver replied, • It is ready for the knacker's : but what must Ido ? My father won't buy any more." The constable afterwards saw the father, who said he knew the horse was working.—lnspector i Wilson, R.S.P.C.A.,said the animal was weak,ernaciated, and completely worn out, and hardly able to drag itself along. It was lame on the near hind lea, and blood and matter was oozing from the skin.—Mr. Kilsall, sen.' said he had had 40 years' experience of horses, and the horse in this case had what farmers called a "shake," for which the veterinary surgeon ordered gentle exercise and work. It never worked on the road, but always on soft ground, was well fed, and was treated humanely and kindly.—Kilsall, sen., was fined 40s. and costs 125., and the son was ordered to pay costs, Bs. 6d.

TFIE REV. PETER MACKENZIE AT NIITGROVE. The Rev. Peter Mackenzie, the well-litiown preacher and lecturer, visited Nutgrove on Sunday, and preached to crowded congregations at the Wesleyan Chapel. He also preached In the same place of worship on Monday afternoon. Collections were made on behalf of the trust fund and realized £l6.—On Monday evening he delivered his lecture on "The proverbs of Solomon and others.' The chair was occupied by Dr. Wyse. of. St. Helens, and there were on the platform the Revs. W. Arthur, W. Holroyd, G. Hammond, T. Jackson; Mr. Lee, of Liverpool, and Mr. J. T. Anderton. About .£2O was taken at the door. RUNCORN BOARD OP GUARDIANS.

Colonel Ashton presided on. Tuesday at the fort- nightly meeting of the above-named Board which was held at the Workhouse at Dutton, when there were present.—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner. Messrs. Mc tntyre, Heywood. E. Aaron,J. Baguley, T. Lewis, J. Brandreth, D. FL Jones, W. Wilkinson, Jackson, T. Hewitt, P. Speakman, H. Linaker (clerk), and H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk).
TENDER FOR COAL. The tender of Messrs. Richardson, of Warrington, for coal was accepted.
IMBECILES IN THE WORKHOUSE. The Visiting Committee reported that the imbeciles in the Workhouse, numbering 21, were clean and well- cared for.

div.head: COUNTY COUNCIL AND THB BOARD.
div.p: THE COUNTY COUNCIL AND THB BOARD.

Mr. Brandreth presented the minutes of the Finance Committee, which showed that accounts had been passed for payment of £BO9 Bs. 4d. The amount in the treasurer's hands was £2,896 12s. Bd., which amount had been increased through £1,832 being received from the County Council. A balance was owing to the County Council which the Board were not able to pay for some time. There was no unpaid calls. In the amount of £BO9 Bs. 4d. recommended for payment, £lB3 13s. was for the support of lunatics, 40 of whom were in the asylum. At the beginning of the year there were 43, but three hail since died, there being 20 men and 23 women.—Mr. Mclntyre asked whether that was an increase on previous years. Mr. Brandreth : It is about the same. He noticedthat the accounts were less for grocery and butcher's meat as compared with the corresponding quarter of last year. There had been a decrease of as much as £2O for grocery. He moved that the report be confirmed. Mr. Speakman seconded the proposition, which was carried. • , Mr. Lewis : Have we received all we have to receive from the Cheshire County Council The Deputy Clerk : We have about £9O to receive. VOTRS OF THANKS.

Mr, Brandreth proposed a vote of thanks to the Chair- man for his services during the past year, and observed that he did not think they could ti.aveliad a better chair- man. The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner seconded the proposition, endorsing what Mr. Brandreth had said. Thc motion was carried unanimously. The Chairman returned thanks, and said no chairman could possibly have been better supported than he had been by the members, and any -credit that was due was due to the Board itself. He proposed a vote of thanks to the Vice-Chairmen for their assistance. Mr. Lewis seconded, and on the motion being carried, Mr. Mclntyre, as senior vice-chairman, returned thanks, and said he was perfectly conscious in his own mind, that the vice-chairmen had done no work, and this was owing to the vigilance and regular attendance of the Chairman.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting of the above-named Authority was held at the Workhouse at Dutton on Tuesday, when there were present—The Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, Messrs. Mclntyre, R. Aaron, T. Lewis, J. Brandreth, U. Linaker (clerk), H. G. Linaker (deputy clerk), and J. Farrington (sanitary inspec- tor.) TIE MEDICAL OFFICER'S RE-APFOINTMENT. A letter was read from the Local Government Board Isanctioning the re-appointment of Dr. Adams as medi- cal Officer of health for the union at a salary of £l2O per lannum.

div.head: TYPHOID AND KARIM' ?EVER.
div.p: TYPHOID AND KARIM' ?EVER.

Dr. Adams reported that cases of scarlet fever had broken out at Sutton drid Frodsham. In the first case the infection appeared to have been from Frodsham, and the second case was a descendent of previous cases already notified. A case of typhoid fever had occurred at Cliff View, Frodsham, a widow being the patient. Her three children had been removed to Dutton Workhouse, in order to escape infec- tion and also as a relief. The cause of the disease was obscure, and it was probable that fresh cages might occur. A case of typhoid fever, had also occurred at Netherton, and some slight defects in drainage were dis- covered, and orders were given to remedy them. Another case has occurred be Volunteer-street, Frodsham, where an outbreak of typhoid fever had already been reported.
THE MAIN SEWER AT STOCKTON HEATH. A tender was submitted amounting to £9 for the further improvement of the main sewer at Stockton Heath, and the same was accepted.
NEW NOUSE AT HEMET'.
A certificate of occupation was granted to Mr. Mark Smith for a new house erected by him at Relsby.
NIIISANCRS.

Nuisances were reported as -existing in the townships of Preston-o'ol'-Rill and Helsby, and the Inspector stated that he felt confident that they would be attended to upon the agents' attention being called to them. This was considered to be satisfactory.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS.

A special meeting was held 'on Wednesday even- ing. Mr. J. W. Lightburn presided, and there were present Messrs. P. Speakman; E. Imison, S. Taylor, H. J. Grice, F. A. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor). The Chairman moved that the estimates of the money required for the year ending the 25th March, 1891, be approved :—Estimated expenditure, £5,695; estimated income, £715; amount required, £4,980. He further moved the adoption of the recommendation of the Finance , Committee that a general district rate of 2s. 2d. in the £, is. ld to be collected in the first six months and Is. id. in the second six months. This was an increase of 2d. in the £ over, last year and ws.s accounted for by the increa.seu cost in connec- tion with the 'removal of nightsoil and the provision of new tipping places. There was also the repayment of principal and interest of the cost of the alteration to Waterloo Bridge, and of the proposed new road from Greenway-road to Heath-road.. There was further the cost of the sewerage under the Big Pool. The other ex- penses were practically the same as in previous years. All the figures had been carefully scrutinised; in fact, the members had almost lived in the Boardroom for some time past.—Mr.Taylor seconded the motion.—Mr. Speak- man said throughout his long experience as a Commis- sioner, he never remembered a better working Board than there was at Ne present time. The estimates had been carefully gone through, and if very great care had not been used, they might have had a much higher rate. Grice drew attention to the many improvements being carried out in the town,. and remarked that they could not have the cake and the money too.—The Chair- man said they would reap the advantage of the increased cost by a higher rateable value of property.—The motion was carried.

THE REMOVAL OF NIGHT SOIL. The Health Committee recommended that the removal sof nightsoil be carried out by the Board through its officers, and that 'application be made to the Local Government Board, for its sanction to spread the cost of the appliances over a term of years. It was further recommended that Messrs. Lightburn, Taylor, Speak- man, Wiswall, Meadowcroft, Pritchard, Once, and Imison, be appointed to consider and report as to the practicability of contracting with boatowners for the conveyance of nightsoil over the neighbourhood also to submit recommendations for the purchase of the plant requisite for the carrying out ot the work sanctioned by the Board,—Mr. Taylor moved, and Mr. Speak- man seconded the adoption of these minutes.—The Chairman explained that the reason why the Board had undertaken the onerous duty of dealing with the disposal of nightsoil was simply that the tenders received were so much in excess of previous tenders, and of what the Board anticipated. After con- siderable investigation and ascertaining the cost of other towns in which the local authority had undertaken this duty, the Board came to the unanimous conclusion, that it was to the interest of the ratepayers to do the work themselves. If they had accepted the lowest tender, which was sent in by a contractor, it would have in- creased the rate over 2d. in the £. The Board hdped to save this amount and pertorm.the work better than it had been in the past.—The motion was carried unani- mously.

PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Prescot Board of Guardians was held at the Union Workhouse, Whiston, on Thursday afternoon. There were present the Rev. Dean Finegan (chairman), Rev. S. A. K. Sylvester, Messrs. J. W. Wareing, J. Marsh, J. Ellison, G. E. Chad- wick, G. Davies, J. Burchall, W. Middlehurst, C. B. Johnson, J. Birchall, J. Leatherbarmw, W. Botrows' J. Ranson, J. Peover, H. rbdme, J. Griffiths, J. Mercer, W. Lowe, J. Kenwright, J. Gldsworth, and S. 11. Hartley (clerk.) EXPIANATIONS WkNTED.—Mr. Mercer stated that Dr. Cooper, of Widnes, had ordered a man named Harper into the Workhouse hospital, but on his arrival at the Workhouse, he was ordered by Dr. Hall, the Workhouse medical officer, to go into the body of the house. He thought an exp'anation was desirable from Dr. Hall, and moved that. Dr. Hall be asked to attend the meeting of the Board.—Mr. Middlehurst seconded the motion, which was passed.—Dr. Hall subsequently attended the meeting, and with a subcommittee consisting of the Chairman and Messrs. James Burchall and Marsh, visited the man Harper, who was in the Workhouse hospital. The Chairman, on their return, reported on the explana- tions they had received, and the Guardians considered them satisfactory. , .

div.head: iryn TT 1 c2tl(l
div.p: iryn TT 1 c2tl(l

RELIEF.—The Workhouse Master (Mr. Hale) reported there were 550 inmates of the house this week, 552 last Week, 550 in the corresponding week last- year, and 72 vagrants had been relieved, against 71 last year. 'film ST. HELENS RELIEF OFFICES.—On the recommen- dation of the Building: Committee and the St. Heleas Guardians, it was unanimously resolved that Mr. T. C. Wilcock's offer to provide increased accommodation for relief purposes at St. Helens, at a total rent of £45 a year, be accepted. ' hrroxicArrrs IN THE WORICHOGSE.—A circular letter was read from the Workhouse Drink Reform League, drawing attention to the use of stimulants for paupers and pointing out that thousands of pounds of the funds compulsorily contributed by ratepayers to the poor's rate were annually spent upon intoxicants for the use of inmates of the workhouses of Great Britain. The co-operation of the: Prescot Guardians was sought to realise a uniformly economical use of intoxi- cants in pauper institutions, and it was stated that in the last year for which the Government had published a return the cost of alcoholic stimulants for the 441 inmates of Present Workhouse exceeded that for 11,924 inmates of 52 other British workhouses. The Clerk said the Prescot Union was considerably below the average in the cost of alcoholic drinks. There were 850 workhouses, and only 181 were below them in the cost. The matter was really a medical question. No in- toxina.nts were supplied except what were ordered by the Medical Officer.—The matter then dropped. THE EMIGRATION QUESTION.—A letter was read from the Rev. R. B. Baron, of St. Cieopas' Vicarage, Liver- pool, stating that in June next he expected to sail for Canada in charge of boys for Manitoba, where they would be placed in good homes, and asking if the Board could give permission for four boys who were eligible and three of whom had expressed their willingness to go under his care. The letter was referred to the Visiting Committee. Tan PARR OVERSEERS.—The Clerk entered into a long explanation with reference to remarks made at the Parr township meeting in regard to the precept served upon the overseers. He considered that the overseers were t emselves to blame for the misunderstanding which had arisen. The Board adopted a resolution that the ex- planation was perfectly satisfactory. THE CATHOLIC POOR LAW SCHOOLS.—III reply to Mr. Wareing the Chairman referred to the movement inaugu- rated by the Catholic Bishep of Liverpool for the erec- tion of Catholic Poor Law Schools in the diocese and said it was not intended to be in opposition to any of the existing Union institutions. VOTES OF Tue./qtrs.—This being the concluding meet- ing of the Union business year, hearty votes of thanks were tendered to the Chairman and Vice-chairman, for their services during the past twelve months. This was the principal business. The meeting lasted for a longer period than any previous meeting for many years
pit.

WIDNES FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE. The last meeting of the members of this Cmn- mittee for the financial year just closed was held in the Town Hall, Widnes, on Wednesday afternoon, presided over by Mr. H. Wade Deacon, J.P. The other members present were—Messrs. J. Pankhurst, J. Morrison, D. J. Brooks, W. Sadler, J. Midwood, S. Sadler, .1. T. Allen (clerk), and Miss Proctor (librarian.) —Miss Proctor, in her third annual report, stated that the library and reading room had been epen 302 days during the.past year. The total number of attendances was 154,418, or an average daily attendance of 511, being an increase on the previous year of 14 daily. Three hundred and sixty-nine volumes had been added to the library during the year, 332 by purchase and 37 by gift, making a total of 3,946 volumes in the library. During the year 51,774 volumes had been issued for home reading, and 1,024 for the reading-roots, making a daily aver3ge of 175, a decrease on the previous year of 13 per day. The total number of borrowers now on the register was 2,445. The Chairman pointed out that there was a decrease of something like 5,000 books igsued amongst readers, who were practically the working-classes of the town. The total number of issues last year was 57,678, against 52,798 in the year just closed, or another decrease ot nearly 5,000. The decrease was chiefly in Class C., or books of fiction. The disappointing feature about the report was the decrease amongst the labourers, builders. joiners, and chemical workers, for whom the free library ought to serve. Perhaps there was some reason for it, but he thought the number of books issued ought to have been equal to list year. The Chairman also referred to a belief which seemed to prevail amongst some that the library was not free, and submitted a suggestion from the librarian that cards should be distributed amongst the householders inform- ing them to the contrary.—lt was decided, on the motion of Mr. Morrison, that 6,000 cards be printed and dis- tributed as suggested.—The Chairman said the estimate of the expenditure for the year just closed was £443, and the actual money spent was £442 6s. 7d., which lefts balance in hand of 13s. sd. The estimate for the year 1890-91 was again fixed at £443, which would leave a balance for the purchase of books of about £l2O 6s.—The salary of Miss Walker, the assistant librarian, was in- creased ss. per week.—On the motion of Mr. Sadler, seconded by Mr. Pankhurst, a vote of thanks was ac- corded to the Chairman for his services during the past year.
WIDNES POLICE COURT. I.loNDAY.—Before Messrs. S. Pilkington (chairman)

and H. Wade Deacon. DRUNKENNESS.—Martin Phi!bin, 43, Nelson-st.; Thomas Breet, 91, Midvrond-st. • Catherine Lynch, Warrington- rd. ; Patrick Duffy, 22;Victoria-st.; Richard RaHinson, Sutton's-lane; Margaret Ilardiman, no residence; Bridget Oates, Victoria-st. ' • were each fined ss. and costs, or seven days, for belbug drunk and disorderly. —Martin Riley, for a similar offence, was fiaed 7s. fid. and costs; whilst James Carney, of no settled residence. was ordered to pay 10s. and costs, or in default 14 days, for a like offence. BREACHES OF THE PEACE.—Mary Ann Rollinson and Annie Gallagher both pleaded guilty to creating a breach of the peace, by fighting, on the 6th inst.—Both defend- ants were bound over to be of good behaviour for three months, or in default 14 days' imprisonment. • ASSAULTING THE POLICE.—Mary Jane Riley, of Water- at., was charged in custody with being drunk and dis- orderly at Widnes, on the sth inst., and also with assaulting P.C. Gillies whilst in the execution of his duty. —The police constable stated that shortly after six o'clock on Saturday night, he found the prisoner drunk in Marsh-st. She was making use of indecent language and causing a great disturbance. When he took her into custody she struck him on the clivt and kicked him' about the legs vi 31ent" v.—P. C. Beaton gave corroborative evidence."-Inspector keighley said the prisoner had been fourteen times before the court and this was her seventh appearance since May last.—The prisoner was ordered to pay a fine of 10, and costs for assaulting the police, and ss. and casts for being drunk, or go to gaol for three weeks.

div.head: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. TIIBSDAY.—Before Mr. Henry. Reynolds and Mr. James
div.p: RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. TIIBSDAY.—Before Mr. Henry. Reynolds and Mr. James

Reynolds DRIINRRNNESS.—James Percival Sant, William Week, and Ralph Delight, " scabs " from Liverpool, who said they were on their way home to Birmingham and London, were charged with being drunk and disorderly in Regent- st., and were each fined ss. and costs.—Thomas Corbett, George Taylor and Michael •Burke were each fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly. SIISPICIOIIS.—Thomas Malone, a young man, was charged on suspicion of stealing a harness tug— Inspector Bowyer said on Saturday night the prisoner was going about offering the " tug " for sale, and when arrested he said it belonged to a man named Morris. Morris. however, said it did not belong to him and the police had been unable to find an owner.—He therefore asked that the prisoner be discharged.—Discharged : accordingly. How VAGRANTS ARE MADE.—Caroline Mackey, a middle-aged woman, was charged with causing her son ' Henry Mackey to beg alms. On Saturday night, between eleven and twelve o'clock, P.C. Edwards saw the boy apparently about six years of age, singing in Bridge-st. People who were passing gave him coppers. Subsequently the boy informed Inspector Bowyer that his mother had sent him out to get some money, and he had got sixpence. His mother, he said, got her living by begging in public houses, and she was in Kelly's lodging-house. The Inspector found the woman at that place lying on a form drunk.—lnspector Bowyer said there was no doubt the woman tramped about the country begging.—She was sentenced to seven days hard labour. Inspector Bowyer said he would see the relieving officer with regard to the boy and girl.

WIDNES PETTY SESSIONS. TiacasnAy.—Before Mr. W. L. McClure and Mr. H. Gasket!, jun. Scam. Bastin CASES.—A number of parents were summoned for not sending their children regularly to school, and the usual fine of ss. was imposed in each case. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—Martin Slattery, 23, Nelson- at., Maria Bell, llarrison-St., Ditton, were each fined Ss. and costs for this offence; and Robert Wan-, Walml3leY- st., was fined 7s. 6. and costs.—Catherine Hines, of Marsh-st., made her 23rd appearance and was committed , to gaol for a mon h in default of finding sureties to keep the peace for three months. The woman threatened "to do" si x months for the policeman when she got out. —Mary McDermott, of the Old Marsh, was bound over to be of good behaviour for three months for creating a breach of the peace. STRAY DoGs.—A fine of 2.5. 6d. and costs, 7s. 61, was imposed upon each of the following for allowing his dog to be at large uninuzzled i—John'Lecomber, Victoria- road; John Devereaux, Moss Ban-road; Edward B. Rigby, Elizabeth-terrace, Ditton ; and Ralph Smith, 103, Hurst-st. PITCH AND TOSS.—For playing this game four young men named James Smith, Thomas Smith, James Taylor, and John Tobin, were each fined is. and costs. AN OFFENDING ESYCYCLIST.—CharIes Joseph Johnson, 13, Vine-st., was fined 2s. Bd. and costs for riding a bicycle without a light.
CRITCHLRY, Practical Tailor, Bold-st.,Warrington.—Advt. THE WINLLLIE CYCLE Co.'s Spring-frame machine is uni- versally acknowledged to be the best and cheapest in the market.—Advt.

account so that it could be entered with the rest.—The Vicar said he had not given the churchwardens any return of the Library Charity, because it was in no sense a parochial charity. By reading the inscrip- tion over the door, they would find that the Library was for the benefit of literary men in the neighbourhood and for divines of the Church of England. An opieion had been expressed that it was originally intended for the parish of Halton, but the founder must have been out of his mind if he intended it for that pur- pose as most of the books are written in Latin, and Greek, and one in Hebrew and various other languages, which be could not conceive that the founder ever thought the people of Halton would ever be able to read. The income was £l2 a year which was to be spent in keeping the library in repair, and In that manner it had been spent. The accounts could be seen by anyone who wished to do so. Mr. Tomlinson's proposition was seconded by Mr. J. M. Baguley and carried unani- mously. Votes of thanks to the various officers, the choir, the lay reader (Mr. J. W. Haddock), Mr. Evans, and the Vicar were passed, and the meeting concluded. FRODSHAM PARISH CHURCH.

div.head: , EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS
div.p: , EASTER VESTRY MEETINGS

HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN. The annual vestry was held on Wednesday night, the Rev. Dr. Preston, vicar, presiding. There was a g.ood attendance. Mr. fV. Fisher (vicar's warden), vre.Writed the accounts, which showed that the collections for church expenses amounted to £63 13s. 80., and pew rents realised £lB Bs. 7d., total £B2 2s. lid. The dis- bursements amounted to £I3I 7s. 10d., leaving a balance in hand of 14s. 50. The collections for special objects realised £22 19s. 80. The total number of collections during the year was 106.—The accounts were passed on the motion of Mr. E. Timmins. seconded by Mr. Hankin- son. The Vicar congratulated the parish that for the first time in 18 years there was a balance in hand and showed that although a struggling people, they were yet a progressive people. He tendered his heartiestthanks to the wardens and other officials for their kind co-operation during the year. He spoke in high terms of praise, and appointed him his warden for another year.—Mr. Buckley was unani mously appointed people's warden, but declined to again undertake the office; and proposed Mr. J. Meadowcroft, who was eventually unanimously elected. The following sidesmen Were appointed—Messrs. W. Hankinson A. Salkeld, W. Lea, John Savage, John Buckley, N. Large, R. Kilcross, who with Mr. E. Tim- ' mins and Mr. A. Brigley formed the church council.— Mr. Hankinson and Mr. Fisher were elected lay repre- sentatives to the Diocesan Conferances. The customary votes of thanks were accorded, and the meeting ter- minated.

div.head: ST. AMBROSE'S CHURCH, WIDNES.
div.p: ST. AMBROSE'S CHURCH, WIDNES.

. The annual Easter vestry meeting of St. Ambrose's Parish, Widnes, was held in the vestry on Wednesday evening, presided over by the Vicar, the Rev. S. A. Le Bert. There was a good attendance. The Vicar's Warden (Mr. Johnson) submitted the statement of accounts for the year just closed. They commenced the year with a balance in hand of £4 14s. 11d., the offer- tories had amounted to £Bl 13s. 2d., and the total receipts to £l3B Is. id. The total expenditure was £132 35.. which left a balance in hand of £6 is. The Vicar expressed his pleasure at seeing them again, and referred,to the death of an old member of the council, Mr. Lee. During the year they had had two distinct additions to the church, namely, the decorations of the chancel, which cost £lOO, and the erection of a bell by Mr. and Mrs. G. J. Neil, which had been given unfettered by any condition, and for which he felt sure they were all thankful, as well as to those who had helped through- out the past year. He nominated Mr. Johnson again as his warden, stating that he desired no change.— Major Wareing moved the adoption of the accounts. Mr. Beech seconded the motion, which was carried.—Mr. Valentine proposed Major Waring as people's warden for the ensuing year, which was seconded by Mr. Williams, and carried.—The follow- ing gentlemen were appointed sidesmen : Vicar's nominees, Messrs. Booth, Warner, Pankhurst, Hirst, Foster, Beech, Goff, Carlile, and Kidd. Parishioners' nominees, Messrs. Mercer, Minton, Niel, Pile, Riley, Shuttleworth, Smith, Valentine, and J. J. Latham.— Messrs. Niel and Christie were unanimously appointed lay representatives, on the motion of Major Wareing and Mr. Williams.—The usual vote of thanks concluded the proceedings.

div.head: WIDNES PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: WIDNES PARISH CHURCH.

_ The annual meeting of the vestry of the parish of Widnes, which includes St. Mary's and St. Paul's churches, was held on Tuesday evening, in the National Schools, Waterloo-road, and was well attended. The Vicar (Rev. G. H. St. Patrick Garrett) presided.—Mr. H. N. Wharton submitted the balance sheet from St. Mary's Church, which showed the income for the year to have been £B6 12s. 30., of which £72 19s. 70. was from offertories. The total expenditure was £B3 9s. 30., which left a balance in hand of £3 98. 3d.—Mr. F. Neil, representing St. Paul's Church, said the expenditure for the year just closed had been £2O less than in the pre- vious year, but there had been a corresponding falling off in the offertories. There was a balance due of £2 us. 100.—On the motion of Mr. Beech, seconded by Mr. Beattie, the accounts were passed.— The Chairman after referring to losses by death, said he thought the Easter vestry meeting was a very particular time for bringing prominently before them the laymen's stake. The church was not the clergy's, but theirs. It belonged to the people and they had a right to exercise their franchise and privilege. He felt thankful to God that he had been spared to meet them, and for their kindness, help, and cordiality in the work of the past year. He concluded by nominating Mr. F. Neil as his warden.—Mr. Dwerryhouse proposed the re-election of Mr. Wharton as people's warden.—Mr. Ward seconded the motion.—Mr. Wharton said it was his decided wish that a change should be made in the election of people's warden for the ensuing year. He proposed that Mr. Dwerryhouse be elected people's warden.— Mr. Tracey seconded the motion, which was supported by Mr. Beach.—Mr. Dwerryhouse was then elected almost unanimously.—Mr. Beech proposed that Mr. Wharton and Mr. Kilcrass be elected lay representatives for the current year.—The resolution • was seconded by Mr. Beattie, and carried.—The following gentlemen were elected sidesmen and members of the Church Council :—St. Mary's : Parishion- ers' nominees, Messrs. W. Treacy, T. Bruce, J. Farrant, J. Ward, F. Beattie, and D.J. Brooks. Vicar's nominees: Messrs. W. Chadwick, J. Hartland, J. L. Brissoe, A. Borthwick, Frank Cave, and J. Starkie. St. Paul s Church: Vicars' nominees : Messrs. R. Carlile, J. Hutchinson, W. Lowe, J. Williams, Thomas Hughes, and James Burrows. Parishioners' representatives: Messrs. A. Beech, Adam Case, R. Faulkner, J. Treacy, S. Upward, and S. Arnell. Mr. G. Joynson (vestry clerk), and Messrs J. Farrant and W. Treacy (auditors), were also re-appointed. The Vicar exhibited a neat drawing cf the new Parochial Room, by Mr. Paul Ogden, archi- tect, of Manchester, and pointed out the wing of the building which it was proposed to designate the" Imison Memorial Room." He said they had at present £750 clear in the bank, and the building was estimated to cost £1,750. At least £2,000 would be required to build, furnish, and complete it, which left them £1,200 to get by June next, when he hoped to start the building. Out of that £1,200 Mr. Timmis had intimated his intention to give one-half of the sum, on condition that they raised the remainder. He hoped they would all earnestly take the matter up. The usual votes of thanks were passed.

div.head: HALTON PARISH CHURCH.
div.p: HALTON PARISH CHURCH.

The annual meeting of parishioners was held in the girls schoolroom on Tuesday evening. The Rev. G. D Wray, the vicar, occupied the chair, and amongst those present were Messrs. C. L. Evans, J. Stokes, T. Wright, J. W. Haddock, J. Peacock, Rutter, J. M. Baguley, J. Pritchard, J. Baguley, B. Haddock.

TELE ACCOUNTS. Mr. T. Wright read the churchwardens accounts, which showed that the total receipts amounted to £175 15s. 4frd. and after paying all expenses there was a balance in hand of £29 Ss. aid.

WARDENS AND SIDEMEN. The Vicar nominated Mr. T. Wright AA his warden for the ensuing year. Mr. Wright had discharged his duties in a most efficient manner in the past, and he should be glad to have his assistance in the future.—Mr. Wright said he should be very pleased to do what he could.—Mr. Evans proposed that Mr. Stokes be the people's warden. No person could better fill the posi- tion. (Applause.) Mr. .1. M. Ba,s,ruley seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously.—Mr. stokes thanked the vestry for the honour conferred upon him and said he would endeavour to give satisfaction in the future as he hoped he had in the past. (Applause.) The following sidesmen were appointed: Messrs J. Rutter, J. Ackersley. J. M. Bagulev, E. Buckley, William Nickson, and J. Hougliton.—The churchwardens were appointed , lay representatives for diocesan purposes. THB CHARITIES.

The Vicar said the accounts of the charities of the township had been asked for, and a return had been made to the churchwardens, and Mr. Evans was present to answer any question that might be asked. This was simply a matter of courtesy. It was a right of every ratepayer to seethe accounts and there was no desire to conceal anything.—Mr. Tomlinson said he brought forward the matter at the meeting of ratepayers in order that past irregularities might be swept away. Ere moved a vote of thanks to the Vicar and the trustees for their prompt attention.—The Vicar said in future a statement would be forthcoming at the annual rneeting of rate- payers.—Mr. Wright said the accounts had been rendered to the Charity Commissioners every year, and they would have been produced to the ratepayers if they had been asked for. He gave the following statement of the charities :—Bolton's Charity : received one year's rent of Bolton's field £9, paid ; St. Thomas' Charity £3 ; Halton Grammar School, £3; Vicar of Halton £3. Eaton's Charity: cash Mr. Robert Davies and CO., £6 15s. 14., paid. St.Thomas's Charity £3 7s. 6d.; Halton Grammar School, £37s. 74. St. • Thomas's Charity: balance in , hand £1 6s. 4d., received from Bolton's Charity, £3 ; Eaton's Charity. £3 7s. 64. ; Mersey Docks and Harbours Board, one ypar's interest £l5 2s. 44. total £22 16s. 2d. Distributedl 2nd December, 1889, £2O 19s. 6d. and there was a balance in hand of £1 16s. 2d. Stock- ham Charity ; balance in hand £74 16s. 94., received from Mr. Linaker £6; total £BO 16s. 9d. Paid for adver- tising Commissioners' notice 17s. 4d. leaving a balance in haid of £79 19s. sd.—Vicar and wardens Coal Charity showed a balance in hand of £1 103. lid.—Mr. Wright said he had attended St. Thomas's Charity meeting for 20 years !Ind the money was distributed very carefully without regard to creed.—The Vicar and the Stockham Charity was for the poor widows of Stockham but there were none and thus the money had accumulated. It was for widows who are members af the C:mre.h of England, and was a secterian charity in the strictest sense of the word.—Mr. Evans said there was a scheme before the Charity Commissioners with regard to this charity. There was one charity which he had left off the list read by Mr. Wright. It was the Almshouse Charity left' by John Brooke in 1771. It brought in an income sufficient to pay each tenant of the almshouses 3s. 64. per week, but Sir Richard Brooke made the sum up to 4s. per week. Under the original deed all the cost of repairs should come out of the fund, but Sir Richard had always defrayed the cost of repairs out of his own pocket. It was a private charity rather than a public one, as Sir Richard,or the owner of Norton propertv,had full control. He, however, promised to let Mr. Wright have an

div.head: MR. FOULKES TO THE FORE-LIVELY SCENE.
div.p: MR. FOULKES TO THE FORE-LIVELY SCENE.

The annual vestry meeting in connection with Prod- sham Parish Church was held on Monday, in one of the side chapels. The vicar, Rev. H. B. Blogg, presided, and there was a good attendance ; amongst those present being Colonel Ashton, Messrs. H. Linaker, D. c. E. Linaker, H. G. Linaker, G. H. Danby, J. B. Holland, T. Riley, S. Davies, T. Lewis, H. G. Heywood, C. Timmins. Robert Foulkes, &c.
MR. FOITLEES' FIRST OBJECTION.

Mr. Robert Foulkes, at the outset, said if there were any persons present except ratepayers and reporters, they had no right there.—The Vicar's Warden (Mr. C. E. Linaker) said any parishioner had a perfect right there, but he could not vote unless he was a ratepayer. Surely a parishioner had as much right to be there as a reporter.

div.head: ACCOUNTS.
div.p: THE ACCOUNTS.

The Vicar's Warden then read the accounts, which showed a balance on the wrong side. The receipts showed that the Parish Church offertories realised £l5l ss. 2d., and special collections had been taken as follows: —Chester Diocesan House of Mercy, £4l7s. 9d.; National School, £ll 4s. 9d.; Church Missionary Society, £l2 19s. ad.; Chester Diocesan Society, £lO ks. Bd.; Chester Infirmary, £l6 13s. 6d.; Church Temperance Society, £8 195.; Church Sunday Schools, £9 3s. 3d. ; Curate's Augmentation Fund, £l3 13s. 2d. The total receipts were £284 16s. sd. The payments included sexton, £4O; organ blower, £4; choir, £24 17s. 10d. ; ringers, £22 119 s. 3d.; lighting, £l3 4s. 7d.; heating, £lO 9s. id. ; washing surplices, £5 us. 6d.

div.head: SURPLICES.
div.p: SURPLICES.

Mr. H. Linaker referred to the item of £24 for the choir. He thought they had a voluntary choir.—Vicar's Warden: So we have; but we have to pay the boys and provide for them. We have had to buy new surplices and pay £5 for teaching the boys.—The Vicar said each boy received half-a-crown a quarter.—Mr. Foulkes: Surplices might be done away with and save that cost.— Mr. R. G. Linaker : That is a matter of opinion.—Mr. Foulkes: They are not required for devotion.—Mr. 11. Linaker : That is not the question before the meeting. It is a question of accounts, and I move that they be passed.—Mr. Riley seconded the motion, which was carrind.

div.head: TIE CHARITIES.
div.p: TIE CHARITIES.

The accounts of the Frodsham and Stockham Charity were presented by Mr. H. Linaker, and showed that the rent of the land had been received. One moiety had been paid over to the Stockham trustee, Mr. Evans, and the other £6 had been distributed amcngst six widows, according to the requirements of the trust. The Vicar reported that with regard to the Harrison Charity £2 19s. Bd. had been received from dividend on the amount invested and had been distributed on Christmas day. The Organ Trustees account showed a balance in hand of £39 4s. 4d. Mr. Pollard reported that on Overton Sunday School account, there was a balance of 19s. 6d.

div.head: BOTTOM SCHOOL.
div.p: THE BOTTOM SCHOOL.

Mr. Foulkes asked where were the accounts of the bottom school. A resolution was passed two years ago that they should be presented.—Vicar's Warden : We will make you a deputation to ask Miss Crosfield to present them.—Mr. Foulkes said ke had no objection to the way in which the school was managed, but he thought it was a downright shame that the vicar should take upon himself, without consulting Miss Crosfield, to send any teacher out of that school.—The Vicar said he had no doubt Miss Crostield would let Mr. Foulkes see the accounts.—Mr. Foulkes said they should be presented in a business-like manner.
A HANDSOME LEGACY.
The Vicar's warden reported that an old parishioner, Mr. Wm. Upton, had left a legacy of £6OO to the parish, the proceeds of which were to be distributed e mongst the poor.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF OFFICERS.

The Vicar re-appointed Mr. C. E. Linaker as his war- den, and spoke of him in high terms of praise.—Mr. Linaker suitably acknowledged the honour.—Dr. Robin- son was re-elected parishioners' warden, and the Vicar's warden nominated Mesrss. G. Gleave and H. E. Hey- wood as Vicar's sidesmen, and on the motion of Mr. Danbv, seconded by Mr. Lewis, Messrs. Watson and Bate were re-elected parishioners' sidesmen.—Messrs. A. Pollard and Samuel Davies were appointed auditors.

THE LAY REPRESENTATIVES. Mr. H. Linaker asked for a report from the lay repre- sentatives to the Diocesan Conferences, but it transpired that only one representative had attended, and he was not present.

div.head: FLOWERS AND DISTRACTION.
div.p: FLOWERS AND DISTRACTION.

Votes of thanks were accorded to the various office- bearers. The Vicar proposed that a vote of thanks be accorded to the ladies who had so kindly presented and arranged the flowers.—Mr. H. G. Linaker seconded.— Mr. Foulkes said they could not find in St. Paul's In- structions to the Churches that they had to have flowers inside. Flowert might do very well in a Roman Catholic church, but in the Church of England they were out of place. In that church they had a cross which was not legal, and to get out of it they had to put up a little rear • table, lie moved tlrat the ladies keep their flowers at heme, as they were not required for the purposes of worship, and tended to distract the mind.—Vicar's War- den : Some people's minds are quite distracted with other things, Mr. Foulkes.—The Vicar : lam sorry Mr. Foulkes's mind is distracted by anything of the sort.— Mr. Foulkes (hotly) : It is not distracted. The Vicar's might be distracted if you took that cross out there.— Mr. Foulkes did not find a seconder, and the vote of thanks was accordect—The Vicar said he had the inte- rgst of the parish at heart, and his great desire was that they should have a service which would redound to the honour and glory of God, In this great wish he had the support of the wardens and sidesmen.
HYMNS AND POPBUY.
MR. FOULKES EXCITED.

Mr. Foulkes, amid interruption, proposed that a new hymnbook be introduced into the church instead of "Hymns Ancient and Modern," at present in use.— Mr. H. G. Linaker made some remark as to Mr. Foulkes now attending another place of worship, and Mr. Foulkes retorted that he was a ratepayer and as good a Church- man as any man in the vestry. There were lies in the Hymns Ancient and Modern, which he had come there to prove. Hymn 318 taught the doctrine that Christ is priest, a victim in the Eucharist feast, but in Hebrews 14 it was stated that if Christ were on earth again He could not be priest. There was a direct lie.—Mr. H. Linaker : I hold that preaching belong S to a certain class, and not to a layman. If Mr. Foulkes has anything to propose, let him propose it, and not give us a sermon. —Mr. Foulkes : I am proposing it, and if you don't like to hear what I have to say you should stop at home. (Laughter.) In hymn 349 it was stated that Christ dwelt in temples made with hands. Now the Acts of the Apostles said—Mr. They : Make your proposition.—Mr. Foulkes : You are a paid servant of this vestry,' and you ought merely to come and sit down—Mr. Heywo•d: Is there a proposition P—Mr. Foulkes : Yes, there is a prcposition.—rhe Vicar : Well, put it down.—Mr. Foulkes was proceeding to state that there were 109 Popish hymns in the Hymns Ancient and Modern, but there were interruptions from every quarter, and Mr. Foulkes said he would not be put down by Vicar or any- one else; and a parishioner asked if he proposed to make a night of it. (Laughter.,—Vicar's Warden : If we don't wish to hear what you have to say what do you mean to do ?—Mr. Foulkes said he had every right to be heard.—A Parishioner: If you will get a seconder, I will propose an amendment.—Mr. H. G. Linaker : We don't want a speech.—Mr. Foulkes : You don't want facts. —Mr.. H. G. Linaker : I don't want your facts.—The parishioner: You are going to Communion somewhere else.—Mr. Foulkes: lam as good as you and I don't want to be driven into Popery .—Vicar's Warden: If you would bring some one here to support you, it would be better; but you have not a single supporter in the vestry.—Mr. Foulkes: There are people here who will support me.,—Vicar's Warden : Then get them to second the motion.—Mr. Foulkes: I have proved lie No. I.—Mr. Heywood : Don't use such language here.—The Vicar : The language is quite out of keeping in church.—Mr. Foulkes (excitedly): It is not more out of keeping than you teach- ing lies on a Sunday.—The Vicar: If no one wishes to second this resolution it is at an end.—The Vicar : I move we go on to the next business.—Mr. Foulkes : That isnot fair ;it is a Jeusuitical trick.—Vicar's Warden : I will not stop and hear you.—The meeting then broke up, a vote of thanks being, hurriedly passed to the vicar for presiding.—Mr. Foulkes, who at the outset was a considerable dikance from the chairman, had advanced step by step in his excitement until he was almost touch- ing the table, and as the parishioners were leaving the sacred edifice he used seine strong expressions, for which he'avas reproved by the vicar. Finding no one would. listen to him, Mr. Foulkes departed.

Mr. H. M. Stanley arrived at Brindisi from Cairo on Thursday, and left for Naples the same evening. The sub-Prefect and Mayor,with the secretary and two mem- bers of the Italian Geographical Society, went on board the Hydaspes to welcome Mr. Stanley, and present thei gold medal awarded to him by the society.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

THE LODGER HAD AN OBJECTION. On Wednesday, at the Warrington Police Court, Peter Eden, a forgeman, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly inFlorence-St., Latchford, on the previous evening; and with having caused wilful damage to a door to the amount of 6s. 6d. It was stated that the prisoner's landlady had recently been married. The lodger seems to have taken offence at this, and exhibited his disappointment by getting drunk and kicking one of the panels of the front door. He pleaded guilty, and was ordered to pay a fine of 108. and costs, including the amount of the costs.

div.head: LOCKED UP ON SUSPICION.
div.p: LOCKED UP ON SUSPICION.

Matthew Callaghan, shoemaker, last from Stockport, and Margaret Clark, last from Widnes, were brought up in custody, on remand, at the Warrington Police Court, on Tuesday morning on a charge of having offered in pledge at the Tower, Bridgefoot, on Thursday evening in last week, a pair of men's boots, regarding their posses- sion of which they did not give a satisfactory account. They were also charged with having in their possession a number of pairs of shoes supposed to have been stolen. From a statement made by Mr. Hunt, the Chief Con- stable, it appeared that the boots were in the possession of the male prisoner, who made the acquaintance of the female prisoner in a vaults at Warrington. They sent a woman to pledge a pair of boots, and the suspicions of the pawnbroker being aroused, he communicated with the police. It was found on inquiry that Callaghan had a number of other boots in his possession, and the couple were locked up on suspicion. Callaghan now asserted that he bought the goods at a public auction in Man- chester. The Bench considered that the case was one of suspicion, but they did not think there was sufficient evidence to commit them upon any positive charge. They would, however, be bound over to appear if called upon, and in the meantime the boots would be retained by the police.

THB GIRL KLEPTOMANIAC. A girl of about 20 years of age, whose parents live nea:r Manchester, and who gives the name of Edith Walworth, was brought up on remand at the Warrington Police Court, on Saturday, on a charge of wandering in Irlam-street without visible means of subsistence. Early on Wednesday mprning a policeman found her sitting on some steps in Irlam-street, and took her to the police station for safe custody. A few hours later she was brought before the magistrates, who were informed by the Chief Constable that the girl had been sent to prison for eight months for stealing something, and that she told him it would be useless for her to go home, as her parents would not receive her. She made threats as to what she would do to herself, and seemed to nave got the idea that she was without a friend in the world. She was, without a doubt, troubled with kleptomania, which seemed to be her only fault. When she saw a thing she could not help taking it. Under these circum- stances the case was remanded until Baturday, when the girl adhered to the opinion that her parents would not have her at home, although she would be willing to go. The Bench granted a further remand, instructing the Chief Constable to communicate with the parents. On Monday the Bench discharged the prisoner, and she was given money with which to go home, but it was stated that her father had expressed himself as unwill- ing to receive her.

WARRINGTON. STRONG COMMENTS BY THE CORONER.

Mr. Brighouse held an inquest at the Unicorn Inn, on Saturday, on the body of Mary Ellen Little- fair, (4), daughter of Thomas Littlefair, alebrewer, living at 39, Watkin-st. As narrated in our last issue, the deceased went, on Thursday after- noon, with several other children to a brickpit (belonging to Messrs. E. Bolton, Sons) off Orford-lane, to catch " jacksharps." The deceased slipped into the water and was drowned before assistance could be obtained. One of the witnesses who was called (Mrs. Elizabeth Morris) characterized the pit as "a disgrace to the town."—lnspector Spinks said one or two persons had been drowned in the same pit during the past ten years.—The caretaker for Messrs. Bolton and Sons was in attendance, but as he could not say what the firm intended to do to prevent accidents in the future, the Coroner told him it would have been more decent if Mr. Bolton had attended the inquest, or sent a solicitor to represent him. It was all very pretty to say the pit was on private pro- perty, but they did not livein this world to be guided by legal principles exactly. They did many things in this world they were not legally bound to do. It was per- fectly ridiculous to remain passive and allow these chil- dren to be drowned. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and added the following present- ment :—"That, considering the number of persons who have been drowned in the pit, the jurors think Messrs. Edward Bolton and Sons ought to take immediate steps to have the pit fenced and railed round in such a manner that will prevent children getting into the same." The Coroner, at the close of the inquest, visited the pit, and on his return said it was a frightful place. He would communieate with the Town Clerk, and ask if the Cor- poration could interfere under any of their bye-laws. If they could not do so, the. matter would, he added, have to be left to Mr. Bolton's sense of right. It should be added, that it was stated during the inquiry, that Messrs. Bolton had put up a fence round the pit, but it did not prevent the children getting to the water side.
