Secretaries of Football Clots are requested to note that reports of matches Vlayed on Saturday must be sent to the head office, Bewsey-street, Warrington, not later than ten o'clock on Wednesday morning.
RUGBY. RUNCORN "A" V. LANCASTER.—On Monday, the Run- corn" A" team met Lancaster at Runcorn, on the Irwell-

4ane ground, when there was a large number of specta- tors. The game throughout was of an interesting i , description, and resulted n a win for Runcorn, the score being Runcorn, one goal, one try, to two tries. WIDNES V. WORTLEI7.—A match between these teams took place at Widnes on Tuesday evening and there was a good attendance of spectators. In consequence of the high wind, the game was divided into four quarters. The home team had the upper hand throughout and retired the victors by one goal, seven tries, and two minors to nil. Clarke, Brennan, and Peters were the principal try getters. RUNCORN "A " v. TUEBI;00/{.—On Saturday, in splendid weather, these teams played the return match at Runcorn. The play for a time was of an even nature, during which Pendlebury for Runcorn and Morris for Tuebrook shone conspicuously. Davies punted, and after a scrimmage Hollingsworth passed to Crompton, who dropped a splendid goal. The visitors were severely pressed, but eventually succeeded in relieving the pressure, and forced their way to the centre, where scrimmages ensued, and the visitors attacked the home lines in a determined manner. The result being that „ . . .

Ellams grounded the ball over the Runcorn line, Eccles then put in a goal. Pendlebury subsequently scored a try near the corner flag, the result of some fine passing between May, Lee, and himself. Riley also crossed over but the kicks at goal failed. The second part of the game was equally exciting, and the result was ; Run - corn, 2 goals, 3 tries, and 2 minors ; Tuebroolc, 1 goal, 1 try, and 2 minors. WIDNES v. ASPIILL.—The return league fixture be- tween Widnes and Aspull was piayed on the Widnes ground, in Lowerhouse-lane, on Saturday, before about 2,000 spectators. Smith started the ball for the home team. Brennan failed to take a pass, which placed the Widnes line in danger. Peters, however, relieved, and showed excellent form throughout the game. Brennan next attempted at goal, but the ball went wide. Peters made his mark in the visitors' quarter, but the ball fell rather short. The kick was followed up, and Gordon subsequently got over the line, but the point was not improved upon. Smith for the visitors next got over but was called back. At half-time the score was—Wid nes, one try and two minors, to the one minor. On changing ends, Stubbs headed a aribble to the visitors' line, when a scrimmage ensued, from which Gordon got possession, and scored. Brennan again failed at goal. A penalty kick was given to Widnes for the visi- tors' full back holding the ball, from which Farrell kicked a goal. The home team continued to have the best of the game, when Clarke secured in his own quar- ter, and made a magnificent run from line to line, tack- ling and dodging his opponents in a manner which called forth the enthusiastic cheers of the spectators. The place kick proved successful, and the game ended in a brilliant victory for Widnes by two goals, two tries, and two minors, to Aspull one minor; or 24 points to one. Teatns—Widnes : Hartles, back; Peters, Brennan, and Clarke, three-quarter backs ; Farrell and McGurl, half backs ; Gordon, Hewitt, Stubbs' Whelan, Pearson, Farmer, Smith, Gandy, and Carroll, forwards. Aspull : Taylor, back; Roberts, Birchall, and Morris, three- quarter backs ; Cartwright and Taylor, half backs; Webster, Turner, Lindsay, Mulroy, Nicholson, Smith, I Monks, Pilkington, and Mather, forwards.' Referee. Mr. Seddon, Broughton Rangers. WIDNES v. MOSSLBY.—The return match between Widnes and Mossley was played at Widnes, on Monday, in beautiful weather. Widnes won the toss, and elected to play with the wind. The visitors were at once called upon to defend. Brennan passed to Clarke, who got over, but no goal resulted. From the drop out Peters returned to the line, where a scrimmage ensued and Brennan got over. The kick at goal again failed. Whelan next got possession in the loose in the visitors' 25, and scored the third try, Farrell this time placing a goal. Peters was next conspicuous after receiving a pass from Howard, and scored easily, but the goal kicking was still faulty. At half-time the score was Widnes one goal, three tries, and two minors to nil. On i• tri4ing ends the visitors had the wind at their back, and play now assumed a very even nature. Hartles and Stubbs saved

some pressure, and Brennan got possession from a scrim- mage opposite the home goal, but failing to get through passed to Clarke, who grounded the ball behind the posts. Farrell again did the needful. Hartles saved, after which Brennan again got away, but the ball was oalled back. Some pressure on the part of the visitors was relieved by Gordon and Hewitt, and from a scrimmage opposite the home goal, Brennan got the leather, and successfully passed the visitors' backs, and groun6led the ball behind the posts. Farrell again took the place kick, which was successful. Just before the call of "no time," Howard scored a try, but the attempt at goal was futile. The game ended in an easy victory for Widnes by three goals, four tries, and three minors, to Mossley two minors. Teams :—Widnes, Hartles' back; Clarke, Brennan, and Peters, three-quarter backs; Howard and Farrell, half- backs; Stubbs, Pearson. Whelan, Smith, Carroll, Gor- don, Holt, Gandy, and Hewitt, forwards. Mossley : Taylor, back; Halton, Lawton, and Pichford, three- quarter backs; Pilling and Mills, half-backs: Batley, Barker, J. Corscadden, A. Corscadden, M. Bowman, J. W. Newby, S. Dawson, H. Halliwell, and Coke, for- wards. Referee, Mr. A. B. Dewhurst.

WARRINGTON "A " V. STOCKPORT "A."—The first fix- ture between the above "A " teams was played at Stockport, on Saturday, before a large concourse of spectators, numbering quite 3,000. Warrington won the toss, and Stockport kicked off. Fine open play was wit- nessed on the visiting side, Thorniley, Ashton, and Russell, particularly distinguishing themselves ; Thornley eventually raced over the line, Heesom placing a pal. Knowles returned the kick off, and the home backs mulling. Heesom and Rowe followed up the ad- vantage gained. From some infringement of the rules the homesters were allowed a free kick, but Heesom re- turned to Downes, who mulled ; and the visiting for- wards hastily followed up the advantage gained by dribbling to the line) Thornley grounding safely. Isher- wood, however, failed at goal. Rowe sprinted nicely, but failed to pass at the right moment, and a good oppor- tunity was lost. Eventually, however, Thorniley ran in somewhat easily, Heesom placing a second goal. The Stockport forwards seemed again to liven up and t combine better, for Morley and Imison broke away and dribbled neatly. Again good passing among the home backs gained ground, Hockenall spoiling by throwing forward. With a good dribble, Ashton and Isherwood retaliated, but Rowe spoiled a good chance by passing forwards. Kicks were how exchanged between the res- pective backs, and eventually Ashton, with an excellent dribble safely piloted the ball over the line, Isherwood failing to add the premier point. The pace seemed now to increase ; determination and pluck on the homesters' part was at length rewarded, for Goodall scored at the corner flag, Mills making a splendid attempt at goal. Half time was called, the score showing that Warrington had 2 goals, 2 tries to their credit, while Stockport had one try, Thorniley restarted and Beard charged down, and the home team gained a slight advantage, which Webster finally alleviated. After a smart run, Lally tackled Hockenall, but Downes following up the advantage forced the visitors to concede a minor. Through a mistake by Sampson, Heathcote scored rather an easy try, Downes failing to increase the point. This reverse somewhat stirred up the visiting forwards, for Ashton, Russell, and Bate came away beautifully with the ball among them, thus gaining considerable ground. Hockenall essayed a drop at goal, adding a minor to the score. The visiting forwards now dribbled nicely to half-way, but Stockport playing vigorously soon neutralized the benefit gained Downes sprinted along touch, but Thorniley and Davies gradually worked the leather back again. So.ne loose play ended by Goodall and Beard making strenuous efforts to cross the visitors' line, Webster and Knowles tackling and saving respectively. After some spirited and energetic play, time was called with the score : Warrington, two goals, two tries ; Stockport, two tries, two minors. Teams : —Warrington Full back, Sampson; three-quarter backs, Webster, Heeson, Lally; half backs, Knowles, Rowe ; forwards, Thorniley (captain), Ashton, Nield, Isherwood, Russell, Oxley, Davies, Bate, Wilkinson. Stockport : full back, Goodall ; three-quarter backs. H. Downes, Burrows, Brookes ; half backs, Hockenall, Ligatt ; forwards, Mason (captain), Mills, Marsley, J. Downes, Robert Downes, C. Goodall, Beard, Morley. WARRINGTON v. MARYLEBONE.

Continuing their Easter tour, the Marylebone (London) club encountered the Warringtonians on their spacious enclosure at Wilderspool. Fully 5,000 holiday-seekers partook of the afternoon's sport, and Marylebone losing the toss, Lumley kicked off towards the pavillion goal, the homesters having the advantage of a strong wind. Boscow's reply found the game at half-way flag, but some strong forward work by the visitors caused Warrington some anxiety. Evans strove hard to relieve the pressure, but the tackling was of too safe a nature to allow of the desired effect. A slight mistake by Fowler gave the Warringtonians a footing in the opposing 25 but from a pack, a rush by the visiting forwards again called upon Boscow, but the home custodian was exceptionally safe. Some ground gained by Barnes and Massey was neutralized by the loose play which immedi- ately followed, and the visitors taking advantage of the many mistakes and careless play of Warrington, once more took the oval to near the pavillion goal. Thorniley came away from a pack, and dribbling past Williams, a certain chance of scoring presented itself, but being joined in the movements by his colleagues, apparent eagerness spoiled the opportunity. However, as time went on, the play improved, and from a smart rush of the home forwards the visiting defence was broken through, and Fair. Turner scored the first point of the match, his brother failing to augment the point. Following the drop-out, Littlewood and

Dillon spoiled Pilkington, and again the Marylebene goal was endangered. Judicious kicking on the part of Bruce improved the visitors' position, but Dillon running in fine style took play to the half-way flag, only to see Draper throw across to Fowler, who, with an excellent run, brought the teams on level terms. A huge drop- out by Frank Turner sent the oval well into the London 25, where Barnes got clean away, after" Williams" and Bate had exhibited some rare passing. Barnes' final pass, however, was not taken, and although Bate a moment later got away, the coveted point was not to be scored until a spell of grand passing by "Williams," Barnes, and Massey resulted in the latter scampering round his opposing three-quarter, and baffling Williams, he wound up a grand piece of work by scoring near the corner flag, Frank Turner again failing at the place kick. From the reply to the drop out Bruce made his mark, but the advantage gained was promptly neutralized by "Williams "and Bate, who passed neatly, working the oval in clever fashion to the Marylebone line. Barnes essayed a drop at goal, but the shot going wide, Evans rushed up at top speed, and taking advantage of the hesitating of the visiting backs, gathered in grand style, and succeeded in placing the third try to his side's credit, Barnes this time placing the goal. Thorniley charged the kick off, and Barnes and Massey each in turn almost got in. W. Dillon headed a dribble of the Warrington forwards, and a minor being forced, half-time was called with the score as War- rington, 1-2-1; Marylebone, 0-1-0. Now that the visitors had the .wind in their favour, the chances pointed to a game of a more even nature ; but Warrington, who had displayed anything but their proper form during the first portion of the game, now set to work in a determined manner. Frank Turner's kick-off was followed by a grand piece of work by Bate and Evans, and " Williams" missed a rare chance. Bate tricked through the opposing defence, and being ably seconded by Berry, the visitors'defence was severely tested. Williams got the oval away in grand style, but the relief was only momentary, for after Fair. Turner, Donohue, and Berry had effected a smart dribble, a grand piece of work by Evans and Massey sent the oval to Fowler, who mulled, and Donohue snapping the oppor- tunity, galloped over the line, but through some previous informality the point was disallowed. Warring ton had some satisfaction shortly after, for the forwards rush- ing through the defence set against them, brushed aside all oppositien, and Littlewood succeeded in gain- ing a try near the posts, Barnes, with his usual precision, kicking a goal. The visitors were now a beaten team, and Warrington, who seemed to be getting into some- thing like working order, forced the pace, and Fair. Turner putting in a strong run all but scored. Eventually Bate passed across a scrimmage to "Wil- liams," and the last-named running strongly finally landed the oval to Barnes, and a capital piece of play re- sulted in the popular Warrington centre scoring behind the posts, a third goal resulting from his place kick. After Boscow had been called upon to defend his charge, Bruce had a shot at goal, and a minor was conceded. This was followed by a determined attack on the pavil- lion goal, and after several attempts to score, "Williams" raced away on the call of time, and feigning to pass during his progress, the visitors were baffled in their en- deavours to stay him, and another pass was the result, Barnes adding a fourth goal, which point brought the game to a conclusion, the final score reading—Warring- ton, 4-2-2 ; Marylebone, 0-1-1. On the Warrington side all the backs played well, whilst Berry, Dillon, and Thorniley were the pick of the forwards. Teams : Warrington: Boscow, back; Evans, Barnes, and Mas- sey, three-quarter backs ; "Williams' and Bates, half backs ; Fair. Turner, F. Turner, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, Donohue, Littlewood, Berry, Thorniley, and Povey, for- wards. Marylebone : Williams, back ; Bruce, Fowler, and Pilkington, three-quarter backs ; Draper and Murphy, half backs ; Lumley, Rouse, Wilson, Wilde, ' Pendom, Gossage, Weech, Gamble. and Barnes, forwards. Referee, Mr. Williamson, Manchester. WARRINGTON V. STOCKPORT. The first meeting of these clubs took place on Satur- day, in splendid weather and before a large assemblage. The Stockport club has not long been formed, but the rapid strides they have made in the football world caused notice to be taken of their doings by leading organiza- tions and it certainly was some encouragement to the Cheshire Club, when Warrington consented to meet them in friendly rivalry, although it was never for one mom- ent thought that they could cope with their more ex- perienced antagonists. The latest victories of the Stock- port men over Widnes and Mossley had a tendency to confirm the self-confidence which apparently appeared in the Stockport ranks, and as they had caught Warrington short handed—Lawless, Antrobus, and Bandies all being absentees—there was not wanting a few who pinned their faith to the chances of the Cheshire men. However, the preliminaries having been gone through, Potts on behalf of Stockport started the game by kick- ing off towards the pavilion goal, Teare assisting the kick-off with a neat dribble to the home quarter flag. Nevins made his mark, and his kick being well followed up, the Stockport men were at once placed on the de- fensive. The Stockport goal was further hampered by a strong endeavour on the part of Evans. who, receiving a pass from Fair. 'Turner, was pulled up a yard from the line. Wickman ran the oval out, but his effort was neutralized by a clever run by Berry. Stockport responded with a strong forward rush the game for the first quarter of an hour being confined to the front rank, making it very tedious. A fine dribble by W. Dillon relieved the monotony, and eventually Evans and Massey enlivened the pro- ceedings with neat runs and kicks on their respective wings. Parrott and Cockerill made some little headway, and a pass to Barnes from Bate being intercepted by Murray his career was notchecked until Bosco° with a smart tackle pulled him up at the half-way flag. The homesters now seemed to warm to their work, for after Eyre had effected a neat run, further ground was gained by Povey, who ran strongly to the line, and passing at the right moment to Bate the last named crossed the line, but the plea of" pass forward "was sustained. Nothing daunted by this ill-luck, Warrington played with re- newed vigour, and from a pack the home forwards buckled to, and rushing their opponents over the line, E. Dillon succeeded in scoring the first tangible point, Barnes causing renewed cheers by placing a goal. Following the restart, Bate, Barnes, and Massey, put in some grand passing tactics, and being ably backed up by Nevins, Littlewood, and Frank Turner, the Stock- port defence wss severely tested, Ogden and Murray by their clever iday staving off, at least fora time, the re- peated endeavours of the " wirepullers " to augment their score. Eventually, from a pass from Barnes, Massey raced to within a yard from the line, and although both he and Barnes had several chances afforded them, none were taken. A moment later, Fair Turner threw grandly to Massey, who rounded his opposing threequarter, and baffling his namesake, the opposing custodian, a brilliant effort resulted in his gaining a grand try, Frank Turner making a good bid for goal. The Brothers Dillon met the drop out with a grand dribble through the Stockport defence, and from some loose play, the home skipper threw across to Evans, and another brilliant try resulted, Frank Turner's kick at goal falling a little short. Murray put in a grand run, following the kick off, but Boscoe was safe, and half-time arrived with the score as— Warrington, 1-2-0 • Stockport, 0-0-0. Frank Turner restarted, and the first item of notice was a clever piece of work by Barnes, who dodged through his men in fine style. Abbey, however, cleared his lines, and although he got clear of everybody with the exception of Boscoe, the home custodian, with that apparent coolness lie displays in all his games, waited the Cheshire man's coming, with the result that a brilliant tackle staved off the misfortune which had every appearance of bringing disaster to his side. A grand piece of passing between Barnes and Massey on the popular side was neutralized by Ogden, and although Frank Turner got away from a line-out with a clear field befoie him, the chance of scoring was not taken, and the Stockport quarter flag saw the scene of hostilities. Evans made a desperate effort to score, and Fair Turner by a strong run was brought down near the line. However, from a line out, Berry secured and grounded,Frank Turner's kick at goal being futile. By the aid of judicious kicking, the Stock- port men assumed an aggressive attitude, and Boscoe saved at a critical moment. Littlewood, Donoghue, and Dillon dribbled well, but to no purpose, for pretty passing by Ogden and Murray changed the venue ta the home quarters. Cockerill tried hard to force an opening, but Nevins' safe gra' prevemed his travelling far. The game now slo- down considerably, and little interest was taken. sue home backs, were, compara- tively speaking, idle, and as the game was confined to the forwards it calls for little comment. Towards the

lose Massey and Littlewood successively made efforts to score, but only a minor accrued, and time brought the game to a close, the telegraph board denoting the score to be as follows :—Warrington 1-3-1, Stockport 0-0-0. That the better team won there is not the least doubt, for Warrington showed a distinct superiority all round, both in the backs and forwards. Still, there was a decided falling off in their play generally, and one branch was especially weak, viz., tackling. This has been one of the " wirepullers" strong points, but on Saturday it was one of th:•ir weakest. Individually Boscoe at back played grandly, and too much praise can- not be bestowed on him. He never made the semblance of a mistake, and his play again served to prove what an able substitute he is for so responsible a position. Evans was the best of the other backs, whilst in the for- wards, the brothers Dillon, Eyre, and Fair Turner were the pick. On the Stockport side Ogden,Murray,isolassey, McClure, and Teare were the pick. Teams :—Warrington. Boscoe, back; Massey, Barnes, and Evans, three-quarters ; Bate and Nevins, half backs; Fair Turner (captain), F. Turner, W. Dillon, E. Dillon, T.Donohue, R. Littlewood, W. Povev, B. Eyre, B. Berry. forwards. Stockport : Massey, back ; Ogden, Murray, and Ceckerill, three-quarters ; Wickman and Parrott, half backs ; Potts, Dr. Smith, Abbey, Bailey, Mills, Teare, Ingram, Duckers, and McClure, forwards. Referee, Mr. H. Lord, Broughten.

FOOTBALL.-RUGBY.
To-day's matches :—Warrington v. Dewsbury at War- rington • St. Helens v. Hunslet at St. Helens; St. Helens Recs. v. 'Castleford at St. Helens ; Widnes v. Manchester Rangers at Manchester. . .

During the holidays, Warrington added two more to their pretty satisfactory record of victories. On Satur- day the Stockport team, which has won renown lately, were rather easy victims,tholsgh they displayed a consider- able amount of vigour in the opening part of the game They were defeated by one goal, three tries, and a few minors to nil. On Monday the Warringtonians had a still easier conquest of Ma.rylebone a score of four goals, and two tries being compiled against the solitary try of the Londoners.

There was a tremendous turn-out at Halifax on Satur- day to see the final tie for the Yorkshire Cup between Huddersfield and Wakefield Trinity. There would be fully 20,000 spectators, and enthusiasm ran very high. Anticipation pointed to the success of Huddersfield, who, it is claimed, have the finest set of backs seen under the same banner br years, and for once the prophets were right. Wakefield could make no impression on the superb defence of their rivals, and were beaten by a goal, the result of a grand try by Richmond, the point being easily converted by Brooke. Archer also crossed the Wakefield line, but the try was disallowed. Richmond was in great form for the winners; indeed, all the backs except Dyson, who got few chances, did uncommonly well. Stafford was of great service to Wakefield. and in one case hit the post with a drop at goal. The Hudders- field forwards were the sroarter lot, and got over the ground at a very fast pace. This is the first time that the cup has gone to Huddersfield—the first occasin n on which they have appeared in the last round; and their success was particularly well received.

The supporters of the leading St. Helens Clubs are well satisfied with the result of their holiday engagements. This is especially the case in regard to the Recs. who handsomely won three out of their four fixtures. Their defeat by Heckmondwike was not altogether unexpected as their hard work on the previous Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, prepared the way fordefeat by the strong Yorkshire organisation.

An amusing incident occurred on the Recs. field on Good Friday. The visitors were Holbeck and the specta- fors were convulsed with merriment at half-time when it became known that they were objecting on ridiculous grounds to the county man " Jimmy" Pilkington carry- ing the ball with one hand! " Jimmy " was too quick for them altogether—proof of this being found in the fact that he scored three tries. If Holbeck's objection had held good poor " Pilky " would have had to curtail the " feelers" with which nature has blessed—or cursed— him.

An all-absorbing interest centred in the visit of the Cheshire Champions, Runcorn, on Thursday night. An even and hard fought game was expected, and opinions were divided as to the probable result of the encounter.

A meeting of the West Lancashire League Committee was held at the Star and Garter Hotel, Tyldesley, on Saturday evening, when the following team was chosen to represent the rest of the League against Wigan, the winner ef the West Lancashire Cup, the match to be played at Wigan on the 16th inst. :—T. Coop (Leigh), back ; J. Roberts (Aspull), F. Shaw (Tyldesley), and D. Worthington (Leigh), three-quarter backs; J. Berry (Tyldesley) and D. Hulme (Aspull), half backs; G. Wood- ward, P. Battersby (Tyldesley), L. Webster (Aspull), J. Gregory, WMaster (Leigh), W. Graham, J. Brownbill (St. Helens), Williamson, and Prescot (Walkden), for- wards.

div.head: FOOTBALL-ASSOCIATION.
div.p: FOOTBALL-ASSOCIATION.

The St. Helens Associationists have made arrangements for taking the admirable ground in Park-road, vacated by the defunct Globe Recreation (Rugby) Club. They played their opening game thereon on Good Friday, and were defeated by Haydock by two goals to none.

The visit of the famous Preston North End Reserve team to Earlestown on Saturday occasioned great inter- est. The North Enders met the littls Champion Reserve team of the Earlestown Club and the latter sustained their known reputation by defeating their more noted— though no cleverer—opponents. Well done Earlestown Juniors!

The Stanley team was defeated by the Earlestown Club on Monday, by three goals to one. In the early history of the Earlestown organisation the games with the Stanley Club seemed to excite widespread interest but what a change has taken place ! The old enthusiasm which would have been aroused by a visit from Stanley has disappeared, and the supi:orters of the Earlestown Club only discussed as to how many goals the " boys" would win by.

The match, England versus Scotland, drew together a vast number of patrons of the game, Hampden Park be- ing occupied by over 28,000, whilst many thousands were unable to gain admission. So great was the crush, that it was only with much difficulty that play was carried on. The game can be dismissed in a few words. After Wood had opened the scoring, excitement was very keen until the Scotchmen equalised, the score at the in- terval being a goal each. And here it remained till the curtain fell, the defence on beth sides being of the finest possible character. One hardly knew which to admire most—the fearless, risky style of the brothers Walters, or the cool, calculating method adopted by Arnott and M`Keown. Each was equally effective in its way. Moon had more to do than Wilson between the posts, and did it extremely well. He was pitilessly assailed during the last twenty minutes, but never lost his head. Howarth vied with Kelly for the honours in the half-back depart- ment, both doing wonders. Of the English forwards Wood and Daft were by far the best wing, Currey being a failure, and spoiling the good work of Bassett. Lind- ley did not shine in the centre. The money taken at the gate was said to amount to £1,400, irrespective of the stands.

div.head: CRICKET.
div.p: CRICKET.
WIDNES VICTORIA CRICKET CLUB.

The opening game of the above club took place on Saturday, the Captain's team playing the Sub-Captain's team. For the Sub-Captains team ffirmett was the only one to make a stand, Sadler's splendid complete- ly beating the batsman, he taking seven wickets for three runs. Teasdale and Bingham batted very well for the Captain's team. Score :—Captain's team 52 ; Sub- Captain's 25.

INTOXICANTS IN LOCAL WORKHOUSES.

STRANGE DIVERSITIES IN THE SUPPLY. Most extraordinary discrepancies exist between th e quantities of stimulants consumed at Work- houses of similar size and like situation. At one Workhouse hundreds of times as much per head of inmates will be spent upon intoxicants as at adjacent ones, and intoxicants for a single Work- house will cost more than for 300 other Workhouses. At the majority of Workhouses the expenditure is far higher than at many special and general Hospitals, and at not a few the cost of malt liquor is greater than that of all the Workhouses put together throughout an area 'extending over half the kingdom. A great deal of this expenditure is illegal, being incurred contrary to the official regulations, and if the local ratepayers objected, the Master, as has in some cases happened, would be surcharged with the cost. From the Non-alcoholic System of Workhouse Manage- ment,we learn that 1,000 ratepayers were summoned in one day for the payment of rates, and also that excessive administration of stimulants in hospitals his been condemned by the Lord's Committee on Intemperance, the Inspectors to the Local Government Board and other authorities, and also that Masters of Workhouses, Medical officers, Chairmen and Members of Boards of Guardians give abundant testimony to the value of a system by which intoxicants are excluded from Workhouses. A circular sent to the Chairman of most of our local Workhouses says that "unfortunately investigation reveals the fact that whilst the general tendency is a diminution in the consumption of Workhouses-20 per cent. in England in 10 years and a further reduction of 25 per cent, in four years with a larger number of in- mates—there are some Workhouses where the expenditure under this head is still greatly in excess of any reason- able allowance, and very many where it has not been reduced to so low a point as it might be." A comparison Is also instituted between the local Workhouses and others, and attention is called to the fact that at many Workhouses no intoxicants are administered at the ratepayers' expense, with advantage to all concerned. The following are some of the statistics laid before the Guardians: Cost of Intoxi- Exceeding that cants for for 2,214 paupers in West Derby 42,300 elsewhere 3,788 „ Liverpool 33,900 ~ 3,322 „ Manchester 29,500 „ ' 709 „ Toxteth Park 27,800 „ 426 „ Wigan 22,613 • 1,587 „ Salford 18,819 „ 392 ~ Warrington 15.042 „ 411 „ Preseot 11,934 „ 200 „ Leigh 11.758 „ 264 „ Ormskirk 11,331 DISCUSSION AT WARRINGTON BOARD OF GUARDIANS. At the meeting of the Warrington Board of Guardian on Wednesday, a communication on the subject of the subject of the supply of intoxicating drinks to inmates of workhouses was read from the Workhouse Drink Reform League. In addition to giving the figures in the above statement relating to Warrington, the communication stated that the 15,042 paupers who consumed less intoxicating drinks than the 292 at Warrington were inmates of 83 other workhouses. , It added that there were, accerding to the last government return, 312 workhouses at which the rate of expenditure per head of inmates upon intoxicants was lower than at Warrington Workhouse.—Mr. W. HOUGHTON said he should not take much notice of a communication of that kind. He thought they on the spot, guided by the advise of their doctors, were the best judges as to what was good for the inmates. He was reminded, however, that they used to have a weekly return showing the quantity of spirits consumed on the premises.—The Woitenouse MASTER said the return had never been pre- sented since his appointment.—The CLERK said it was one of those orders that would have to be renewed after every election.—ln answer to Mr. Blackhurst, the WORKHOUSE MASTER said he should say the consumption of beer and wines and spirits in the Workhouse, taking into account the number of inmates was the lowest in the country, and had been for the hat few years.—Mr. CLARKB: There are some where none is given.—The Wonanousa Mama said there was only two half-pints of beer, seven ounces of whisky, and two ounces of wine used per day at the Workhouse and that was upon the doctor's orders.—The CHAIRMAN said if there was anything in the communica- tion it ought to have attention paid to it, and seeing that no intoxicants were given except upon the doctor's orders, the doctor's attention should be called to the letter and he should be asked to report to the Board.—Mr. Baacx- HURST suggested that it was a case the House Committee might inquire into. If it were really the case that 392 inmates of Warrington Workhouse consumed as much intoxicants as 15,042 in some other workhouses it was a case for inquiry.—Mr. HEATON proposed that the letter be on the table and 'that no notice be taken of it. Be added that if the people who got that informa- tion together got anything which told against the object they had in view they would not send it. He thought the men who sat there knew better whether a pauper should be allowed a few ounces of spirits or half-a-pint of beer than people who simply sat in an office making out statements. He had been in some of those great teetotal workhouses where he had had champagne to his dinner and plenty of good whiskey and'beer, and he had been to some teetotal places where they hadzoedone, which, when they came to drink, they found to be very good whiskey. (Laughter.)—Mr. BLACKHIIRST thought Mr. Heaton had made a very serious charge and he hoped the temperance people of Warrington would take notice of it.—Mr. CLARKE did not consider it was any teetotal place where there was whiskey.—Mr. HEATON : I said reported teetotal places. —Mr. CLARKE : Oh l—The CHAIRMAN .aid it was desir- able to give the doctor an opportunity to reply. It was a serious charge to make that 392 inmates of Warrington Workhouse required as much stimulants as 15,042 inmates in 83 other Workhouses.—Mr. RATCLIFFB did not see that there could be any harm in giving the doctor an opportunity to reply.—Mr. AUKLAND said it was a seri- ous statement to make against any Workhouse.—lt was then decided to refer the matter to the medical officer of the Workhouse for a reply.

div.head: MINERS' FEDERATION.
div.p: MINERS' FEDERATION.

The Miner's Federation of Great Britain opened an adjourned Conference at Nottingham on Thursday, Mr. Pickard, M.P., presided, and delegates representing 118,000 miners attended. Matters relating to the ap- proaching International Conference Of Miners at Brussels were discussed at length, and it was resolved that one of the principal questions brought before that Conference should be that of the eight hours day for miners. Messrs. Hasiam (Derbyshire) and Cowey (Yorkshire) were ap- pointed to give evidence before the Royal Commission on Royalties, &c.

div.p: THE CREWE MURDER.

EXECUTION OF RICHARD DAVIES. Ms LAST STATEMENT. Richard Davies, 19, was executed on Monday morning, within the walls of the Cheshire county gaol, at Knutsford, for the murder of his father at Hough, near Crewe. The Rev. Mr. Truss, prison chaplain, who had left the unhappy young man at a late hour the previous evening, when he adminis- tered the Sacrament of the Holy Communion, arrived at the prison at seven o'clock, and found that Davies had been up and dressed for an hour. His sleep during the night had been very fitful. Just before eight o'clock the Press representatives were admitted to the prison. Berry came down one of the corridors with the pinioning straps in his hands, and as the clock struck eight was intro- duced by the governor to the condemned cell. Davies, who was engaged in prayer with the chaplain, at once rose and quietly submitted to the pinioning, and as the prison bell began to toll the party re-appeared in the corridor, Dr. Fennell, the prison surgeon, walking first with Mr. W. Gregg, Under Sheriff; 'then came Captain Price, Governor of the gaol; Chief Warder Lewis, the Rev. Mr. Truss reading the burial service,/ Davies, with a warder on either side of him, and Berry bringing up the rear. The distance between the condemned cell and the scaffold, erected over the coachhou.se, is some sixty yards but Davies walked the whole way quite without assistance. He was very pale and haggard, but showed the greatest firmness throughout the awful ordeal. As the man approached the scaffolding Berry, to spare his feelings as far as prac- ticable, stepped quickly up to him and pulled the white cap down over his face. Davies staggered momentarily, but Berry, putting out his hand, guided him on to the scaffold. In a moment the rope was about his neck, and as he stepped back to pull the lever Davies could be heard exclaiming "Lord, receive my soul. Lord, I commend it to Thee." The lever was then pulled, and the trap-door falling, the lad shot through into the pit below, falling a distance of six feet. A momentary vibration of the rope was followed by what was obviously almost instantaneous death, the only signs of life for a few seconds being a nervous contraction of the pinioned arms and shoulders. Not more than two minutes elapsed between the leaving of the condemned cell and the execution, Berry being obviously satisfied with the whole of the arrangements. A crowd had gathered outside to witness the hoisting of the black flag, while as many as possible stood as close to the prison wall as possible to listen to what they believed to be the falling of the drop in the old coachhouse. The poor lad had become extremely penitent, and the chaplain and all those who came in contact with him are convinced that the letters which have recently appeared in the papers accurately represented his feelings. While under sentence of death his attention to the chaplain's ministrations were most marked, and the greater part of his time during the last day or two was occupied in re- ligious exercises. To the last he protested his innocence of any actual participation in the crime, a fact which is certain to strengthen the opinion held Joy a large section of the public that George, who has been respited, was the actual murderer of his father. At ten minutes to eight o'clock be rose from his knees,where he had been praying, and wrote out and handed the following statement to the chaplain: "I truthfully declare in my last hour that I never struck my father on the night of his death, and that I never had the axe in my hand." He at the same time handed another letter to the chaplain addressed to his mother embodying this statement. On Saturday, I Richard Davies made a mech longer statement to the I same effect, which was telegraphed to the Home Secre- tary immediately. The poor lad felt his position keenly. During his imprisonment he suffered greatly, and when Berry entered his cell for the purpose of pinioning his arms it was found that he had become so extremely thin that a folded sheet had to be put on his back under his waistcoat before the belt could be secured. George Davies has, says the officials, been stolid from the begin- ning, and has expressed no penitence for his crime. A correspondent visited The Hough on Monday, and had an interview with members of the Davies family. After the terrible suspense of the past few days the widow is utterly prostrate and ill, and frequently breaks o 0 into hysterical weeping. The night before the execution was one of intense anxiety ; the widow and family sat up through the night, several kindly neigh- bours staying with them. It was known that the near- est telegraph station was *pen. No reply had been received to the appeal sent to the trieen, and it was expected to be delivered during the night. As the hours passed the hopes of the family grew fainter, and after maintaining a constant vigil until an hour or two after daybreak without any message of any kind being re- ceived either from the Queen or the Home Secretary, the little party broke up disconsolate and dejected, feel- ing that all hope even for a temporary respite must be abandoned. The Davies family drew down their blinds as a sign of mourning, and the villagers who had shared the vigil showed sympathy in the same way. The widow and family continue to receive a large number of mes- sages of sympathy. MR. WLAREN, M.P., AND THE HOME SECRETARY. Speaking at Crewe on Tuesday night, Mr. W. S. B. M'Laren, M.P. for the division, condemned the Home Secretary's decision in the Crewe murder case. He could not conceive any reason that could induce the some Secretary to take up the position he had done. He could have understood his action although he could not have agreed with it, if he had refused to reprieve either of the prisoners, but had allowed the law to take its course. Of all the acts which the Home Secretary had considered it his duty to perform in the revision of criminal sentences since he took office, he did not think he had ever performed one so unwise, so wrong and cruel, as to respite one of those unhappy boys and not the other. (Cheers.) He felt strongly that both youths should have been reprieved. Their youth, the circum- stances of their home life, the great provocation to which they had undoubtedly been subjected, should have been taken into account, and haying been taught I by the awful experiences through which they had passed 1 they might have become useful members of society, and might have lived to atone by useful lives for the awful crime which they had committed. The verdict of the jury had not peen carried out on the evidence presented to them. Bound by their oaths the jury had no alternative but to find the boys guilty of murder; but they felt still, having regard to the evidence, that, bound by conscientious scruples, the extreme penalty of the law should not be carried out, and so recommended them to mercy. Their recommendation to mercy was as much a part of their Verdict as their express belief in the prisoners' guilt. But a jury should not be tied to pass a verdict which involved a sentence of death whilst an equally important part of their decision, a recommendation to mercy, should be overridden and disregarded. (Cheers.) The Rome Secretary's decision compelled the consideration of the whole question of our criminal procedure, and the whole question of right and wrong of capital punishment, to which he.was strongly opposed, for he believed it had no deterrent effect upon the commission of murders. He regarded it indeed as being only one degree less wicked than the crime itself. Capital punishment was contrary to civilization and the principles of Christianity. It was a last remnant of a barbaric age, and shpuld at once be swept away for more just and Christian methods cf punishment. (Loud cheering.) Mr. M'Lazen con- cluded by expressing his deep regret at the sentence having been carried out upon Richard Davies, and his deep sympathy for his mother, brothers, and sisters, because of the hardness of their lot in this life.

div.head: FATAL PRIZE FIGHT.
div.p: A FATAL PRIZE FIGHT.

John Hopkins, one of the principals in% prizefight on a hill near Mountain Ash on Sunday, died on Tuesday from injuries he received in the encounter. The other combatant, John Collins, was brought before the Aber- dare magistrates on Tuesday on the charge of man- slaughter. The fight lasted for half an hour.
MR. GLADSTONE AND HIS CONSTITUENTS. REPLY TO ADDRESS OF CONGRATULATION.
Mr. Gladstone has sent the following reply to the address received by him on Saturday, signed by the conveners of the Midlothian Liberal Committees :

"It is most true that the electors might well, had they thought fit, have called for my appearance amongst them at a much earlier period, but while I thank them for their forbearance I can assure them that, warmly as I have been received elsewhere, it is among them before all others that I desire to render an account of my political conduct, and to explain the views that I am bound to take of public affairs. At my age, nature begins increasingly to shrink from effort, yet I can truly , say that I look forward with deep interest to the opportunity which we trust the present year may give me of noting the extraordinary progress which our cause has made since the election of 186, and endeavour- big to express the obligation now resting upon every man in our enlarged constituencies to give his vote as though the entire issue of the great political controversy depended upon it. It is a cause of satisfaction to me that the effect of the Irish controversy has been to define more clearly the position of Scotland, and to improve her means of pressing what she deems, and may deem, to be her reasonable claims and her substantial interests. Nor can I he otherwise than pleased that our opponents have given signs of life, and intend to challenge a verdict at the poll, which I feel assured will be not less emphatic than those of former 'Tars."

div.head: TRIPLE ALLIANCE.
div.p: THE TRIPLE ALLIANCE.

General Wedel; as special envoy from the German Emperor, has presented an 'autograph letter from his Majesty to the Emperor of Austria, and about the same - time Prince Reuss, the German Ambassador, handed W Count Kalnoky a letter from General Von Caprivi. Both letters express confidence in the mainieuance of the Triple Alliance and of European peace.

SHOCKING SUICIDE OF A WOMAN. On Monday night, Mary Gee, wife of a collier, Parr Bridge, Tyldesley, 50 years of age, threw herself in front of a goods train near a level crossing at Parr Bridge. Her head was frightfully crushed, and she died immedi ately. The train was only travelling at the rate of seven miles an hour. The deceased, who had been in a des- - pondent state some time, left home half an hour befose, saying she was going for a walk.

div.head: VOLUNTEER MA.NCEUVRES.
div.p: THE VOLUNTEER MA.NCEUVRES.

The Easter Volunteer manceuvres at Portsmouth on Monday, resulted in a practical victory for the invading army, who succeeded in turning the left flank of the defenders, and driving them back upon the right of their position. The Duke of Cambridge witnessed the shan2 fight, and afterwards reviewed the whole of the trooPs• The Chief incident of the manceuvres at Eastbourne wan a magnificent flank movement by the northern force, which would have decided the day had supports arrived at the proper moment. In the result the battle was a drawn one.

div.head: LORD R, CHURCHILL AND THE LAND BILL.
div.p: LORD R, CHURCHILL AND THE LAND BILL.

Lord Randolph Churchill, in a further letter on the Land Purchase Bill, strongly advises the Government to withdraw the measure. He says that in Ireland land purchase should not be a precursor to local government, but an adjunct and a supplement. All schemes for land purchase and other special purposes in Ireland should be' made dependent on the will of the Irish people, sch°' should be allowed to speak through the medium of popular and representative local government on the lines of English and Scotch local government. This, Lord Randolph. Churchill conceives, is the only foundation upon which a tranquilized and regenerated Ireland oan be constructed.

div.head: ANOTHER AFRICAN EXPEDITION.
div.p: ANOTHER AFRICAN EXPEDITION.

Stanley's penetration of South-east Atrica to the dominions of the Mandi is to have imitators from the West Coast, as there is now a project on foot which is to start from Monrovia, the capital of Liberia, West Africa. - and eventually penetrate the great unknown country until the city of General Gordon's death is reached. The new exploration is to be undertaken by a compani which is now being formed in England. The explcrers will start from Monrovia to Borporah, open up the country between Liberia and the Niger, and then cross over with an expedition which is to negotiate with the interior tribes, and eventually come out at the Red Sea. The expedition wilicotnprise experts in botany, miner- alogy, and agriculture. Communications are at the pre- sent time passing between the promoters of the company and the Colonial Office, and it is expected that a great development of trade between England and West Africa will•result.

div.head: SHOCKING BOAT ACCIDENTS.
div.p: SHOCKING BOAT ACCIDENTS.

By the upsetting of a pleasure boat during a squall 0" the river at Montrose on Monday, William Beattie, fisherman, was drowned. The accident was witness from the shore, and the other occupant, Alexander Scott, a draper's assistant, clung to the upturned iv° ' until he was rescued. A fatal boating accident occurred on the same daV off Penarth. Mr. Boyer and Mr. Alfred Thornley, eldest sod of Major Thornley, of the Submarine Mining Engineers, and himself a lieutenant in the corps, were boating off Penarth, when their light craft was caught in a sudderl squall, and upset. Both, being good swimmers, ulacil for the shore, but Mr. Boyer, seeing that his boat nib' righted, suggested swimming back to it. Ts this young Thornley agreed, and was carrying out the suggestion when he was swept away by a treacherous current and drowned. Several boats had put off to his assistance, but failed to arrive in time.

DEATH OF THE PRESIDENT OF THE PRIMITIVE METHODISTS. We regret to hear of the painfully sudden death of the Rev. Joseph Tou!son, President of the Primitive tvletho- dist Conference, on Saturday afternoon. He was at the time of his death on his way to Liverpool-st. Station t° take the train for Dereham, where he was to preach ott, Sunday. He was carried to the London Hospital, all the fact of his death was there medically declared. few days days ago, feeling unwell, he had called on the 1e Thomas Guttery and asked him to take his place at 16., public meeting, but otherwise showed no symptom °I ill-health, and up to the time of his death seemed to be quite cheerful. His age was 87 years. He had been M the ministry 48 years. He was elected President at the last Conference. The many public duties demanding attention in addition to the duties of general boo' steward have been a great strain upon him during the year. The denomination, never had a more popular President.

div.head: MR. GLADSTONE AT TRING.
div.p: MR. GLADSTONE AT TRING.

Mr. Gladstone travelled from Weybridge to London 01 Tuesday. Replying to an address from the Liberals the Weybridge district, he said the Lib,lral cause was advancing, but their opponents would not giv them the opportunity of showing it by a general electiLn. In the evening the right hon. gentleman journeyed to Asto.o,. Clinton, on a visit to Mr. Cyril Flower, M.P., and his presence at Tring station was taken advantage of by 1.113 Liberals of that part of the country to present him an .address. In responding, Mr. Gladstone touch briefly on the Irish Land Purchase Bill. To judge frO11) the reception it had met with, that measure waadle said, not in a very healthy, but rather in what might be considered a somewhat fishy, condition. Hs wanted .te know what sort of security there would be for thirty-three millions of money if the Irish people werela a position to say that we chose to send the money over there but that they by their representatives protested against the whole proceeding, and that therefore it vfa4 impossible thatwe could pretend to extract it from thell?; This was" avery stiff, awkward, and indigestible point, and he commended it to the attention of his audience/ impressing upon them the fact that they had got to advance the money—" every one of them."

THE CONDITION OF BRIDGE-STREET.

Sir,—l am extremely reluctant to make any complaint, but I do think the Corporation might consider the requirements of and also assist the tradesmen by keep- ing the thoroughfares in as good condition as possible. The'condition of Bridge-st. at the present time is simply disgraceful and slovenly. To-day (Friday) at 9 a.m. half the width of the street is taken up to lay a short length of supply pipe, and the process takes a whole day. Why cannot this be done at night when there is no traffic? But apart from this, Bridge-st. requires attending to very urgently, as the present state of things is a great drawback to the development of busi- ness, and I personally feel it very discouraging. The more attractive the town is made, the more business will be done in it. I think the Ccrporation will do only right by helping us a little in this respect, and not hindering us by allowing the present state of things to exist.—Yours respectfultv, Bridge-st., Warrington.
W. HODGKINSON.

div.head: WATER CHARGES LIVERPOOL VERSUS WARRINGTON.
div.p: WATER CHARGES LIVERPOOL VERSUS WARRINGTON.

Sir,—ln your issue of March 29th, 1890, under the above heading you make the following remarks in refer- ence to a letter of mine of March 29th :—" The whole difference between us and Mr. Greaves is one of mode of payment. In Warrington the consumer pays Is. 20. in the £ in one sum; in Liverpool he pays 7P. as consumer and a Bd. rate as a ratepayer, showing a difference in this respect of A of a penny only in favour of Liverpool. We grant that something may be urged in favour of beginning, as in'Liverpool, with a special levy of a fixed sum, and should be glad to hear something more as to this phase of the question." I cannot compliment you on your logic or arithmetic in the above remarks. It passes my comprenhension to understand by what pro- cess of reasoning you arrive at the conclusion that a rate of 3d. in the £ levied on and raid by the landlord is paid by the consumer. You will persist in asserting that to be the fact, and also in asserting that there is merely a fractional difference between the cost of water in Liverpool and Warrington. I repeat again the cost to the consumer in Liverpool, this year is 70. in the £ and granting (which I do not), that you are right if you add the occupier's rate of 3d. in the £ it would still leave a difference in favour of Liverpool of 4d. in every L. You will perhaps be good enough to acknowledge your error —at least to the extent I have pointed out.—Yours, etc. THOMAS GREAVES. The Tower, Warrington, April 3, 1890.

[We still state that tlse whole diffevnce between us and Mr. Greaves is one of mode of payment ; but we must go a little further back to make the issue clear. Originally our Correspondent stated that the payment for water in Liverpool was 6d. in the £ only, as against Is. 2icl. in Wairington. We found, on making inquiry, that Mr. Greaves had omitted to state that in Liverpool there was in addition " a charge of 6d. over all pro- perty whether they take water or not." This reduced the difference between Warrington and Liverpool to 2id. But Mr. Greaves has since found that he should have said the charge to Liverpool consumers was 70. in the ; and, as he cannot deny that there is a further charge of 61. in the £, it comes to what we said, name- ly that the total charge in Liverpool is is. lid. in the £as compared with ls. 20. for Warrington—a differ- ence of nine-tenths of a penny only in favour of Liver- pool. Granted that in Liverpool the fixed charge of 6d. is divided between the owner and the occupier, it does not affect the fact that the total payment for water in Liverpool is Is. IV. in the R. As our Corres- pondent has utterly failed in showing, as he sought to show, that water is much cheaper in Liverpool than in Warrington, the less he says about " logic or arithme- tic " the better.—En. Ex.]

div.head: MORE FACTS.
div.p: MORE FACTS.

Sir,—All Protestant readers of your columns must feel grateful to your correspondent " Robert Foulkes" for his able expo-ure of the Romanising practices car- ried on in the Church of England. Many people can scarcely credit that such practices are perpetrated in what should be Protestant churches, but that they do exist, and that they call for the light of day, the follow- ing extracts will prove. In a paper that professes to represent the feeling in the Established Church, viz. : "The Church Times," I last week read an account of a working-man's funeral in which were these extracts "On Friday night his body was carried from his house to the church "and " met at the porch by the Vicar vested in a black cope, three assistant clergy, and the choir, and marching slowly up the church the Vicar reciting the opening sentences of the burial service. The coffin was placed near the chancel screen and was surrounded by six wax tapers. Vespers for the dead were sung," and" the body was watched all night and part of Saturday, by members and hon. members of the branch, including all four clergy." The account goes on to say that a Special Mortuary Eucharist was cele- brated at 7 a.m on Saturday, and in the procession at the funeral were cross bearer and acolytes, Vicar in cope and biretta, supported by the three assistant clergy in birettas. If this is not downright Roman Catholicism, I don't know what is. It reminds me very forcibly of a funeral I recently saw in the streets of Rouen. In another article, or rather editorial, a writer refers to the "calvaries and crucifixes of Brittany, where a crucifix is set up at every cross road," and he as good as laments that the peasantry do not fall down and worship these brazen images; but these same peasantry show their self-respect by " not even lifting their has or paus- ing to make the sign of the cross," to blocks of wood and stone. It would do a lot of English people good to take a trip to Normandy or Brittany to see the practise of Roman Catholicism in its unadulterated state. There, no mention is made of Christ, as in Engiand, as a blind to the unwary, but rank Mariolatry prevails. When in France some time ago, my comp° yne de voyage paid her first visit, and was greatly taken with the churches. Indeed, there was no keeping her out of them, and con- sequently Ihad my fill of saints, symbols, and smells. We saw marriages and funerals innumerable, and the effect upon my travelling companion was beneficial. Though I read to her numerous offers of " indulgences " for prayers to the saints, none had such effect as a claimant for the "honour." At the tomb of St.

Genevieve, in Paris, I told her she could claim 50 days indulgence for as many prayers to the saint, and just as she was asking whether any person in his senses would do such a thing, she was spell hound by seeing a man apparently tired of the rigid rectitude of daily life, fall down at the gilded shrine and qualify for a 50 days' fling of folly on these conditions. In the cemetery of Dfontmarte she had another shock—this time by a funeral. Anxious to see a real Catholic funeral ceremony, she took up a good position by the grave side and a- waited the arrival of the procession. It arrived ; the mourners handed to the officials the body, enveloped in a coffin in every way similar to an orange box, and be- fore it was lowered to its last resting place, they walked off round the Cemetery—not a word being said! I would advise all your readers who would like to know what Catholicism did for England to read and study Macaulay's History, from the death of Charles the Second to the accession of William the Third, and if they never thought much of it before, I will guarantee they will entertain feelings of the greatest admiration for English Protestantism and freed,m, blessings of which the clergy of the Church of England now seem bent on depriving us. But that they will never succeed is the conviction of thousands of Englishmen besides April 9th, 1890.
A DISSENTER.
FATAL FIRE IN LONDON.

Flames broke out shortly before one o'clock on Thurs- day morning at 85, Landor-road, Clapham. London, occupied by Mrs. J. E. Weller. Her two daughters, on returning with a gentleman from the theatre, discovered the outbreak. The gentleman ran upstairs and brought down a little boy, but was unable to make Mrs. Weller hear. The local fire brigade poured quantities of water into the house, and then found the charred remains of Mrs. Weller on the ground floor. The origin of the dis- aster is unknown.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
THEL WALL.

Over the holidays the canal in the Thelwall district was visited by large numbers of people, and a thriving business was done at the excellent coffee rooms on the canal, the conveniences of which are now thoroughly appreciated by visitors. It might almost be said that amongst the visitors there were persons from all parts of the country. Work was resumed on the canal on Wednesday, after the holidays.

div.head: MISSION MEETINGS.
div.p: MISSION MEETINGS.

For some ten months past Mr. Jos. Wibberley, of the Independent Methodists, has been working among, the navvies now assembled in such large numbers, by hold- ing mission meetings at the various lodging-houses. So far the meetings have been a success, and have been entered into with spirit by those for whom they were intended. The meetings held on Wedhesday evening at the Old-road lodging-house, Latchford, were especially successful and gave great encouragement to those engaged in the work.

div.head: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.
div.p: DARESBURY HIGHWAY BOARD.

The last meeting of the members of this Board for the year 1889-90 was held in the Board room, Daresbury, on Thursday afternoon. Mr. John Mclntyre presided, and there were also present Messrs. J. Cooper, T. Moore, T. Hall, E. Clarke, J. Clarke, P. Percival, J. Darbyshire, W. Bradford, J. W. Haddock, J. Parr, W. Tickle, W. Pier- point, J. L. Jones, P. Darbyshire, T. S. Burgess, W. Beswick, E. Aaron, sen., J. Barber, and H. Linaker (clerk).—A letter was read from Mr. Robert Dobson, deputy coroner for the Halton division of Cheshire, con- veying the recommendation of a jury at a recent inquest on the body of a man who had been drowned, calling attention to the unprotected state of Whitley Reid Brook, and suggesting that steps be taken by the Board to prevent drowning cases there in the future.—Tha Sur- veyor (Mr. Swinton) was instructed to visit the place referred to, and report about its condition to the next meeting of the Board.—Acting on a suggestion from the County Council, the Board decided to cancel their two years' contract for the repair of the main roads in the district.—Tenders for the supply of broken stone were opened, and after some discussion the tender of Messrs. 13rundritt, of Runcorn, was accepted, at an average of from Bs. 10d. to 10s. per ton, by nine votes to eight.— The Surveyor's estimates for repair and maintenance during the coming year were submitted, the total amount being £4,693 against £3,979 15s. last year. The chief increase was in the township of Appleton, being £l,OOO against £625 last year.

div.head: FLEEING FROM JUSTICE TO DEATH.
div.p: FLEEING FROM JUSTICE TO DEATH.

A very tragic event occurred at Widnes on Satur- day evening. About half-past six Constables Beaton and Gillis heard a disturbance in Wellington- st., and proceeding there, discovered the cause to be a woman named Mary Jane Riley, who was drunk. They took her into custody, and Patrick Killele, her paramour, came up and attempted to drag her from the grasp of the officers. Beaton pushed him away several times, and threatened that if he did not cease his interference he would be arrested. There- upon Killele kicked Beaton on the leg, and a second time attempted to strike him, and Beaton, leaving the woman with P.C. Gillis, seized his assailant,and a fierce struggle on the ground ensued. For a quarter of an hour they wrestled and rolled over each other on the , ground, and a large crowd assembled to witness the struggle, and their sympathies being with the pri- soner, they interfered and set him at liberty. Killele at once ran away and shortly afterwards Constables Beaton and Robinson set to work to trace and recapture him. At the outset they searched through Messrs. Hutchinson's Works, and in the revolver shed they saw their quarry, but he quickly ran off with the officers in hot pursuit. He climbed a wall and alighted on the canal bank, aad being closely pressed,he shouted," Here goes ;if you can follow me," and jumped into the canal He swam vig- orously to the centre of the canal, when a person called to him to stay in the middle and he stopped a moment, and then threw up his arms and sank. He quickly rose to the surface, and a plank and an oar were sent to him, but he sank again and did not rise again to the surface. Shortly afterwards Mr. W. E. Oakden, of Messrs. Hutch- inson's works,recovered the body by means of a boathook. Attempts were made to restore animation, but without effect. It was observed that his trousers had slipped down to his ankles and had perhaps been the cause of his sinking.—On Tuesday Mr. Brighouse held an inquest on the body at the police station and evidence was given bearing out the above facts. Mary Ann Noon, 5, Nelson- st., said the deceased was her brother and was 18 years of age and a chemical labourer. He was a good swim- men—The jury returned a verdict to the effect that the deceased was accidentally drowned, whilst trying to escape from the police.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN. BY AN OCCASIONAL CORRESPONDENT.

Mr. Robert Foulkes, a well-known character in Runcorn neighbourhood for his hatred of Ritualism and Popery, was both "seen and heard" at Frod- sham Vestry meeting on Monday. He appears to spend a great part of his existence in a crusade against Ritualism, but he is a general without either staff or rank and file, and single-handed he braved the Frodsh am Vestry. Dreadfully in earnest himself, Mr. Foulkes is one of those men whom his fellows will not take seriously, and he had to betake himself home without ventilating the long list of abuses which he alleges are perpetrated in the ancient church every Sunday. Whatever Mr. Foulkes may think of Vicar Blogg and his services, the parishioners appear to be well satisfied, and if he wishes to bring about a reform to his " Evangeli- cal " standard, he will have to adopt a different method of attack and bring his supporters "up to the scratch."

For the first time in the history of Halton, the law has been complied with in regard to the paroch- ial charities and t he parishioners have been supplied with particulars of the accounts except in two par- ticulars. Mr. C. L. Evans, agent to the Norton Estate, from the proceedings at the vestry on Tues- day, would appear to be the channel through which the charities of by-gone benefactors flow, but the public were not enlightened as to his official posi- tion, and it would be interesting toknow in what capacity he acts as the guardian of the bequests. Both the Vicar and Mr. Evans made statements which are fit subjects for inquiry. The former alleges that the Library is not a parochial charity ; and the latter states that the almshouses are under a private trust. In the face of these confident assertions, it is strange that each charity is in the list of parochial charities issued by the Commis- sioners, from which it may naturally be inferred that they are of a public character. The district rate for Runcorn for the next twelve months will be 2s. 2d. in the an increase of 2d. in the Lon last year. At one time the estimates showod that a heavier call would be requisite to meet the demands of the growing town, but the Commissioners being large ratepayers themselves, are desirous of keeping the rates as low as possible, and they have succeeded, after making the Board room their home for a few days (according to the Chairman),in making the rate announced equal to the requirements of next year.
THE NATIONAL GYMNASTIC COMPETITION. WARRINGTON TEAM'S PROSPECTS.

The final struggle between Liverpool. Warrington, and Dundee, will take place to-night (Saturday), at the gymnasium, Myrtle-st., Liverpool. The contest has this season created an unusual amount of in- tetest ;indeed, gymnastics seem likely to share the honour with football in the near future as a popular winter pastime. To gain their present position in the competition Liverpool have beaten Aberdeen and Newport.; Dundee have beaten Leeds, Hudders- field and Dublin ; Warrington have beaten Exeter Hall, Lendon'(previous holders), Bournemouth, and Sefton Hall. Among the defeated teams Aberdeen and Exeter Hall are undoubtedly the bst. The contest between Liverpool and Aberdeen was a very close one. Both teams broke the previous scoring record, Liverpool scoring in the aggregate 320 i points and Aberdeen 311 points. The Warrington team suddenly became famous by unexpectedly beating Exeter Hall on their own ground, scoring 275 k points to their opponents , 270 points. Judging from the scoring in the previous rounds, Liverpool seem to have a fairly easy thing on in the final, unisss Dundee or Warrington, both of which clubs have had easy victsries in the last two rounds, have a lot in hand. There will, however, be a severe fight between Dundee and Warrington for secorufplace. In the barbells and rope climbing, the two teams are about equal: in the high jump, Warrington will have a lead of a few points ; and the scoring on the parallel bars will practically decide which team takes the Bronze Shields. Dundee have in the previous rounds gained considerably more marks than Warrington on the bars, but this fact is no index to what the scoring will be in the final. Judges adopt very different standard ; and when pitted against Liverpool and Warrington it is thought that the marks previously gained by Dundee will he very cousiderably reduced. Dublin gained more marks than Dundee on the bars, and good judges who saw Dub- lin compete against Chester assert that the Warrington men work much better than even Dublin. If this is so, either Dundee have been judged on a very high standard or Warrington on a very low one. T. Locker has almost recovered from the accident which prevented him from competing against ziefton Hall, and will again take his place in the Warrington team. James Holmes, who acted

Podmore, that the Committee have wisely decided to give him Podmore's place in the team; rather hard lines on Podmore,who has competed in all the previous rounds, but no doubt when he considers how valuable the extra 5 points thus gained become under the circumstances, he will act in a sports- manlike manner and give way with a good grace. Corn

On Thursday a painful sensation was caused in the neighbourhoods of Moore and Daresbury, by the discovery of the bodies of two women floating in the Bridgewater Canal. The discovery was made by a passing boatman, who at once gave information to Constable Jackson, of the Cheshire police. That officer had the bodies taken from the water as soon as possible, and conveyed to the Ringo' Bells public- house at Daresbury, where they were subsequently identified The unfortunate women were Mrs Maria Buckner and Miss Mary Massey. Mrs. Buckner was the wife of Mr. Henry Buckner, a gamekeeper in the employ of Sir Richard Brook,and Miss Massey, who lived at Salford, and was in the neighbourhood on a visit, was formerly in the em- ploy of Sir Gilbert Greenall,Bart.,as a laundress. On Wednesday Miss Massey paid a visit to Warrington, it being market day, and returned to Daresbury by the train due there at eight o'clock in the evening. At Daresbury she was joined by Mrs. Buckner, and the two went to a public-house in the vicinity kept by Mr. Jones, for the purpose of obtaining a lamp. They decided to walk home to- gether, a distance of about a mile, as the way they had to take was the same. The night was very dark and stormy, rain falling heavily, and Mr. Jones, the landlord of the inn where they had sheltered, lent them a lamp to assist them in finding their way. The road which they took runs for some distance along the banks of toe Bridgewater Canal, and it is supposed that they were unable to see their way clearly and walked into the water. Mr. Buckner naturally became anxious when his wife did not arrive home at the time when she was expected, and he went in the direction of the station in the hope of meeting her, but was unable to obtain any tid- ings of her. The search was renewed next morn- ing, with the result stated. Both the deceased are said to be between sixty and seventy years of age, No marks of violence were found, and there is nothing to suggest that the women came by their death otherwise than accidentally. Mr. Worsley, Coroner for that portion of Cheshire in which the deaths took place, ha ti the facts communicated to him by the police, and will hold an inquiry into the ' sad affair this (Saturday) morning.
