div.head: DUNDEE'TEAM 17121-JECE.
div.p: THE DUNDEE'TEAM 17121-JECE.

As it is anticipated that the real- -;;;; " at to- day's contest will be to determine the relative places of the Dundee and Warrington teams,the following extrac s from a descriptive account of the Scotch team at prac- tice preparing for the final may be read with some interest

"Only five of the members were present, and these were engaged in jumping when we entered. When the warmth of their greetings had subsided, this was re- sumed, and I had time to admire the grace and agility with which each sprang. The various gymnasts are too well known to rgluire any description. Suffice it to say that a more manly, well-developed set of young men would be difficult to find. The lath had attained a height of 54 inches, and as yet there were no failures. It was now raised another inch, and one dropped off. Four feet nine proved fatal to another one; but a second, though he failed to clear it in three attempts, by sheer strength of will, for the first time in his career, on his fourth essay managed to land safely across. Another who, after failing in his first trial and slightly hurting himself, re- lieved his feelings by what could hardly be termed Parliamentary language, on his performing it at the second jump was told if he would only do it religiously he might possibly clear five feet. Sixty-one inches found only one competitor, and he was not successful. The parallel bars were then brought forward, much to the satisfaction of those who had failed earlier in the trial. All in their order had a preliminary turn,and then each started to his combination. The exercise of the first (the smallest of the team) was performed with re- markable neatness, and when he vaulted over the bars, the self-constituted awarded him twelve marks. Strength ' and agility combined were the prevailing features of the next two, and the humour of the others also gave them twelve. "A Dublin exercise," remarked the new corner, but, after the opening inovements—a back roll into a straight-arm balance and a plank—done with such ease as a professional might have envied, were immediately recognised, and called forth shouts of "Dundee for ever." The enormous development of the chest and arms of the next performer was in itself a surety to us of a brilliant performance; nor were we disappointed. A complete circle from the straight-arm balance and round to the same position, balances varied by promenades all round the top of the parallels, and terminating with the pretty shoot through between the bars, which has become so

familiar with Dundee audiences, went to fill up an exer- cise which fairly entitled the performer to rank amongst the best parallel workers in Great Britain. The parallels were now given up, and attention was turned reluctantly to the rope. While they were still discussing who was to have the honour (?) of climbing anamusing incident occurred. The pianist, who was present, took a towel, and, rolling it up, threw it at one of the team. It was instantly converted into a foot- ball, and round the jumping utensils, extemporised for the time being into goal posts, a battle royal was waged. The feature of the tussle was the dribbling abilities of one of the members, who for some time kept the ball from all others. Despite the warnings of one or two of their more sedate companions, who reminded them that the competition took place an Saturday next, the game was continued until the clock struck ten, and the appear- auce of an attendant, asking if he would turn off the light, recalled them to the more serious task of rope- climbing. In this also the team showed "a, marked ad- vance. Six marks was the minimum, while others reached 40 feet (8 marks), and one who was unable to be present is said to climb to a height of 50 feet."

div.head: WARRINGTONIANS IN AMERICA.
div.p: WARRINGTONIANS IN AMERICA.

LETTERS FROM MR. WINSTANLEY. Quite a number of people were interested in the last letter that Mr. Winstanley, formerly of War- rington, but new living at Salem, Oregon, sent to his friends at Warrington, the substance of which was re-produced in these columns. As many who read the last letter have expressed themselves desirous of knowing how the writer had since got along, Mr. J. Gandy, of Church-st., has furnished us 1 with a few extracts from two letters recently re- ceived from Mr. Winstanley. In the first one, dated February 23, Mr. Winstanley writes :—" I don't know how you are getting your mails, for I know some of the lines across the continent have been blocked for nine or ten weeks.

IgOt -yours on January 19, this week, over a month old, so if you do not get our correspondence as regularly as you ought, you must put it to the fault of the weather. The weather is much better now, but we are still having very sharp frosts, and the foothills and mountains are still covered with snow, showing that it is very cold over there. Last year we had no frost after the 15th Feb. This year we have had almost as much frost since the 15th as we had all last winter. Oh dear; the experiences of the past month I hope never to go through again.

THE FLOOD HAS BEEN DREADFUL. It has almost swept some farms out of existence. Houses and barns, horses, cows, hogs, sheep, and poultry by the hundred have been swept away, in some cases leaving the farmer nothing but what he had on when be escaped. It made a wreck of our place—clearing away the fences in fine style. It also washed away about one and a half acres of the best land on the place, and where I had planted the orchard it washed out the soil, leaving a gravel pit in its place. Altogether I put the loss at 250 dol- lars—actual loss. If I tried to sell now lam afraid

I should lose more than double that sum. During the past two weeks, I have been re-fixing the fenc- ing, and I have now nearly got it all fixed. There is now only about 100 yards down, and one or two weak spots to repair. One of our neighbours, a mean Oregonian, keeps nine cows and two horses, and a lot of hogs, and he does not herd or pasture them at all. He just turns them out, and if they can get on anybody's land, why, all the better for them. They got in our young orchard, and did more harm to the trees than the flood. When I told his son of it, he said You should keep your fences up.' I said 'lf I had a gun I would shoot them.' I just felt as though I would, I was so annoyed at the whole business. My little boy Harry is rather sick just now. Ido not know what is the matter, whether it is fever or not, but I hope he will soon be better. He said I must tell little Katie he had got a pet lamb. I wish somebody else had it; it is such a nuisance about the place. My son John now gets 324 dollars per month, so I think he is doing very well. The second letter bears date March 3rd. In it Mr. Winstanley says:—" I should have written sooner, but I have been laid up with a bad cold— about the worst I have ever had. But I will explain how I got it. [have been

ELECTED SCHOOL DIRECTOR for this district. There was a sharp contest between two parties—the religious and the non-religious. It was feared that if the non-religious ele- ment won the seat, the bible would be excluded from the day schools, and the Sunday Schools shut up altogether. So the religious element mustered all their strength, and "ran me in" at the head of the poll—much against my will, for the office brings no pay, but lots of enemies. On the evening of the day of my election I received a visit from an indig- nant school mistress. Because I had not voted for her to teach the school, she gave me the rounds of the kitchen, and threatened to tear my hair off, and she was quite capable of doing it, too, for she was a big, stout, muscular looking woman. However she thought better of it, and, after giving further expressions to her injured feelings, the gentle crea- ture drove off—to my intense relief. The next day I went down to the schoolhouse, and found it in a broken down condition, with four or five inches of mud left on the floor by the flood. The windows were all in a bad condition, so I .et to work and put them in repair, and got a severe cold for my trouble. I went home and was confined to my bed for several days with fever and

div.head: INFLAMMATION OF THE LUNGS.
div.p: INFLAMMATION OF THE LUNGS.

lam better now, though very weak. What kind of weather are you having? We have had sharp frosts and snow since the Ist of the year. The old settlers say they have had not such a winter since '6l. In 'B2 it was very bad, but not so bad as this year. But just across the mountains they have had it much worse than we have. There is a tract of country between the Blue Mountains and the Cascadlo, ex- tending from Florida right up into British Colum- bia, and the cold there has been most intense. So late as the latter part of February, the thermometer has been 40 degrees below zero,'and the sufferings of the people have been dreadful. In our valley it has not been nearly so bad—though even now, the mountains and foothills are covered with snow. I was very sorry to read of dear old McNlinnies' death. lam afraid you will have a difficulty in replacing him. My family are all well."

STEAM TRAM-CAR OFF Tau LINE.—On Saturday night the 7 p.m. steam tram-car running from Peasley Cross to Prescot ran off the rails up to the King's Arms, Prescot, thus delaying it for nearly three hours, and the trams that had come up in the meantime had to back all the way to the sheds at St. Helens. Happily no one was hurt.

div.head: BREACH OF THE FACTORY ACTS AT
div.p: BREACH OF THE FACTORY ACTS AT
WARRINGTON.

Yesterday morning, at the Warrington Police Court, Henry [Ernest :Lees, cotton spinner, Florence Mills, Warrington, was summoned for having, on the 10th March, unlawfully allowed Bridget Walsh to remain during a meal time jin a room where manufacturing purposes were being carried on. There was a similar charge in respect to five other girls. Mr. W. H. J. Jenkins appeared for the defence, and pleaded guilty. An inspector under the Factory Act stated that from information received he visited the mill, and on questioning the manager, the engineer, and several workpeople, he found that on several days the engine had been run during the meal-time, while the women were kept employed. Mr. Lees had previously been fined for a similar offence, and the Bench were now asked to inflict the full penalty—£3 and costs—in each case. Mr. Jenkins, for the defence, said that an offence had been committed, but the motive was that a certain number of the hands should not lose time. It was a very difficult thing to work a cotton mill and comply with all the regulations by which em- ployers were, to some extent, hampered. He gave an assurance that the offerwe would not be repeated. The Bench imposed a fine of £3 and costs in the first case, and of £1 and costs in each of the other cases, making £ll Bs. altogether.

div.head: WILL OF THE LITE MR. BLECKLY.
div.p: WILL OF THE LITE MR. BLECKLY.

The will, with a codicil, made the sth June, 1889, of the late Mr. Henry Bleckly, of Bellefield, Altrinc- ham, J.P., chairman of the Kirkdale Quarter Sessions, who died on January 24 last, aged seventy-seven years, has been proved by the executors, his sons, Mr. William Henry Bleckly, of Thelwall Lea, and Mr. John James Bleckly, of Daresbury Lodge, the value of the personal estate having been sworn at £74,592 is. 3d. The testator bequeaths to his wife, Mrs. Ann Sanderson Bleckly, the money in the house and at his bankers, his furniture and household effects, the use and enjoyment for her life of his books and pictures, and the income for life of his residuary estate. On the death of Mrs. Bleckly the testator's books and pictures are to be divided amongst his children ; a sum of £1,500 is to be held in trust for his grandson, the son of his deceased daughter, and a sum of £1,500, fifty A shares and 100 B shares of Pearson and Knowles, Limited, are to be held in trust for Mr. Frederick Allis Gower. The testator's daughter Mrs. Amelia Temple Johnson, is then to take I fifteen A shares and 100 B shares in Pearson and Knowles, , Limited ; his daughter, Mrs. Emma Deane Bourne, wife ' of Mr. H. R. Fox Bourne,forty A shares and 100 B shares ; Mr. William Henry Sleekly, 60 A and 158 B shares •, Mr. John James Bleckly fifty A and 120 B shares; Mr. Charles Arnold Bleckly forty A and 100 B shares; and Mr. Herbert Sanderson Bleckly, thirty-seven A and 100 B shares. The testator devises and bequeaths the ultimate residue of his property, real and personal, in trust for his last- named six children in equal shares,

div.head: A. DAIRYMAID'S CLAIM FOR WAGES.
div.p: A. DAIRYMAID'S CLAIM FOR WAGES.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Nfoulkes, a case was heard in which Sarah Elizabeth Thompson, a young lady, claimed damages for alleged wrongful dismissal from the Lancashire and Cheshire Farmers Co- operative Association, Limited. Mr. A. Browne appeared for the plaintiff, and the defendants were represented by Dr. Thomas, barrister, of Liverpool, instructed by Messrs. Jenkins and Cnsworth. On the application of Mr. Browne, his Honour amended the claim by adding the words "and for balance of wages due," in which respect 21s. were claimed.—Mr. Browne, in submitting his case, said that the action was brought against the Farmers' Stores, Cernhill, Warrington, by the plaintiff, who was formerly manageress of the dairy at the stores, to recover damages for wrongful dismissal, and Ms-) the balance of wages due. The dairy was not opened until four months after the Stores had been started, but the directors had been on the lookout for a person to manage the dairy, and mentioned the matter to Mr. William Thompson, the plaintiff's father, who was then the manager of the Stores. He recommended his daughter, who was ultimately engaged, but, at the request of the directors, she was sent to Aylesbury Dairy, London, to learn the business. The directors having paid for her learning her business, would not engage for less than six months, and in conse- quence, Mr. Browne contended, she was entitl, d to six months' notice.—The defendants had paid 16s. into Court—one week's wages. Mr. Browne then called evidence.—William Thompson, Avenue Farm, Orford, manager of the Farmers' Stores up to 1888, detailed the circumstances of the plaintiff's engagement, at 7s. 6d. a week for the first six months, and 12s. 6d. for tne second, that salary to be raised subsequently if things went on prosperously. Witness received the wages on behalf of his daughter, but during the second half year, through a mistake' he only received 12s. a week.— Plaintiff, examined, said that after her father had left the stores, she received 16s a week salary, and had the sole management of the dairy. On the 15th February, she was offered 16s. in lieu of notice, which she declined, stating that she should require proper notice. By his Honour: By "proper notice," she meant six months' notice.—For the defence,Dr. Thomas contended that the plaintiff was serving as a weekly servant at a weekly vtage. Was it likely that a girl in her position should be entitled to such -a period of notice, when even her father who was the man- ager was only entitled to one month's notice. . Evidence for the defence was then given by John Marsh, farmer, Grappenhall, who said that after plaintiff had , served twelve months, he always understood that she was a weekly servant, like the others, and by Thomas Dutton, farmer, Newton-by-Daresbury ; Joseph Know- les, farmez, Appleton ; Charles Dutton Parkinson, secre- tary of the Association • and Robert Henry, a clerk to Mr. Parkinson. The fatter witness spoke to having tendered the plaintiff a week's wages in lieu of notice. She declined to take the money, and demanded a month's ; notice. She did not say, "I demand proper notice."— ' Lily Caldwell, a dairymaid at the Stores at the time in , question, gave evidence in corroboration of the state- ment.—His Honour having summed up at length, the [ jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff, for £1 is. 6d., s balance of wages, and one month's wages in lieu of notice.

div.head: LONDON BOOT AND SHOEMAKERS' STRIKE.
div.p: THE LONDON BOOT AND SHOEMAKERS' STRIKE.

About 5,000 nen-union men will have to be relieved to- day (Saturday) by the Strikers' Committee of the London boot and shoemakers. Processions, with collecting boxes, have paraded the streets, and the Metropolitan Branch of the Shoemakers' Union has voted £lOO. Six firms have conceded the men's claims. THE FIRE AT BARON DE_ ROTFISCHILD'S. _

Serious damage has been caused by a fire at Waddes- don Manor, Baron de Rothschild's country seat near Aylesbury. Some French workmen lighted a fire in a new west hall, and the flames were drawn through a draught-hole into the Baron's private room. The pannol- ling, tapestry, and pictures, by Gainsborough, valued at between £9,000 and £lO,OOO, were destroyed.

div.head: FEDERATION OF THE CENTRAL AMERICAN REPUBLICS.
div.p: FEDERATION OF THE CENTRAL AMERICAN REPUBLICS.

A New York telegram says :—The Ministers at Wash- ington who represent Costa Rica and Nicaragua regard a federation of the five central American Republics under a constitntion resembling that of the United States as assured. Only formalities remain to be arranged. Guatemala, Honduras, and Salvador have already ad- hered to the proposal.

div.head: NARROW ESCAPE OF MR. LEGH, M.P.
div.p: NARROW ESCAPE OF MR. LEGH, M.P.

Mr. T. W. Legh, Conservative M.P. for the Newton Division, experienced a narrow escape from personal injury at Earlestown, at noon yesterday. The hon. gentleman was driving in a cab along Earle-st. when suddenly the axle broke, precipitating the vehicle with a heavy crash to the ground. Quickly estimating his perilous situation, Mr. Legh sprang from the carriage, and thus averted what might have proved a serious accident.

div.head: FOOTBALL FATALITY.
div.p: FOOTBALL FATALITY.

The Deputy City Coroner of Manchester (Mr. Sidney Smelt) held an inquest yesterday, on the body of John Smith, age 15, son of James Smith, a mill overlooker, of 90, Queen-st., Bradford. The deceased was playing football on Sunday afternoon, the 30th of March. On the following Tuesday he complained of a pain just above his knee, and died on Monday. He did not appear to have been kicked whilst playing at football, but he was seen to fall on his knee after kicking at the ball. A veidict was returned in accordance with the medical evidence, which was that blood poisoning followed up the injury.

div.head: LYMM.
div.p: LYMM.

VAGRANCY.—At the Lymm Police Court, on Tuesday, before Mr. T. P. Norris, Patrick Morley, a tramp, was charged with begging at Warburton on the previous day. P.C. Ennion gave evidence in support of the charge, hut the defendant was dismissed on promising to leave the district. _

A DISORDERLY ExcuustomsT.—Al the Lyrnm Police Court, on Good Friday, before Dr. Brabazon, James Deakin, a tanner, residing at Latchford, was charged in custody with being drunk and disorderly in the village the same day.—P.C. Griffiths proved the offence, and the prisoner was* fined ss. and costs, or seven days' imprisonment. The money was paid. SHEPHERDRY.—At the quarterly meeting held at War- rington, on Saturday, Mr. Frederick George Leigh, of the Shepherds by Night Lodge, Lymm, was duly elected to represent the whole of the Warringten district at the coming A.M.C. at -Manchester. This is the first time that a delegate from Lymm has been appointed to represent so large a district as Warrington, which comprises nearly 1,000 members. THE VISITORS.—Lymm was visited by a great number of holiday makers over the Easter holidays. In accord- ance with the recent memorial which was forwarded to the Chief Constable of Cheshire, several additional police were on duty in the village, but the behaviour of the ' excursionists was very commendable and only one per- son was locked up for being disorderly. As usual, for the convenience of the residents, excursions were run from Lynam to Liverpool, Manchester, and the various watering places. On Monday the Lymm Volunteers proceeded by train to Altcar for class firing. Special services were conducted in all the churches in the dis- trict which were largely attended.

ST. MARY'S VESTRY MEETING.—The Easter vestry meeting was held in the vestry of the Parish Church, Lymm, on Tuesday evening. There were present the Rector (Rev. G. W. Guest) in the chair, the curate (he Rev. R. Coward), Mr. Bayley (rector's churchwarden), and Messrs. J. Rhomer, James Marsh, Thomas Ardern, Levi and Harry Bradburn, Edwin Massey, George Simp- son, Richard Oddie, James Blakemore, Alfred Watkin, James Gregson, Peter Newton, Henry Browning, J. E. G. Groves, M. D. Woodhead, F. Carver, Samuel Hinde, and H. Norris.—Mr. Bayley presented the accounts of the year, which were as follow :—Receipts: Balance from last year, £l4 15s. 6d.; offertories—early celebrations, £2l us. 10d. ; morning service, £177 Os. 7d. ; evening ser- vice, £6l 2s. 5d.; sundries, £4 9s. id.; total, £278 19s. sid. Payments: By sick and needy, £lB 13s. 111 d. ; special collections, £7l is. Bd.; church expenses, £157 6s. 4d ; balance in hand, £3l 17s. 6d. The accounts were adopted.—Mr. S. P. Lee, Brenthurst, was elected people's warden. The Rector again appointed Mr. W. Bayley as his warden. Mr. John Warburton and Mr. Fred. Swallow were elected parishioners' sidesmen, and Mr. Fred. Holt and Mr. Thos. Arden] were appointed by the Rector. Mr. I. H. Evans and Mr. R. Oddie were appointed lay delegates to the diocesan conferences.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

div.head: MR. HIGOINSON'S SUCCESSOR.
div.p: MR. HIGOINSON'S SUCCESSOR.

Mr. Sinclair, the surveyor-elect, wrote stating that his notice at his present situation would expire on the 11th April, and that he expected to commence his duties on that date.—lt was explained by the Clerk that Mr. Irg- ginson's notice did not expire until the Ist May, and Dr. O'Keeffe said they had nothing to do with Mr. Sinclair until that date. They did not want two surveyors.—Mr. Taylor moved, and Mr. Sadler seconded, that Mr. Sinclair commence his duties on the Ist May.—Mr. Brown thought Mr. Sinclair ought not to lose a month's salary, and he proposed that he commence his duties on the 14th inst.—There was no seconder for the amendment, and the original motion was carried. Dr. O'Keeffe voted against, and several other members did not vote.

div.head: ELECTION.
div.p: THE ELECTION.

Mr. Midwood, returning officer, reported the result of the recent election, and said the number of voting papers delivered into the hands of the constables this year was 4,935, last year, 4,763; voting papers filled up in the pre- sence of the returning officer, 70 ; last year, 24, total this year, 5,005; last year, 4,787. The number of papers not delivered through change of residence, &c., was 846 ; last year, 972; number returned blank, 414 ; last year, 479; spoiled papers, 317; last year, 265; papers not accounted for, 253 ; last year, 215. Papers good, 3,175; last year, 2,833. Mr. Midwood asked for a cheque of £6O 6s. 9d. for the expenses of the election.—Mr. Handley proposed, and Mr. Heyes seconded, that a cheque for the amount named be drawn on the treasurer.

div.head: MOSS BANE SEWER DISPUTE.
div.p: THE MOSS BANE SEWER DISPUTE.

The Clerk read a letter from Messrs. S. COwburn and Sons, who stated that "our Mr. W. Cowburn stated that the difference in the items objected to in our account after explanations given by him and since, did not leave any sort of comparison to the amount now sought to be deducted from their account, and they thought it was very arbitrary indeed to have to put up with such treat- ment as they had to do, and be kept out of their money so long. If it is intended that £l5O should be deducted from the account in connection with railway and canal company's charges, this would be quite wrong, as the item was not included in their tender, their price being for pipes and labour only as explained by them and acknowledged by the surveyor as being correct. Add the above named amount (£150) to the amount offered them, and although it was hard that they should have to lose, money which was honestly due to them, they would for an immediate settlement (without prejudice to their claim, of course) agree to split the difference;of balance, viz., £123, making the amount which they agree to accept in settlement of their account £7ll 10s.—Mr. Sadler said the Highway Committee adhered to their original proposition, and offered £5OO for a final settlement. He proposed that the letter lie on the table.—Mr. Taylor seconded.—Carried. Dr. O'Keeffe and Mr. Wright did not vote.

div.head: DEACON-ROAD IMPROVEMENTS.
div.p: DEACON-ROAD IMPROVEMENTS.

Messrs. Sayce and Randle, Appleton Quarry, wrote with regard to Deacon-road Improvements, and stated they would let the Board have the land they required at 4s. per super yard on condition that the Board raised the road and sewered the same in six months time as by then they would have completed their buildings. They would also want the Board to construct them a new road to their steam crane from the level of the raised road. —The letter was referred to the Highway Committee.

div.head: HIGHWAY MATTERS.
div.p: HIGHWAY MATTERS.

The minutes of the Highway Committee contained the following .—Building Plans.—The following examined and approved :—One house -for J. Shaw, Albert-road ; three houses for E. Wood, Birchfield-road ; nine houses for Sayce and Randle. Deacon-road. It was recom- mended that Mr. T. Hughes salary be increased ss. per week. The estimate for the ensuing year, examined and approved, amounting to £5,768 ss. 4d:, which includes £665 for widening certain roads, and which amount the Committee suggest should be paid out of this and next year's estimates. The minute referring to the estimate was referred back for further consideration ; the remain- der were approved.

div.head: FIRE BRIGADE.
div.p: THE FIRE BRIGADE.

The Superintendent of the Fire Brigade (Mr. I. Carr), submitted his report upon the operations of the Fire Brigade during the past twelve months. The total num- ber of fires that have occurred within the rateable dis- trict (exclusive of chimney fires) is seven, none of which were very destructive. The brigade has had four calls, —on two occasions their services were not required, at the remaining two the fires were extinguished by the brigade. Thd estimated total loss from fires is £315. The estimated value of the property at risk is £23,255. The present streugth of the brigade is three officers and eight men. Twelve meetings for drill have been held, the average attendance being 64•3 per cent. Two mem- bers have been dismissed during the year. The condi- tion of the brigade, as regards efficiency and discipline, is fairly good, but not quite so satifactory as last year, as the attendance at drill has fallen off somewhat. I trust, however, when the proposed new fire station and firemen's houses are completed, to be able to make the brigade efficient in every respect. The police, as in pre- vious years, have rendered the brigade excellent assist- ance. The total number of street hydrants is 188 —The report was adopted. THANKS TO THE CHAIRMAN.

Mr. Brown proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman for his services during the past vear.—Mr. Handley. seconded and Dr. O'Keefe supported the motion, which was carried by acclammation.—The Chairman, in re- sponding, said at the expiration of this term, after the election he should have served on the Board 20 or 21 years, and when he came back to the Board on the 24th Inst., he trusted he should come with renewed vigour. (Applause.)

NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that a special meeting of the Council of the Borough of Warrington will be held on Wednesday, the 23rd day of April, 1690, at 7 o'clock in the afternoon, at the Town Hall, Warrington. in pursuance of the provisions of the Act 35th and 36th, Victoria, Cap. 91, intituled "an act to authorise the application of Funds of Municipal Corporations and other governing bodies, In certain cases," for the purpose of considering and confirm- ing the propriety of the promotion by the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington, acting by the Council, of a Bill in the present Session of Parliament intituled " a Bill to extend the boundaries of the Borough of War- rington, to provide for vesting the undertaking of the War- rington Waterworks Company in the Mayor, Aldermen, and Burgesses of the Borough of Warrington, and to make better provision for the health local government and improvement of the Borough, and for other purposes." Dated this 12th day of April, 1890. L LYON WHITTLE, Town Clerk.

TO THE ELECTORS OF THE NORTH-WEST WARD. LADIES AID GENTLEMEN, Having been requested by representatives of all sections of the Electors in the Ward to become a candidate for the seat in the Council, rendered vacant by the lamented death of Mr. John Greening, I have consented to place my services at your disposal. For many years I have taken a deep interest in all political and municipal matters. The course of recent events in the Council, relating to the Extension of the Borough, the Sanitation, and the general Improvement, has been, and will be, watched by me most carefully. I have long been in favor of the Freeing of the Library, and am pleased to see there is now a prospect of its early accom- plishment. The question of the purchase of the Waterworks is most important to all the ratepayers, and I shall give to it my thoughtful consideration. As a member of one of the most numerous and important sections of the community, viz., the working classes, I shall, owing to my acquaintance with our wants, be the better able to keep a watchful eye upon all efforts to improve our dwell- ings, and increase the comfort of our homes. I shall also watch, so far as I can, the general expenditure of the Borough, being assured that efficiency and economy can be made to go hand in hand. I am, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your obedient Servant, SAM. J. BRAMAN. 96, Bewsey April 11th, 1890.

BOROUGH OF WARRINGTON. MUNICIPAL ELECTION. NORTH-WEST WARD. TO THE BURGESSES OF THE WARD. LADIES AND GENTLEMEN, Having been urgently requested by a large and influen- tial body of the Ratepayers of the Ward to become a candi- date for election, as your representative in the Town Council, in place of the late Councillor Greening, I have con- sented to do so, and if elected my constant object will be to do all in my power for the improvement of the town and its trade, thus creating and improving labour and wages for the working-classes, and business for the shopkeepers and com- mercial interest. I will also give my beet attention to the Improvement of the Streets, Gas Service, and Sanitary Ar- rangements, as well as to full efficiency, with due economy in all matters connected with the Ward and Borough. As one who has always taken a deep and active interest in the Institutions of the Borough, and in everything calculated to promote the general welfare and prosperity of my fellow townsmen, added to the long period I have lived among you, I feel that I may appeal with confidence to my fellow workingmen and many good friends for their assisuance in this contest, and to the Burgesses of the Ward for their votes on the day of the Poll. lam, Ladies and Gentlemen, Your Obedient Servant, JOHN ROBERTS. Warrington, April 12th, 1890.

T' v 'TY THOUSAND ACRES AMERICAN PRO- PERTY FREE. In allotments of Farm, Fruit, and Vineyard Tracts of 40, 20, 10, and 5 acres each, and selected Residence or Business Lots. ONE of the above divisions of Real Estate Pro- perty, located either in the Golden State of fruitful California, or in the famous Orangegrovc State of Florida, will be unconditionally given free from any charge for the land I to any respectable person who sends his or her full name and post address to the American Office of the Californian and Southern Land Company at Cincinnati, Ohio, U.S.A. As soon as your name and address are received by the Com- pany, a free Land Warrant for one of the allotments of free property will be returned to you by first ocean post. The only cost for the property will be an expense fee for executing a Warranty Transfer Title Deed in your favour, and having the signatures thereto legally acknowledged before the pi oper officials. Such expense will in no case exceed 125., and is not to be paid until after you have received the Free Land War- rant. When one or more members of the same family, or friends, wish to secure property together, the Company will issue to any applicant as many Free Land Warrants as may be requested, not to exceed ten, to be given by the applicant to those whom he applies for. The object in making this extraordinary offer is to secure a diversified interest and ownership throughout the different countries of Europe in the lands owned and controlled by the above-named Company. When this is accomplished, the Company will open branch offices in various European Cities, and offer its large remaining properties for sale at a uniform price of £5 per acre for Farm and Fruit Tracts, and £6 per Plot for Residence or Business Lots. It is believed by.the Company that the diversified interest that will be thus secured by this preliminary method of advertising will amply compensate for the amount of pro- perty that is now offered FREE. If tha number of names sent for free property is in excess of the amount of such property, those whose names are re- ceived first will secure it. Hence the advantage of sending name and address at once. All that need be sent is an envelope bearing your name and post address ; this envelope to be enclosed in another and the outer envelope to be addressed as follows: THE CALIFORNIA AND SOUTHERN LAND CO., CINCINNATI, OHIO, U.S.A. NOTE.--If preferred, application may be made to the Com- pany's Branch Office in London. A penny stamped self- addressed envelope sent to the Company's London Agent, Mr. W. H. FULLER, 8, College Chambers, high Holborn. Lon- don, will secure a FREE LAND WARRANT, issued by the Home Company, the same as if sent direct to the Head Office.

"TOUCH AND GO." "J. C. and " Workin Mon."—Next week. Typhoid and scarlet fever still cling to Sutton and Frodsham, and the Medical Officer of Health , - remarks that fresh cases might occur. There is 'something wrong—bad drainage perhaps—which requires bottoming. . There is a labourer at Weston Point, near Runcorn, who will have occasion to remember Saturday last, for his wife on that day presented hire with two daughters and a son. Nature has _proved bountiful, and it is understood that Queen's • bounty will follow. There has been another seizure in Warrington of unwholesome fish. The officials are to be com- mended for keeping on the alert. Heavy penalties ought in all such cases, to be imposed, for the man "who has bad food palmed 6n him runs the risk of being poisoned as well as defrauded. The Duchess of Fife will not, it is said, be able to take part in the opening of the Electrical Exhi- bition at Edinburgh. Her health, as the phrase goes, is in "a delicate state." Each man in his time plays many parts. It will be interesting to nee how the Prince of Wales will play his part as a , randfather. ------ ' People will get excited about Church millinery. 'There was quite a stormy scene at St. John's, Peni- eevton, on Sunday morning, consequent upon the , introduction of a surpliced choir. Why do clergy- Inert risk rows about these matters? And how comes it that a surplice is as exciting to some People as a red rag is to a bull? ' But what is a surplice ?" some reader may ask. v all, to speak by the card, it must be described as a loose flowing vestment of white linen, generally aching almost to the feet, with broad full sleeves.' ."1" P.D." says that the description is that of a ; but our " P.D." knows nothing of sacred `ungs—just because he is a The result of the Cameroon election is in the ordinary way of things—that is to say it is a vie- Y for the Liberal party. It will be seen from %us result'of the poll, as declared yesterday, that ~poth parties have increased their votes; but the •14heral increase is so large as to convert a Tory Inniority of 136 into a minority of 18. Well done, Wales ! There seems to have been some oversight or neglect in giving notification of infectious diseases 'tst Helens ; and Dr. Pennington who is concerned inthe matter is to be asked for anexplanation. The Authorities are fully justified in following the _katter up, for negligence in cases of this kind °say lead to an epidemic, and St. Helens has already liefaciently suffered. It is interesting to observe how Liberal Union-I late fight shy of the Irish Land Purchase Bill. kr. Courtney thinks it would be all right if accom- panied by a Local Government Bill (which it is not). Mr. T. W. Russell says it would be all right it were compulsory (which it is not). It comes to this that the Bill. as it stands, is objectionable even to Liberal Unionists. xperituents in hypnotism are now quite the tage in certain learned circles. Hypnotism is an old thing with a new name. Thirty years ago, it Was called mesmerism ; but the learned jumped to the conclusion that it was "all humbug," and ITolild have nothing to do with it. At last their , "e 8 are opened ; but it would 'never do to admit Plat they have been in the wrong; and so the talk not of Mesmerism, but of Hypnotism. • It was suggested at a dance, on Monday night, trnongst the Padgate Primrosers that the Croft raguers might shortly be able to form a habits- Linn of their own—that is to say give "a local uslitation and a name to airy nothing." They Zlll require a motto of course. How would this rrzi Shakespere suit them—" The primrose road the everlasting bonfire ?" It comes so pat that might, indeed, be considered good enough for cdae whole League.
